vici:vici-10517.description: Amphitheater of Marcianopolis (Devnya, Bulgaria), excavated 1958-61 by Goranka Toncheva; measured about 65 by 58m with 12 rows of seating in 14 sections and two arched gates, including the porta libitinensis.

vici:vici-10518.label: Amphitheatre Gorsium
vici:vici-10518.description: Amphitheater of Gorsium (Tác), the Pannonian provincial town that served as center of the imperial cult and, after rebuilding as Herculia, provincial capital; accommodated up to about 2,500 spectators.

vici:vici-10525.label: Amphitheatre Brigetio
vici:vici-10525.description: Amphitheatre of Brigetio, a Danube-frontier legionary and civilian settlement (Komárom-Szőny, Hungary) that became a municipium around 205 AD; a 2009 epigraphic study argues the town had two separate amphitheatres, military and civic.

vici:vici-10604.label: Théâtre Antique (Arles)
vici:vici-10604.description: Roman theatre built under Augustus c. 40-30 BC, one of the earliest stone theatres in Gaul, dedicated to Apollo; seated roughly 8,000 and yielded the Venus of Arles, found in pieces in 1651.

vici:vici-10608.label: Zirkus (Arles)
vici:vici-10608.description: Roman circus of Arles, built in 149 AD on the Rhône bank on thousands of wooden piles; 450m long with tiered seating for up to 20,000, used for chariot races. Its spina obelisk now stands in Arles' Place de la République.

vici:vici-10638.label: Theatre (Le Vieil-Évreux)
vici:vici-10638.description: Theatre of Gisacum, the vast Gallo-Roman sanctuary town near Évreux; among the largest in Roman Gaul at c. 106m diameter, holding several thousand spectators, its entrance aligned on the adjoining temple's axis.

vici:vici-10693.label: Theatre  Les Arenes
vici:vici-10693.description: Gallo-Roman arena-theatre at Thénac ('Les Arènes'), near Saintes; likely built under Nero and abandoned in the 3rd century, cavea roughly 84-90m across, part of a rural sanctuary with baths and a sacred spring.

vici:vici-10762.label: Theatre Lugdunum Convenarum
vici:vici-10762.description: Theatre of Lugdunum Convenarum (Saint-Bertrand-de-Comminges), the Roman town traditionally linked to Pompey's 72 BC foundation; its cavea was remodelled around the mid-1st century AD with a large porticus post scaenam.

vici:vici-10866.label: Circus Antinoupolis
vici:vici-10866.description: Hippodrome (circus) of Antinoöpolis, the city Hadrian founded in 130 AD to honour his drowned favourite Antinous; roughly 307m by 77m, it hosted the Antinoeia games of chariot racing and athletic contests.

vici:vici-10904.label: Private roman theatre Bauli
vici:vici-10904.description: The so-called 'Tomba di Agrippina' at Bauli (Bacoli), long linked in legend to Nero's mother but actually a private theatre-nymphaeum (teatro-ninfeo): an Augustan-era odeion within a seaside villa, later converted into a fountain hall.

vici:vici-10906.label: Amphitheatre Beroea
vici:vici-10906.description: Theatre remains on the citadel mound of ancient Beroea (Seleucid refoundation of an older Aramaean settlement), later renamed Aleppo; Roman-period Beroea had a colonnaded east-west avenue and a monumental triple arch, with the citadel serving as its acropolis.

vici:vici-10918.label: Theatre Bovianum Vetus
vici:vici-10918.description: Theatre-temple complex of the Samnite Pentri federal sanctuary at Pietrabbondante (identified in older scholarship with the town Bovianum Vetus), built in the late 2nd century BC with its cavea cut into the hillside below the larger Temple B.

vici:vici-10939.label: Hierapolis
vici:vici-10939.description: Hierapolis Bambyce (modern Manbij, Syria), hellenized from the Aramaic Manbug and known to Greeks as the 'City of the Sanctuary' for its shrine of the Syrian goddess Atargatis, famously described in Lucian's De Dea Syria; distinct from the Phrygian Hierapolis.

vici:vici-10943.label: Theatre of Kaunos
vici:vici-10943.description: Hellenistic theatre of the Carian port city Kaunos near modern Dalyan, seating roughly 5,000 across nine wedges of 33 rows with eight stairways, overlooking the city's silted harbor.

vici:vici-10959.label: Theatre of Cnidus
vici:vici-10959.description: Lower theatre of Cnidus (Knidos) in Caria, built into the hillside beside a temple of Dionysus and holding an estimated 5,000-6,400 spectators; first surveyed by the Society of Dilettanti's 1812 mission and excavated by Charles Newton in 1857-58.

vici:vici-11050.label: Theatre Gythion
vici:vici-11050.description: Roman-era (2nd-century AD) theatre of Gythion, Sparta's ancient port on the Laconian Gulf; excavated from 1891 by Andreas Skias, its marble cavea held twelve rows in five wedges with a front row of backed seats reserved for officials.

vici:vici-11094.label: Theatre Heraclea Pertinthus
vici:vici-11094.description: Theatre of Perinthus, the Samian colony on the Propontis renamed Heraclea under Diocletian; excavations at modern Marmara Ereğlisi have uncovered the theatre together with public baths and the city's fortification walls.

vici:vici-11100.label: Theatre Hierapolis
vici:vici-11100.description: Theatre of Hierapolis (Phrygia), first built in the 2nd century BC, wrecked by the earthquake of 60 AD, then rebuilt under the Flavians in works lasting until c. 206 AD; among Anatolia's largest theatres, with an estimated capacity of 10,000-12,500.

vici:vici-11143.label: Theatre Limyra
vici:vici-11143.description: A Hellenistic theatre cut into the hillside at Limyra in Lycia, built in the 2nd-1st century BC with a horseshoe cavea holding about 8,000; badly damaged in the 141 AD earthquake and rebuilt with funds from the Lycian benefactor Opramoas of Rhodiapolis.

vici:vici-11149.label: Theatre Lychnidos
vici:vici-11149.description: The Ancient Theatre of Ohrid, built in Hellenistic style at the end of the 3rd or start of the 2nd century BC, the only theatre of its kind in North Macedonia; Romans later used it for gladiatorial games and it was a site of Christian executions under Diocletian.
vici:vici-11149.wikidataDescription: ancient Greek theatre in Ohrid, North Macedonia

vici:vici-11218.label: Theatre Tarraco
vici:vici-11218.description: Built at the end of the 1st century BC under Augustus near the forum and port of Tarraco, seating about 6,000 spectators over three tiers; part of the UNESCO-listed Archaeological Ensemble of Tárraco.
vici:vici-11218.wikidataDescription: UNESCO World Heritage Site in Catalonia, Spain

vici:vici-11241.label: Theater Pollentia
vici:vici-11241.description: Spain's smallest surviving Roman theatre, carved directly into the bedrock at Pollentia (Alcúdia, Mallorca) in the 1st century AD to seat 1,500-2,000; excavated from 1952 and later reused as a late-Roman burial ground.

vici:vici-11249.label: Theatre Mytilene
vici:vici-11249.description: Hellenistic theatre of Mytilene on Lesbos (3rd-1st century BC), its cavea over 100m across; Pompey had its design copied to build Rome's first permanent stone theatre, dedicated in 55 BC.
vici:vici-11249.wikidataDescription: ancient Greek theatre in Mytilene, Lesbos, Greece

vici:vici-11259.label: Theatre Neapolis
vici:vici-11259.description: 2nd-century AD Roman theatre at Neapolis (Samaria, modern Nablus), one of the largest in Roman Syria-Palestine with seating for several thousand; discovered by chance in 1978 during water-canal excavations, later converted into a water basin.

vici:vici-11262.label: Theatre Nicopolis
vici:vici-11262.description: Built under Augustus in the early 1st century AD as part of Nicopolis's Actian Games complex commemorating his victory at Actium, with a 92m-diameter cavea seating roughly 5,000; in continuous use into the 3rd century AD.

vici:vici-11319.label: Theatre of Philippoupolis
vici:vici-11319.description: Small basalt-built theatre (capacity around 2,000) at Philippopolis, the Hauran village emperor Philip the Arab (r. 244-249) rebuilt as a colonia; construction halted, unfinished, at his death.

vici:vici-11414.label: Theatre Thassos
vici:vici-11414.description: Ancient Greek theatre of Thasos, cut into the acropolis hillside; first built early 3rd century BC with a marble stage front dedicated to Dionysus by Lysistratos, later used from the 1st century AD for beast hunts and gladiatorial combat.

vici:vici-11441.label: Theatre Tusculum
vici:vici-11441.description: Best-preserved structure at Tusculum: a Roman theatre with a 45m cavea and 17.5m orchestra, built early 1st century AD and excavated by Luigi Canina in 1839-40 for Lucien Bonaparte's campaign.

vici:vici-11444.label: Hippodrome Tyrus
vici:vici-11444.description: 2nd-century AD Roman hippodrome at Tyre, 480m by 90m and seating 20,000, among the largest and best-preserved in the Roman world; hosted the Heraclia games for Melqart-Heracles every four years.

vici:vici-11449.label: Odeon Theatre Lyon
vici:vici-11449.description: Roman odeon on the Fourvière hill in Lyon (Lugdunum), built early-mid 2nd century AD with a 73m diameter seating 3,000; one of only two paired odeon-theatre complexes in Roman Gaul, alongside Vienne.
vici:vici-11449.wikidataDescription: small ancient Roman theatre in Lyon, France

vici:vici-11462.label: Theatre Vetus Pictavis
vici:vici-11462.description: Gallo-Roman theatre at Vieux-Poitiers (ancient Vetus Pictavis, Naintré), 116m in diameter and seating an estimated 10,000 - larger than the theatre of Orange - hosting drama and gladiatorial combat for two centuries.

vici:vici-11463.label: Theatre Vicus Augusti
vici:vici-11463.description: Theatre of the Roman vicus Augusti (modern Sidi el-Hani, Tunisia), with a 58m cavea and 22m orchestra; its ruins, with radial vaulted substructures, were first studied by Saladin and Cagnat in 1882.

vici:vici-11524.label: Odeon of Herodes Atticus
vici:vici-11524.description: Stone Roman theatre built AD 161 on the south slope of the Athenian Acropolis by Herodes Atticus in memory of his wife Aspasia Annia Regilla; seated about 5,000 and still hosts the Athens Festival today.

vici:vici-11525.label: Odeon of Pericles
vici:vici-11525.description: Athens's original odeon, built 435 BC by Pericles for the musical contests of the Panathenaea, its square timber roof said to imitate Xerxes's tent; burned during Sulla's siege in 86 BC and later rebuilt.
vici:vici-11525.wikidataDescription: ancient odeon in the Acropolis of Athens

vici:vici-11769.label: Odeon - Ephesus
vici:vici-11769.description: Small covered theater built c. 150 AD by the wealthy Ephesian Publius Vedius Antoninus and his wife Flavia Papiana; seated roughly 1,400–1,500 and served both as a concert hall (odeon) and as the city's council chamber (bouleuterion).
vici:vici-11769.wikidataDescription: building located beyond Basilica Stoa used for assemblies and performances in Ephesus

vici:vici-11776.label: Plovdiv Zirkus  [Philipopolis]
vici:vici-11776.description: Roman stadium of Philippopolis, built in the early 2nd century AD under Hadrian, about 240 m long and seating up to 30,000; its curved northern end (sphendone) survives exposed beneath Plovdiv's main pedestrian street.

vici:vici-11840.label: Stadium  -  Aphrodisias
vici:vici-11840.description: Stadium of Aphrodisias, built in the later 1st century AD, c. 270 x 60 m with 30 tiers of seating for up to 30,000; considered the best-preserved stadium of the ancient world and used for athletic and artistic contests.

vici:vici-11843.label: Theatre - Assos
vici:vici-11843.description: Hellenistic theatre of Assos, built around the late 4th–3rd century BC on a slope overlooking the Aegean with views to Lesbos; seated roughly 5,000 and gained a two-storey stage building in the Roman period.

vici:vici-11846.label: Theatre - Myra
vici:vici-11846.description: Greco-Roman theatre of Myra, badly damaged in the 141 AD earthquake and rebuilt with funds from the Lycian benefactor Opramoas of Rhodiapolis; seated up to about 12,000, making it the largest theatre in Lycia.

vici:vici-11879.label: Theatre Cherre'
vici:vici-11879.description: Theatre at the Gallo-Roman sanctuary complex of Cherré (Aubigné-Racan, Sarthe), a 1st–3rd century AD rural cult and market center excavated since 1977 that also included two temples, baths, an aqueduct, and a forum.

vici:vici-11915.label: Theatre Caesarea Maritima
vici:vici-11915.description: Roman theatre built by Herod the Great (37–4 BC) at Caesarea Maritima, among the earliest Roman-style theatres in the region; seated roughly 3,500–4,000 and, after restoration, is still used for performances today.

vici:vici-11916.label: Hippodrome Caesarea Maritima
vici:vici-11916.description: Monumental hippodrome/stadium built by Herod the Great, dedicated with the city in 10/9 BC and roughly 315 m long; hosted the quadrennial Actian Games (chariot racing, athletics, gladiatorial combat) and was later remodeled as an amphitheater.

vici:vici-11918.label: Theatre Anderitum
vici:vici-11918.description: Theatre serving Anderitum, Gallo-Roman capital of the Gabali civitas at Javols; built between the 1st and 3rd centuries AD, possibly a mixed theatre-amphitheatre, with only the perimeter wall and foundations surviving.

vici:vici-11924.label: Theatre Chanata
vici:vici-11924.description: The rock-hewn theatre (or odeion) of Roman Canatha (Qanawat) in the Hauran, cut into the wadi slope with nine tiers of basalt seating around a 19m orchestra; likely 3rd-century, possibly cult-related.

vici:vici-11932.label: Theatre Mantinea
vici:vici-11932.description: Ancient Greek theatre of Mantinea in Arcadia, built into the city's agora complex after its 371 BC reconstruction following destruction by Sparta; unusually raised entirely on an artificial mound rather than a hillside.
vici:vici-11932.wikidataDescription: ancient Greek theatre in Mantinea, Arcadia, Greece

vici:vici-11933.label: Theatre Milyas
vici:vici-11933.description: Small theatre cut into bedrock at Melli (Kocaaliler) in Pisidia; a 2000 Pisidia Survey Project excavation suggested a Severan-era (early 3rd-century AD) construction date, though the city's ancient name remains unknown.

vici:vici-11972.label: Cockpit theatre Faversham
vici:vici-11972.description: A rare rural Romano-British theatre-sanctuary near Faversham, Kent, excavated 2007-2013; a circular 'cockpit-style' auditorium set within a religious complex with two temple enclosures and a sacred spring, apparently used for ceremonial gatherings.

vici:vici-11974.label: Amphitheatre Rotomagus (Rouen)
vici:vici-11974.description: Large elliptical Gallo-Roman amphitheatre of Rotomagus (Rouen), built late in the 2nd century AD and among the largest in Gaul at roughly 130 by 120 metres; abandoned by the 4th century and later buried under Philip Augustus's castle.
vici:vici-11974.wikidataDescription: former Roman amphitheatre or theatre in Rouen, France

vici:vici-11986.label: Kleines Theater Pula
vici:vici-11986.description: The Small Roman Theatre of Pula, built in the 1st century AD on the hillside below the citadel; seated an estimated 4,000-5,000 for drama and recitations, with 2011-2022 excavations restoring the site.

vici:vici-11991.label: Theatre - Vize
vici:vici-11991.description: The only known Roman-era theatre in Thrace, built in the 2nd century AD at Bizye (Vize); discovered in 1998, its marble cavea seated some 4,000, with stage reliefs now held in Kırklareli Museum.

vici:vici-16644.label: Theatre, Agen - Aginnum
vici:vici-16644.description: Roman theatre in Aginnum (Agen), built in the 1st century AD with a diameter of about 86m; repaired several times before abandonment in the early 2nd century, its foundations remain buried near Place Armand-Fallières.

vici:vici-16656.label: Cadeyrac Theatre - Catiriacum
vici:vici-16656.description: Gallo-Roman theatre near Rodez, with an estimated 2,000-seat cavea, built within a rural sanctuary complex in the 1st-2nd century AD; discovered in 1865 by Abbé Cérès, with a coin of Marcus Aurelius (145 AD) aiding its dating.

vici:vici-16718.label: Theatre, Brion
vici:vici-16718.description: 1st-century Gallo-Roman theatre near Saint-Germain-d'Esteuil in the Médoc, 57m in diameter with an estimated 2,200 seats, built in opus mixtum masonry; the only known Gallo-Roman theatre south of the Garonne, identified in 1966.

vici:vici-16736.label: Cult Theatre, Vienne
vici:vici-16736.description: Small hemicycle of tiered seating (a fifth of a circle) built in early-1st-century Vienne, interpreted as a theatre for the mystery rites of Cybele and Attis or as a civic auditorium; now part of the Jardin archéologique de Cybèle.

vici:vici-16740.label: Barzan Theatre
vici:vici-16740.description: Roman theatre on La Garde hill within the Gallo-Roman port city at Barzan (site du Fâ); hemicycle radius of at least 50m, among the largest in Gaul, rivaling Vienne, Orange and Autun; built late 1st century AD.

vici:vici-16744.label: Theatre, Les Sarrasins, Moingt
vici:vici-16744.description: Mixed Gallo-Roman theatre at Aquae Segetae (Moingt), built mid-1st century, enlarged in the 2nd, seating up to ~8,000 in a 42m-radius semicircle; its ruined wall, known locally as the Mur des Sarrasins, was classified a historic monument in 1981.

vici:vici-16771.label: Cirque antique, Lyon
vici:vici-16771.description: Roman circus for chariot racing at Lugdunum (Lyon), attested by inscriptions but never securely located archaeologically; probable remains found near rue Pauline-Marie Jaricot may correspond to it.
vici:vici-16771.wikidataDescription: Roman circus located in Lyon, in France

vici:vici-16773.label: Montaudou, Ceyrat
vici:vici-16773.description: Roman theatre on the Puy de Montaudou above Ceyrat, near Augustonemetum (Clermont-Ferrand); built late 1st century at 51m diameter, enlarged to 81m in the 2nd; identified as a theatre, not a Mercury sanctuary, in 2005 by Christian Le Barrier.
vici:vici-16773.wikidataDescription: performance building built in Gaul, in the city of Arveni

vici:vici-17038.label: Kérilien Theatre - Vorganium
vici:vici-17038.description: The 80m-diameter theatre at Vorganium, the only known theatre in Osismii territory, stood outside the settlement, identified via a nearby Kerscao milestone naming the site; excavated in the 1960s, never fully cleared, and abandoned after 3rd-century raids.

vici:vici-17042.label: Naix Theatre - Nasium
vici:vici-17042.description: Nasium, first capital of the Leuci civitas, held a theatre on the Mazeroie plateau, identified in 1833 by antiquarian Claude-François Denis at a spot locals called the 'Fosse aux Lions', proving it a theatre rather than a circus.

vici:vici-17065.label: Arnières Theatre
vici:vici-17065.description: The Gallo-Roman theatre of Arnières-sur-Iton was exposed during Paris-Caen railway construction and partly excavated by Théodore Bonnin in 1853; it stood by a roadside settlement on the Évreux-Condé-sur-Iton route, occupied from the 1st to the 4th century.

vici:vici-17072.label: Metz Amphitheatre - Dividurum
vici:vici-17072.description: Built around 100 CE in Divodurum Mediomatricorum's Sablon district, this amphitheatre's 158m major axis made it the third-largest in the Roman world after the Colosseum and Capua; used for games until the 3rd century, rediscovered during 1902 railway excavations.

vici:vici-17090.label: Theatre, Soissons, Augusta Suesssionum
vici:vici-17090.description: Built in the later 1st century in Augusta Suessionum, capital of the Suessiones, its 144m cavea rivaled Autun's as one of Gaul's largest theatres, said to seat 20,000; dismantled for stone from the 3rd century onward.

vici:vici-17091.label: Lyons-la-Forêt Theatre - Ligontio
vici:vici-17091.description: A modest 'rustic' Gallo-Roman theatre seating up to 2,000 stood in Lyons-la-Forêt's Bout-de-Bas district on the Rouen-Beauvais road where it crossed the Lieure; 3rd-century in date, excavated in the 20th century by Marc-Adrien Dollfus.

vici:vici-17319.label: Calahorra Amphitheatre, E - CALAGVRRIS IVLIA NASICA
vici:vici-17319.description: No archaeological remains confirm an amphitheatre at Calagurris; only the Roman circus (traceable in the modern street plan, c. 360 x 80 m) is archaeologically attested, though scholars presume a theatre and amphitheatre existed given the city's civic status.

vici:vici-17321.label: Toledo Circus,E - TOLETUM
vici:vici-17321.description: Built in the second half of the 1st century AD under the Julio-Claudians outside Toletum's walls in the Vega Baja, one of Hispania's largest circuses (up to 427 m long), seating 14,000-30,000 for chariot races until the 5th century.

vici:vici-17322.label: Sagunto Circus,E - SAGUNTVM
vici:vici-17322.description: Circus of Roman Saguntum, built for chariot racing outside the walls near the Palancia (ancient Udiva) river; roughly 354 x 73 m with a 190 m spina, seating an estimated 15,000-20,000 spectators.

vici:vici-17323.label: Guadix Theatre,E - ACCI
vici:vici-17323.description: Theatre of Colonia Iulia Gemella Acci, built around 25 AD on the hillside above the Roman colony founded for veterans after the Battle of Munda; discovered by chance in 2007 during construction work, covering some 6,000 sq m.

vici:vici-17325.label: Badalona Theatre, E - BAETULO
vici:vici-17325.description: Small Roman theatre of Baetulo, built in the early 2nd century AD with an estimated original capacity of about 878 spectators; the second known Roman theatre in Catalonia after Tarragona's, still under excavation.

vici:vici-17344.label: Bosra Stadium - NOVA TRAIANA BOSTRA
vici:vici-17344.description: Hippodrome of Roman Bostra, an elongated arena roughly 420 x 97 m built after Arabia became a Roman province in 106 AD, possibly linked to athletic games founded under Philip the Arab (244-249); one of five known Roman hippodromes in the Levant.

vici:vici-17346.label: Kalaat Theatre,SYR - APAMEA
vici:vici-17346.description: One of the largest theatres of the Roman world, built in the 2nd century AD with a cavea 139 m in diameter seating over 20,000; only the Theatre of Pompey in Rome was larger. Its design gave exceptional acoustics, audible from any seat.

vici:vici-17348.label: La Laouata Theatre,TN - ACHOLLA
vici:vici-17348.description: The theatre of Acholla (Henchir Botria), a Punic-founded city that submitted to Caesar in 46 BC; monumental elite-funded building in the 2nd-3rd centuries AD added this theatre alongside an amphitheatre and bath complexes.

vici:vici-17349.label: El Jem Circus,TN - THYSDRUS
vici:vici-17349.description: The Roman circus of Thysdrus (El Jem), a chariot-racing track almost as large as Rome's Circus Maximus with capacity for up to 30,000 spectators, built as the city rivaled Hadrumetum as North Africa's second city.

vici:vici-17351.label: Cherchell Circus,DZ - Colonia Claudia Caesarea
vici:vici-17351.description: The Roman circus of Caesarea in Mauretania (Cherchell), the capital built up under Juba II and Cleopatra Selene; unlike the theatre and amphitheatre, which align with the city's cardo maximus, the circus follows a different orientation tied to the surrounding land division.

vici:vici-17353.label: Skopje Theatre, MK - SCVPI
vici:vici-17353.description: Theatre of the Roman colony Scupi (Colonia Scupi Aelia), built in the 2nd century AD and identified by seat inscriptions bearing the colony's name; discovered by archaeologist Nikola Vulić and since fully excavated, yielding over 8,500 artifacts, though the structure itself survives only in decayed form.

vici:vici-17358.label: Yatağan,Theater,TR - STRATONICEA BOVLETERION
vici:vici-17358.description: Not a theatre but the bouleuterion (council house) of Stratonicea near Eskihisar/Yatağan, a rectangular hall with semicircular seating dated to the late 1st century BC-1st century AD, its walls inscribed with a fragment of Diocletian's Prices Edict and a Greek calendar poem attributed to the local orator Menippus.

vici:vici-17359.label: Kıyıkışlacık,Theater, TR - IASSVS
vici:vici-17359.description: The Roman-period theatre of Iasos (Iassos), cut into a hillside on the Carian coast with a rock-and-masonry cavea seating roughly 3,500; its ashlar retaining wall was stripped of marble in 1887 to build the quays of Constantinople's harbour.

vici:vici-17361.label: Cavdarhisar,Circus,TR - AEZANI
vici:vici-17361.description: The theatre-stadium complex at Aizanoi joins a 20,000-seat theatre directly to a 13,500-seat stadium via a shared stage building, a design unique in the ancient world; built c.160-250 AD, funded by M. Apuleius Eurycles.

vici:vici-17367.label: Sedir Adası,Theater,TR - CEDRAE
vici:vici-17367.description: Hellenistic theatre of Cedrae (Kedreai) on Sedir Island, built in the 4th century BC on a seaward slope outside the walls; seated roughly 2,500, with cavea, orchestra and skene remains, part still unexcavated.

vici:vici-17370.label: Aliağa,Theater,TR - CYME
vici:vici-17370.description: Theatre of Cyme, chief city of the Aeolian dodecapolis; largely unexcavated but identified and mapped via ground-penetrating radar alongside the city's agora, Isis sanctuary and Roman baths.

vici:vici-17372.label: Ura Theatre - OLBA
vici:vici-17372.description: Roman theatre of Olba (Diocaesarea), built under the joint reign of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus (r. AD 161-169), seated about 2,000; its auditorium and stage building survive beside the city's nymphaeum.

vici:vici-17376.label: Ildır,Theater,TR - ERYTHRAE
vici:vici-17376.description: Hellenistic theatre of Erythrae, one of the twelve Ionian cities, first built in the earlier 3rd century BC and later remodeled with a double diazoma under Hadrian; excavated by Ekrem Akurgal.

vici:vici-17378.label: YeniKöy,Theater,TR - METROPOLIS
vici:vici-17378.description: Hellenistic theatre of Metropolis in Ionia, built into a natural hillside depression in the 3rd century BC; a marble seat of honor carved with griffins was found there in 1995 during Sabancı Foundation-sponsored excavations.

vici:vici-17380.label: Asar Köy,Theater,TR - SYLLYIO
vici:vici-17380.description: Theatre of Sillyon (Syllion), a Pamphylian hill city that alone resisted Alexander the Great in 333 BC; documented by Karol Lanckoroński in the 19th century before a 1969 landslide destroyed it along with the adjoining odeon.

vici:vici-17381.label: Karpuzlu,Theater,TR - ALINDA
vici:vici-17381.description: Well-preserved Hellenistic theatre of Alinda in Caria, seating roughly 5,000, probably built in the early 2nd century BC and later expanded by the Romans in the 1st century AD.

vici:vici-17891.label: Theatre, Baalbek
vici:vici-17891.description: A Roman theater built into the hillside south of Heliopolis's great sanctuary complex, with a parodos leading to the orchestra and stage; largely destroyed during 19th-century hotel construction, leaving only minimal remains today.

vici:vici-17900.label: North Theatre, Gadara
vici:vici-17900.description: The larger of Gadara's two Roman theaters, built in black basalt into the north-eastern slope with an c.85m-wide cavea seating around 6,000; ruined by earthquake and later quarried for stone by the Ottoman-era village built over it.

vici:vici-17902.label: Hippodrome, Gadara
vici:vici-17902.description: Roman hippodrome of Gadara, a Decapolis city, used for equestrian spectacles; today only faint outlines survive west of the city's colonnaded street.

vici:vici-17970.label: Theater van Balbus
vici:vici-17970.description: Dedicated in 13 BC by Lucius Cornelius Balbus with spoils from his African campaign, one of Rome's three permanent stone theaters (with those of Pompey and Marcellus); held over 11,000 spectators and was rebuilt after a fire under Domitian.

vici:vici-17982.label: Teatro Maritimo, Tivoli
vici:vici-17982.description: Circular island retreat within Hadrian's Villa, begun c.118 AD, ringed by a moat and portico with movable wooden bridges for total seclusion; the name 'Maritime Theatre' was coined in the 19th century by architect Blondel after its sea-themed friezes.
vici:vici-17982.wikidataDescription: architectural feature that is part of the villa of the Roman emperor Hadrian at Tivoli, Italy

vici:vici-17986.label: Theatre, Velia
vici:vici-17986.description: Roman theater of the 3rd century CE built directly over an earlier 4th-century BC Greek theater at Elea/Velia; its 47.5m cavea held roughly 3,000 spectators and faces the Tyrrhenian Sea below a Norman watchtower.

vici:vici-11324.label: Theater of Mikrothives
vici:vici-11324.description: Hellenistic theatre (15 tiers, capacity ~3,000) of ancient Phthiotic Thebes, identified and partly excavated in 1992–93; in the Roman period it was remodeled into an arena for wild-beast fights.
vici:vici-11324.wikidataDescription: ancient city in Magnesia, Thessaly, Greece

vici:vici-11325.label: Theatre of Pinara
vici:vici-11325.description: Well-preserved Hellenistic theatre of Pinara in Lycia, built into a hillside in the late 2nd century BC with a capacity of about 3,200; nearly all its stone seating survives intact.

vici:vici-11345.label: Theatre Samos
vici:vici-11345.description: Theatre of ancient Samos near Pythagoreion, on the slope below the sanctuary of Panagia Spiliani; construction is dated to the 4th century BC with Roman-era rebuilding, though little masonry survives today.

vici:vici-11353.label: Theatre Selge
vici:vici-11353.description: Mountain theatre of Selge in Pisidia, built in the 2nd century AD with a 104 m cavea seating roughly 9,000–10,000; later reduced and converted into an arena in the 3rd century.

vici:vici-11403.label: Theatre Bardiaux
vici:vici-11403.description: Rural Gallo-Roman theatre at Les Bardiaux (Arleuf, Morvan), built around the late 2nd century AD with six concentric tiers seating 600–700; discovered in 1971, it likely also hosted public assemblies.

vici:vici-11406.label: Theatre Petromantalum
vici:vici-11406.description: Large Gallo-Roman theatre (110 m diameter, seating up to 8,000–10,000) at the sanctuary of Les Vaux-de-la-Celle, Genainville; sometimes, inconclusively, identified with the Peutinger Table's station of Petromantalum/Petrum Viacum.

vici:vici-11409.label: Theatre Teanum
vici:vici-11409.description: Roman theatre of Teanum Sidicinum (Teano), among Italy's largest with an 85 m cavea seating 6,000–7,000; built from the late 2nd century BC, systematically excavated by Werner Johannowsky, 1961–1976.

vici:vici-11413.label: Theatre Thapsus
vici:vici-11413.description: Despite being labeled 'Thapsus,' this theatre stands at Rusicade (modern Skikda), the largest Roman theatre in Algeria, built under Hadrian; long quarried for stone, only fragments survive today.

vici:vici-11528.label: Theatre Gadara
vici:vici-11528.description: The smaller of Gadara's two Roman theatres, built of basalt on the acropolis's western slope in the Severan period (193-235 AD) with seating for about 3,000; 1960s excavations uncovered a marble statue of Tyche, now in the Umm Qais museum.

vici:vici-11532.label: Hippodrome  Constantinople
vici:vici-11532.description: Begun under Septimius Severus around AD 203 and enlarged by Constantine I after 330 as Constantinople's chariot-racing arena and ceremonial center; site of the AD 532 Nika riots, its spina still marked by an Egyptian obelisk and the Serpent Column.

vici:vici-11548.label: Nysa Odeon
vici:vici-11548.description: Built as a bouleuterion around the 1st century BC and rebuilt as an odeon around AD 160; Strabo calls it a gerontikon, the meeting hall of the city elders, with 12 rows of seats holding roughly 600-700 people.

vici:vici-11555.label: Theatre Hadrianopolis
vici:vici-11555.description: Roman theatre built in the city founded under Hadrian (who visited the region in AD 125); its cavea, 58 m across with 24 limestone rows, seated about 3,500-4,000. Rediscovered after a 1970s landslide, confirmed as Hadrianopolis by 2002 excavations.

vici:vici-11564.label: Theatre Magnesia
vici:vici-11564.description: Late Hellenistic or early imperial theatre of Magnesia on the Maeander, left unfinished and only discovered by excavation in 1984; the cavea survives but no trace remains of its probably wooden stage building.

vici:vici-11565.label: Theatre Megapolis
vici:vici-11565.description: Built around 370 BC by the architect Polycleitus the Younger for the newly founded federal capital of the Arcadian League; Pausanias called it the largest theatre in Greece, holding up to about 20,000 and doubling as the League's assembly hall.
vici:vici-11565.wikidataDescription: ancient Greek theatre in Megalopoli, Greece

vici:vici-11571.label: Theatre Patras
vici:vici-11571.description: Roman odeon of Patras built in the first half of the 2nd century AD, praised by Pausanias as second only to the Odeon of Herodes Atticus; destroyed by fire in the late 3rd century, rediscovered in 1889, and restored in 1959-61.
vici:vici-11571.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman concert building in Patras, Greece

vici:vici-11591.label: Theatre Uthina
vici:vici-11591.description: Theatre of Uthina (Oudhna), near the Numidian-Roman colony's forum and capitol; unlike the city's well-preserved 16,000-seat amphitheatre, it survives only as a shallow depression in the hillside.

vici:vici-11593.label: Theatre Acropolis Pergamon
vici:vici-11593.description: Hellenistic theatre on Pergamon's upper acropolis, built c. 225-200 BC and enlarged under Eumenes II; the steepest theatre of the ancient world, with 78 rows seating about 10,000, fronted by a 247m colonnaded terrace and the Temple of Dionysus.

vici:vici-11598.label: Theatre Germanicomagus
vici:vici-11598.description: Gallo-Roman theatre at Les Bouchauds (ancient Germanicomagus) in Charente, cut into a hillside beside a sanctuary; at 105.6m diameter the largest theatre in Aquitaine, seating 5,000-6,000, discovered in 1865 and protected as a historic monument since 1881.

vici:vici-11671.label: Zirkus der Tiberius
vici:vici-11671.description: Circus built by Tiberius in AD 14 at Bovillae, ancestral town of the Julian family, in honor of the deified Augustus; measured c. 337 x 69m, with yearly imperial-cult games instituted there from AD 16.

vici:vici-11713.label: Amphitheatre Tarentum
vici:vici-11713.description: Roman amphitheatre of Tarentum (Taranto), southwest of the Chiesa del Carmine, possibly built over one of the city's two unexcavated Greek theatres; no remains are visible today.

vici:vici-11759.label: Theatre Peramon Centrum
vici:vici-11759.description: Small Roman theatre within Pergamon's Asclepieion healing sanctuary, seating about 3,500; built into the sanctuary's northwest corner, with performances forming part of the complex's ritual therapy during its Hadrianic-era remodeling.

vici:vici-11768.label: Hippodrome - Ephesus
vici:vici-11768.description: Stadium of Ephesus, first laid out by Lysimachus in the 3rd century BC and rebuilt for chariot races, athletics, and beast/gladiator fights under Nero; U-shaped, 229 x 28m, its southern seating cut into the slope of Mount Pion.
vici:vici-11768.wikidataDescription: large stadium located on the north-west side of the Panayirdag in Ephesus

vici:vici-12001.label: Hippodrome Laodicea
vici:vici-12001.description: Built in AD 79 and dedicated to Vespasian and Titus, funded privately by the citizen Nikostratos; at roughly 285 x 70 m this was one of Roman Anatolia's largest stadiums, seating up to 25,000 for games.

vici:vici-12005.label: Theatre Hierapolis - Kastabala
vici:vici-12005.description: A 1st-century AD Roman theatre built into a hillside at Hierapolis Kastabala in Cilicia, seating roughly 5,000 across ima and summa cavea; excavations have recovered 36 theatrical stage masks, including five found in 2025.

vici:vici-12007.label: Odeon Anemurium
vici:vici-12007.description: A small, well-preserved covered odeon/bouleuterion at Anemurium in Rough Cilicia, excavated with the rest of the city (UBC excavations, 1965-1993), seating roughly 900-1,100 for council meetings or performances.

vici:vici-12008.label: Theatre Anemurium
vici:vici-12008.description: Anemurium's main Roman theatre, a semicircular structure about 60 m in diameter, built in the 3rd century AD at the height of the city's prosperity.

vici:vici-12019.label: Zirkus Sardes
vici:vici-12019.description: A Roman-period stadium at the foot of the Sardis acropolis, south of the gymnasium, with a U-shaped, double-sided cavea built against vaulted substructures on the slope.

vici:vici-12020.label: Theatre Sardes
vici:vici-12020.description: Theater built at Sardis during the Hellenistic period as part of the city's conversion into a Greek-style polis; it stood alongside a stadium among Sardis's Roman-era civic monuments.

vici:vici-12057.label: Theatre - Shuni
vici:vici-12057.description: Roman theater at Shuni (ancient Kfar Shumi) built with an adjoining semicircular pool used for the Graeco-Syrian Maiumas water festival honoring Dionysus and Aphrodite; excavated from 1986 by E. Shenhav for the JNF.

vici:vici-12877.label: Theater Virunum
vici:vici-12877.description: The only known Roman theater in Noricum, built in the 2nd century AD with a semicircular cavea of 35 m radius and a 32.5 m stage, near Virunum's amphitheater; excavated 1890s–1931 and again since the 1990s.

vici:vici-12885.label: Odeon - Nicopolis ad Istrum
vici:vici-12885.description: Small roofed odeon at Nicopolis ad Istrum (founded by Trajan c. 102–106) seating up to about 350; its stone cavea was supported on arches sheltering eleven shops, separated from the semicircular orchestra by iron-braced stone blocks.

vici:vici-13588.label: Amphitheatre of Tomis
vici:vici-13588.description: Roman amphitheater at Tomis, arena c. 60x40 m within a complex up to 100x80 m and 20–25 m tall, discovered in 1980; a 2nd–3rd century AD section found in 1988–89 was preserved beneath the Ibis hotel.

vici:vici-13914.label: Aquileia Circus
vici:vici-13914.description: Roman circus built around 293 AD under Maximian near his Aquileia residence for chariot racing; still in use in 425, when the usurper John (Johannes) was executed there on Valentinian III's orders.

vici:vici-14461.label: Theater? (Rottweil)
vici:vici-14461.description: A wall with buttresses at Arae Flaviae (Rottweil), near a sanctuary and blocks resembling seating stones, has been tentatively identified as a theater on the strength of geomagnetic surveys showing a monumental complex, though the evidence remains inconclusive.

vici:vici-14560.label: Châteaubleau Théâtre
vici:vici-14560.description: Gallo-Roman theater built in the 2nd century AD within a rural pilgrimage complex with a water sanctuary; held about 3,000 spectators, was abandoned by the late 3rd century, excavated from the 1950s, and protected as a historic monument since 1983.

vici:vici-14567.label: Théâtre gallo-romain de Brion
vici:vici-14567.description: 1st-century Gallo-Roman theatre (57m diameter) at Saint-Germain-d'Esteuil in the Médoc; the only known Gallo-Roman theatre in the Aquitaine basin south of the Garonne, abandoned by the mid-3rd century and identified during 1966 excavations.

vici:vici-14576.label: Vestiges du théâtre gallo-romain, Cahors
vici:vici-14576.description: Theatre of Divona Cadurcorum (Roman Cahors), built c. 41-54 AD under Claudius; once the best-preserved Roman monument in Cahors until its owner demolished the remaining structure in 1860-1863.

vici:vici-14582.label: Théâtre romain du Puy de Jouer
vici:vici-14582.description: Small Gallo-Roman theatre near Saint-Goussaud (Creuse), reputedly the smallest in France; a semicircular seating structure about 9m wide, excavated in 1901, 1965, and 1980, near a Roman road linking Augustoritum (Limoges) and Ahun.

vici:vici-14785.label: The Odeon of Troy IX
vici:vici-14785.description: Odeon (concert hall) built at Ilion (Troy) under Augustus on the site of the old bouleuterion, extensively renovated by Hadrian after his AD 124 visit; a marble cuirassed statue of Hadrian was found here in 1993.

vici:vici-14869.label: Roman theatre Pergamon Asklepion
vici:vici-14869.description: Roman theatre within the Asclepieion healing sanctuary of Pergamon, built under Hadrian in the 2nd century AD to host therapeutic musical and dramatic performances for patients; seated roughly 3,500 in a hillside cavea with a marble-paved orchestra.

vici:vici-14871.label: Bouleterion, Teos
vici:vici-14871.description: Best-preserved building of ancient Teos in Ionia; a late 3rd-century BC council hall (bouleuterion) seating about 800, later adapted in the Roman period with an added stage building for theatrical use.

vici:vici-15049.label: Hippodrome of Domitian
vici:vici-15049.description: Sunken garden-stadium (160 x 48m) built by Domitian (81-92 AD) on the east side of his Domus Augustana palace on the Palatine; despite its racetrack shape it was too small for chariots and served as an imperial pleasure garden.

vici:vici-15097.label: Paphos Odeon
vici:vici-15097.description: 2nd-century AD Roman odeon at Nea Paphos, Cyprus, built of dressed limestone with twelve rows of seating for roughly 1,200; restored by the Cyprus Department of Antiquities and still used for concerts and drama festivals.

vici:vici-15709.label: Hippodrome Magnesia on the Meander
vici:vici-15709.description: Roman-era stadium (186 m long) at Magnesia on the Maeander seating up to 30,000, built in the 1st century AD for the Artemis Leucophryene games; hosted athletics, gladiatorial fights and chariot races; excavated by Carl Humann in 1891-93, resumed 1984.

vici:vici-15711.label: Phocaea Theatre
vici:vici-15711.description: Ancient theatre at Phocaea (Foça), believed to be the oldest Ionian theatre yet discovered; partially excavated on the acropolis hill, first investigated by Félix Sartiaux in 1913-1920 and systematically by Ekrem Akurgal from 1951.

vici:vici-16324.label: Circus Sousse
vici:vici-16324.description: Roman circus of Hadrumetum (Sousse), attested by circus-themed mosaics of the four racing factions and by curse tablets targeting charioteers recorded in Audollent's Defixionum tabellae; its physical remains have not been precisely excavated in situ.

vici:vici-16584.label: Théâtre grec
vici:vici-16584.description: Greek-style theatre of Massalia (Marseille), built in the Augustan period, about 115 m wide with a 54 m stage, seating roughly 6,000; located near the Vieux-Port, first found in 1946-48 excavations and further excavated 1961-64.

vici:vici-16587.label: Theatre, Béziers
vici:vici-16587.description: Roman theatre of Baeterrae (Béziers), unexpectedly discovered in 2014 during a preventive excavation near Place des Chaudronniers; about a third of the building survives, with a restored diameter of 80-85 m, sited between the forum and amphitheatre.

vici:vici-16613.label: Aix-en-Provence, théâtre antique
vici:vici-16613.description: Roman theatre of Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence), about 100 m in diameter and built in the Julio-Claudian period on a terrace of the western quarter; long only suspected, it was confirmed by excavations at Notre-Dame-de-la-Seds in 2004.

vici:vici-16628.label: Theatre, Nîmes
vici:vici-16628.description: A Roman theatre certainly existed at Nemausus (Nîmes), a major colonial city, but unlike its well-preserved amphitheatre its precise location has never been archaeologically identified, with the site only loosely placed near the cathedral.

vici:vici-16629.label: Apt Theatre - Apta Iulia
vici:vici-16629.description: Roman theatre of Apta Julia (Apt), built in the early 1st century AD, roughly 80x60 m and holding 5,000-6,000 spectators; substantial remains were found beneath Place Carnot in 1869-70 and confirmed by soundings in 1966-67.

vici:vici-16846.label: Les Palais, Saint-Marcel
vici:vici-16846.description: Gallo-Roman theatre-amphitheatre of Argentomagus, rebuilt mid-2nd century CE to an 85m diameter, succeeding a smaller theatre built under Tiberius; abandoned by the early 5th century.

vici:vici-16866.label: Théâtre d'Alléans - Baugy
vici:vici-16866.description: Theatre identified in 1874 as part of a Gallo-Roman religious complex with sanctuary and necropolis near Alléans, one of the most important such sites in the Cher; excavated through the 19th century.

vici:vici-16908.label: Theatre, Champallement
vici:vici-16908.description: Urban theatre of the Gallo-Roman town of Compierre, built in the 3rd century CE with a 72m cavea seating about 5,000; the settlement was abandoned by the late 4th century.

vici:vici-16919.label: La Piletière, Mauves-sur-Loire
vici:vici-16919.description: 1st-century Gallo-Roman theatre near the Vieille-Cour sanctuary to Mars Mullo, excavated from 1886 by Léon Maître; cavea over 61m across, its wooden seating and stage now vanished.

vici:vici-16929.label: Mirebeau Amphitheatre
vici:vici-16929.description: Earthwork amphitheatre within the legionary fortress at Mirebeau, built c. 70 CE for Legio VIII Augusta's roughly 5,000 troops under Vespasian; its embankments are still visible today.

vici:vici-16933.label: Mirebeau Theatre
vici:vici-16933.description: A theatre serving the civilian canabae outside the Mirebeau legionary fortress of Legio VIII Augusta (70–86 CE) was later restored by a Roman citizen's daughter after falling into ruin.

vici:vici-16947.label: Locmariaquer
vici:vici-16947.description: Gallo-Roman theatre of the Venetic settlement near Vannes, its cavea extending past a semicircle beyond the standard hemicycle; excavated by Christophe-Paul de Robien (18th c.) and Closmadeuc, partly overtaken by the village cemetery.

vici:vici-16991.label: La Mardelle, Triguères
vici:vici-16991.description: Gallo-Roman amphitheatre at La Mardelle, 71 by 56m with room for about 8,000 spectators, found around 1850; its dressed stones were later reused to build the 1862 cemetery wall.

vici:vici-17095.label: Theatre, Rouen
vici:vici-17095.description: Catalogued as a possible theatre at Rotomagus (Roman Rouen), but no archaeological remains have ever been confirmed here; the city's only firmly attested Roman spectacle building is its separate amphitheatre.

vici:vici-17097.label: Valognes Theatre - Alauna
vici:vici-17097.description: Gallo-Roman arena-theatre at Alauna (Valognes), built in the later 1st century AD, over 72 m across with capacity of roughly 3,700-4,000; excavated from 1695, largely quarried away in the 1820s-30s.
vici:vici-17097.wikidataDescription: roman-era spectacle building in Valognes, France

vici:vici-17126.label: Canouville Theatre
vici:vici-17126.description: Gallo-Roman theatre built in a single campaign around the mid-2nd century AD and abandoned within about 50 years; 75 m cavea diameter; rediscovered in 1977 under a mound long taken for a medieval earthwork.

vici:vici-17193.label: Théâtre gallo-romain Ribemont-sur-Ancre
vici:vici-17193.description: One of the spectacle buildings of the major Ribemont-sur-Ancre sanctuary, a Celtic ritual site (mass ossuary deposits) succeeded by a Gallo-Roman complex of temple, theatre and baths; identified from 1962 aerial survey.

vici:vici-17194.label: Théâtre La Couture Ribemont-sur-Ancre
vici:vici-17194.description: Theatre of the Ribemont-sur-Ancre sanctuary, seating roughly 3,000; confirmed as a theatre in 1971 excavations, part of a temple-theatre-baths complex built over an earlier Celtic sanctuary marked by mass human bone deposits.

vici:vici-17229.label: Perge Stadium,TR - PERGA
vici:vici-17229.description: 2nd-century AD Roman stadium at Perge, among the largest and best-preserved in Asia Minor at 234 m long, seating around 12,000; its vaulted substructure held shops, per surviving inscriptions.

vici:vici-17230.label: Aspendos Stadium,TR - ASPENDUS
vici:vici-17230.description: U-shaped 2nd-century AD stadium at Aspendos, about 220 x 30 m with an estimated 8,000 seats; far less well preserved than the city's famous Roman theatre nearby.

vici:vici-17233.label: Phaselis Theatre,TR - PHASELI
vici:vici-17233.description: 2nd-century AD Roman theatre at Phaselis in Lycia, built over an earlier Hellenistic theatre; cavea about 46-50 m across in 5 wedges, seating roughly 1,500-2,000.
vici:vici-17233.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman theatre of Phaselis (Lycia, Turkey), built in the 2nd century on the foundations of an earlier Greek Hellenistic theatre

vici:vici-17234.label: Olympos Theatre,TR - OLYMPOS
vici:vici-17234.description: A small theatre with an elaborate entrance, likely Hellenistic in origin but rebuilt under Rome; Olympos held three votes in the Lycian League and was visited by Hadrian in 129 CE.

vici:vici-17236.label: Simena theater,TR - SIMENA
vici:vici-17236.description: A rock-cut theatre with seven rows carved into the bedrock of Simena's acropolis, probably Hellenistic and among the smallest and oldest theatres in Lycia; later enclosed within a medieval castle.
vici:vici-17236.wikidataDescription: ancient city of Lycia in modern-day Turkey

vici:vici-17238.label: Ayaş theater,TR - ELAIUSSA SEBASTE
vici:vici-17238.description: Roman theatre of Elaiussa Sebaste in Cilicia, a modest structure of about 23 rows of seats built in the 2nd century AD; the city has been excavated since 1995 by Rome's Sapienza University.

vici:vici-17271.label: Lindos,Theater,GR - LINDUS
vici:vici-17271.description: Rock-cut theatre below the Lindos acropolis, dated to the 4th century BC with seating for roughly 1,800-2,000; hosted the Sminthia festival of Dionysos with drama, music and athletic contests.

vici:vici-17273.label: Rhodos,Ρόδος, Stadium,GR - RHODVS
vici:vici-17273.description: Hellenistic stadium on the Acropolis of Rhodes, 210 m long and built in the 3rd century BC; hosted the athletic events of the Alieia games honoring Helios, later restored under Italian rule after 1912.
vici:vici-17273.wikidataDescription: Hellenistic stadium from the 3rd century BC

vici:vici-17274.label: Rhodos,Ρόδος,Theater GR - RHODVS
vici:vici-17274.description: Marble odeon on the Acropolis of Rhodes, built in the 3rd-2nd century BC as part of the gymnasium complex; seated about 800 for musical performances and rhetoric lessons, reconstructed under Italian rule.

vici:vici-17313.label: Huesca Theatre,E - Osca
vici:vici-17313.description: Roman theatre of Osca, first identified in 2006 beneath Huesca's old town near Calle Canellas; built in the first half of the 1st century AD, possibly larger than Zaragoza's Augustan-era theatre.

vici:vici-17315.label: Valeria de Arriba Amphitheatre,E - Valeria
vici:vici-17315.description: One of three known spectacle buildings (theatre, amphitheatre, circus) at Valeria, a city founded by proconsul Gaius Valerius Flaccus c. 93-82 BC; still largely unexcavated, with only a small fraction of the hillside site uncovered.

vici:vici-17316.label: Nertobriga Amphitheatre - Nertobriga
vici:vici-17316.description: A possible amphitheatre at the Celtiberian-Roman town of Nertobriga Concordia Iulia, proposed from an oval crop-mark visible in early-2000s SIGPAC aerial orthophotos; never excavated, and its identification as an amphitheatre remains debated among researchers.

vici:vici-17347.label: Suweyda Theatre,SYR - Dionysias
vici:vici-17347.description: Roman theatre south of the agora at Dionysias (Soada, modern Suweida), part of an Odeion-Bouleuterion-theatre-colonnade complex built around 100 CE as the region became the province of Arabia.

vici:vici-17382.label: Marmaris,Theater,TR - PHYSCOS
vici:vici-17382.description: Physcus (Physkos), a Carian port under Rhodian control with a harbour sacred to Leto; its Hellenistic walls crown Asartepe hill above Marmaris, besieged during Alexander's Carian campaign of 334 BC.

vici:vici-17384.label: Hyllarima,Theater,TR - MESEVLE
vici:vici-17384.description: Marble theater of Hyllarima, built in the 2nd-1st century BC and implying a town of roughly 1,500 people; excavated by a French-Turkish team led by Pierre Debord and Ender Varinlioğlu from 1997, published 2018.

vici:vici-17388.label: Ankara Theatre,TR - ANCYRA
vici:vici-17388.description: Roman theater of Ancyra (Ankara), dated to the 2nd century AD with about 20-22 rows seating 3,000-5,000; excavated 1982-86 and 2009-10, yielding fragments of a cuirassed statue of Hadrian.
vici:vici-17388.wikidataDescription: Roman open-air theatre in Ankara, Turkey

vici:vici-17390.label: Gölhisar,Circus,TR - CIBYRA
vici:vici-17390.description: Stadium of Cibyra (Kibyra), about 200m long with 21 rows of seats cut into the hillside and a U-shaped sphendone; used for races and, per its famous friezes, gladiatorial combats.

vici:vici-17392.label: Gölhisar,Odeon,TR - CIBYRA
vici:vici-17392.description: Odeon-bouleuterion of Cibyra, built mid-2nd century AD as the city council chamber and later given a stage; one of Turkey's best-preserved roofed theaters, its orchestra holds the world's only surviving Medusa mosaic in opus sectile.

vici:vici-17393.label: Sagrak,Theater,TR - ADADA
vici:vici-17393.description: Theater of Adada, a Pisidian hill town near Sütçüler allied with Termessos against Selge from the 2nd century BC and prosperous under Trajan, Hadrian and Antoninus Pius; its ruins also include a forum, basilica and acropolis.

vici:vici-17394.label: Konuralp,Theater,TR - Prusius ad Hypium
vici:vici-17394.description: Theater of Prusias ad Hypium, locally called "The Forty Stairs"; begun in the Hellenistic period and expanded under Rome to 100m x 74m with 36 rows seating about 10,000, its scaenae added around 190 AD.

vici:vici-17396.label: Kapıkırı,Theater,TR - HERACLEA AD LATMUM
vici:vici-17396.description: Theater of Heraclea ad Latmum (Latmos), a Hellenistic city founded in the early 3rd century BC at the foot of Mount Latmus by Lake Bafa, near the temple of Athena Latmia; its seating remains largely unexcavated.

vici:vici-17400.label: Plovdiv,Circus,BG - PHILIPPOPOLIS,TRIMONTIUM
vici:vici-17400.description: Roman stadium built in the early 2nd century AD under Hadrian, seating up to 30,000 for athletic games; its northern curved end (sphendone) survives beneath Plovdiv's main pedestrian street, discovered in 1923.

vici:vici-17439.label: Pozzuoli Stadium,I - PUTEOLI
vici:vici-17439.description: The Stadium of Antoninus Pius, built c. 142 AD at Puteoli to honor Hadrian and host Greek-style games (the Eusebeia); one of the largest Roman masonry stadiums after Domitian's, only unearthed in 2008.

vici:vici-17440.label: Rome,Piazza Navona,Stadium of Domitian,I - Roma
vici:vici-17440.description: Built by Domitian and inaugurated in 86 AD for Greek-style athletic contests (the Capitoline Games), seating c. 30,000; its elongated plan is preserved by Piazza Navona above, with ruins visible underground.

vici:vici-17441.label: Rome Circus of Villa of Septimius Bassus,I
vici:vici-17441.description: A rectangular circus/hippodrome garden (95 x 327 m) within the huge Villa dei Sette Bassi on Via Tuscolana, second-largest suburban villa after the Villa of the Quintilii; the medieval name likely derives from Caracalla, not a prefect Septimius Bassus.

vici:vici-17446.label: Luni Theatre,I - LUNA
vici:vici-17446.description: Covered theatre (theatrum tectum) at the Roman colony of Luna, built c. 40 AD for readings and music, richly decorated with marble sculpture; excavated from the 1950s-70s and converted to housing, then a Lombard necropolis, by the 6th century.

vici:vici-17449.label: Catania,Odeon I - CATINA
vici:vici-17449.description: 2nd-century AD odeon adjoining the Roman theatre of Catania, seating about 1,500 for poetry and music contests and rehearsals; built partly of volcanic stone with a purely decorative lava architrave.
vici:vici-17449.wikidataDescription: ancient Greek odeon in Catania, Italy

vici:vici-17457.label: Sant'Antioco Amphitheatre,I - SULCI
vici:vici-17457.description: Roman amphitheatre of Sulci (Sant'Antioco), identified in 1983-84 on the slope below the Punic acropolis and necropolis; dated to the 2nd-3rd century AD, likely built largely in wood so little of the superstructure survives.

vici:vici-17462.label: Nocera Superiore Theatre,I - NUCERIA
vici:vici-17462.description: Hellenistic-Roman theatre of Nuceria Alfaterna, built into the Samnite city walls in the 2nd century BC and rebuilt in brick under Augustus; among Campania's largest at 96m diameter, with a marble-paved orchestra and twin vaulted parodoi.
vici:vici-17462.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman theatre in Nocera Inferiore, Italy

vici:vici-17466.label: Nora Theatre,I - NORA
vici:vici-17466.description: The only known Roman theatre in Sardinia, built in the early 1st century AD; its two-tiered cavea (37.7m diameter, 11 andesite-block steps) held roughly 1,000-1,200 spectators and is still used for summer performances.

vici:vici-17469.label: Posillipo Theatre,I - PAUSYLIPUM
vici:vici-17469.description: Theatre of Publius Vedius Pollio's seaside villa at Pausilypon (Posillipo), built c. 31 BC; part of a 9-hectare estate with baths and an odeon, its cavea overlooking the Bay of Naples seated about 2,000.

vici:vici-17470.label: Posillipo Odeon,I - PAUSYLIPUM
vici:vici-17470.description: Small odeon adjoining the theatre within Vedius Pollio's Pausilypon villa complex, built c. 31 BC as a roofed hall for music and recitation on the same Posillipo estate later inherited by Augustus.

vici:vici-17472.label: Lipari Theatre,I
vici:vici-17472.description: Remains of a Greek theatre (4th-3rd century BC) at the southern end of ancient Lipara's acropolis, its sea view later blocked by 16th-century fortifications; Lipari is separately famed for its hoard of Hellenistic terracotta theatrical masks.

vici:vici-17473.label: San Giuseppe Jato Theatre,I - IAITAS
vici:vici-17473.description: Greek theatre of Iaitas, built before 300 BC on the model of Athens' Theatre of Dionysus; its 35-tier cavea, excavated by the University of Zurich since 1971, seated an estimated 4,000-5,000 spectators.
vici:vici-17473.wikidataDescription: ancient Greek theatre in the province of Palermo, Italy

vici:vici-17474.label: Torino Theatre,IT - AUGUSTA TAURINORUM
vici:vici-17474.description: Roman theatre of Augusta Taurinorum, built c. 13 BC as one of the new colony's first public buildings under Augustus; its four-sector stone cavea seated about 3,500 and was rediscovered in 1899 during construction of Palazzo Reale's new wing.
vici:vici-17474.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman theatre in Turin, Italy

vici:vici-17480.label: Saida, صيدا‎,Theater,RL - SYDONE
vici:vici-17480.description: Roman theatre remains uncovered on the north flank of Sidon's castle hill in modern excavations; little else about the structure has been published.

vici:vici-17481.label: Jubayl, جبيل‎ ,Theater,RL - BYBLOS
vici:vici-17481.description: Small Roman theatre built around AD 218, excavated by Pierre Montet in the 1920s; only five tiers of seating survive today, and it was later dismantled and re-erected closer to the shore during subsequent excavation.

vici:vici-17486.label: Shahhat,North  Theater,LT - CYRENIS COL.
vici:vici-17486.description: The largest and oldest of Cyrene's five theatres, cut into the Acropolis slope in the late 6th century BC as a Greek theatre; converted into a Roman amphitheatre for gladiatorial games in the late 2nd century AD.

vici:vici-17489.label: Al Bayda,Theater,LT - BALAGRAE
vici:vici-17489.description: An odeon within the Asclepieion sanctuary at Balagrae, used for musical performances and sophists' recitations as part of the healing cult of Asclepius; a hoard of Roman coins was discovered there in 1956.

vici:vici-17490.label: Ptolemais,Odeon,LT - PTOLEMAIS
vici:vici-17490.description: The smallest of Ptolemais's three theatres, built as an odeon for music and oratory; in the 4th-5th century AD its orchestra and stage were lined with waterproof cement to form a pool, possibly for mock sea-battles or acoustics.

vici:vici-17496.label: Teatro Camunnorum
vici:vici-17496.description: Roman theatre of Civitas Camunnorum, built around the mid-1st century AD on a terraced hillside; roughly a third survives, including the portico behind the stage and lateral staircases, now part of an archaeological park opened in 2003.

vici:vici-17567.label: El Kantara,Theatre,TN - MENINX
vici:vici-17567.description: A small Roman theatre in the northeastern quarter of Meninx, the island of Jerba's Roman-period administrative centre and a major Mediterranean production site for purple (murex) dye.

vici:vici-17568.label: El Kantara,Stadium,TN - Meninx
vici:vici-17568.description: A Roman circus/stadium in the northwestern quarter of Meninx, the island of Jerba's Roman-period administrative centre and a major Mediterranean production site for purple (murex) dye.

vici:vici-17570.label: Medeina,Theatre,TN - ALTUBUROS
vici:vici-17570.description: Roman theatre atop a hill at Althiburos (Kef region, Tunisia), c.60m in diameter with surviving arcaded galleries; under excavation and architectural study by a University of Palermo mission since 2007.

vici:vici-17606.label: Teatro Grumentum
vici:vici-17606.description: Julio-Claudian-era Roman theatre at Grumentum, a Lucanian municipium in Basilicata; partly excavated by Sestieri and Caputi in the 20th century and restored 1964-68 alongside the town's forum and amphitheatre.

vici:vici-17659.label: Teater Acquae Statiellae
vici:vici-17659.description: Imperial-era Roman theatre of Aquae Statiellae (Acqui Terme), uncovered in the late 1990s near the Bollente thermal spring; some spectator seats were cut directly into the hillside, its stage now buried under modern buildings.

vici:vici-17668.label: Anfiteatro (Agro Nocerino-Sarnese)
vici:vici-17668.description: Neronian-era amphitheatre of Nuceria Alfaterna (Nocera Superiore), c.125x102m and among the largest in Campania, built after Nero banned spectacles at Pompeii following the AD 59 riot; rediscovered in 1929, still mostly buried.

vici:vici-17731.label: Circus Trier
vici:vici-17731.description: Roman circus of Augusta Treverorum (Trier), a c.450m hippodrome monumentalized in the early 2nd century AD and depicted on the Polydus charioteer mosaic; no above-ground remains survive today.

vici:vici-17746.label: Odeion of Agrippa
vici:vici-17746.description: Roofed concert hall built c.15 BC in the Athenian Agora, a gift of Marcus Agrippa; its two-story auditorium seated about 1,000 until the roof collapsed c.150 AD, later rebuilt with colossal Triton/Giant statues at its entrance.
vici:vici-17746.wikidataDescription: odeon in the Ancient Agora of Athens

vici:vici-17773.label: Epidauros Stadium
vici:vici-17773.description: Ancient Greek stadium at the Sanctuary of Asklepios, Epidaurus, built mainly in the 4th-3rd century BC with stone seating for foot races, wrestling and boxing held every four years during the Asklepieia games.

vici:vici-17781.label: Odeon, Epidaurus
vici:vici-17781.description: Small Roman-period roofed odeon (c.30x39m) built within the courtyard of the Hellenistic Gymnasium at the Asklepieion of Epidaurus, dated to the late 2nd/early 3rd century AD and used for pantomime and singing contests.

vici:vici-17788.label: Stadion, Messene
vici:vici-17788.description: Hellenistic stadium-gymnasium complex of Messene, built in the 3rd century BC and used into the 4th century AD; among the best-preserved ancient stadiums in Greece, with 18 rows of seats and Doric stoas housing the city's gymnasium.

vici:vici-17796.label: Stadion, Olympia
vici:vici-17796.description: Site of footraces and other athletic contests at the ancient Olympic Games from 776 BC; the track measures one Olympic stade (192.27 m) between marble starting and finish lines, with embankments once holding up to 45,000 spectators.
vici:vici-17796.wikidataDescription: ancient Olympic venue in Olympia, Greece

vici:vici-17809.label: Odeon forum Thessaloniki
vici:vici-17809.description: Roman-era odeon built in the 2nd century AD within the forum of Thessaloniki, on the site of an earlier bouleuterion; inscriptions and statues of the Muses found there confirm its use for musical contests and gladiatorial spectacles.

vici:vici-17815.label: Roman theatre, Dion
vici:vici-17815.description: Roman theatre built near the sanctuary of Zeus at Dion in the 2nd century AD, reusing material from the older Hellenistic theatre it replaced after the city became Roman; excavated south-east of that earlier structure.

vici:vici-17830.label: Stadium, Isthmia
vici:vici-17830.description: Stadium of the sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia, home of the Panhellenic Isthmian Games from 582 BC; two successive stadiums are attested, the later Hellenistic one fitted with a hysplex starting-gate mechanism for footraces.

vici:vici-17838.label: Stadion, Nemea
vici:vici-17838.description: Stadium of the sanctuary of Zeus at Nemea, built around 330 BC for the Nemean Games; athletes reached the track through a unique 36 m vaulted tunnel bearing ancient graffiti, including the victor's name Telestas.
vici:vici-17838.wikidataDescription: Ancient Greek stadium in Nemea, Corinthia

vici:vici-17877.label: Hippodrome, Beirut
vici:vici-17877.description: Roman hippodrome of Berytus, discovered in 1988 in Beirut's city centre; covering roughly 3,500 m² it was the largest known hippodrome in the Roman Levant, laid out with a circuit resembling Rome's Circus Maximus.
vici:vici-17877.wikidataDescription: a circus in the Roman colony of Berytus (modern-day Beirut)

vici:vici-17884.label: Square Arena, Tyrus
vici:vici-17884.description: Unique rectangular arena at Tyre's Al-Mina site, roughly 45 by 35 m with five rows of stone seating for about 2,000 spectators around a central pool; likely 4th-century AD in its present form, function unknown — possibly a water-sport venue.

vici:vici-18116.label: Theatre Laodicea
vici:vici-18116.description: Theatre of Laodicea ad Mare (modern Latakia), a Seleucid-founded port that later became capital of Roman Syria under Septimius Severus; its cavea, built against the southeastern hill, measured c. 100 m across but survives only in traces.

vici:vici-18359.label: Theater Zeugma
vici:vici-18359.description: Theatre of Zeugma, the Hellenistic-Roman city on the Euphrates named for its bridge of boats; excavated by Ankara University since 1987, the site is famed for its mosaics and was partly submerged when the Birecik Dam was completed in 2000.

vici:vici-18399.label: Seleucia on the Tigris, theater
vici:vici-18399.description: Theatre of Seleucia on the Tigris, the dynastic capital founded by Seleucus I Nicator; the Hellenistic theatre stood on the town's south side beside a porticoed square and was uncovered by University of Michigan excavations (1927-1937) and later Italian missions.

vici:vici-18400.label: Seleucia in Pieria, theater
vici:vici-18400.description: Theatre/amphitheatre of Seleucia Pieria, Antioch's fortified port founded by Seleucus I Nicator; twenty-four tiers of benches partly survive, and Antiochus III camped nearby before his 219 BC assault that retook the city from Ptolemaic Egypt.

vici:vici-18566.label: Stadion Arykanda
vici:vici-18566.description: Hellenistic stadium of Arykanda (3rd-2nd century BC), unusually short at just over 100 m; the city was famed for its wrestlers, and a shrine with eight niches built into the seating was dedicated to their patron gods Heracles and Hermes.

vici:vici-18582.label: Suburban Theatre, Hierapolis
vici:vici-18582.description: The lesser of Hierapolis's two theatres, sited east of the Basilica Baths on the mountainside; unlike the city's well-preserved main theatre, it was almost completely destroyed by earthquakes, leaving only a few stairs.

vici:vici-18651.label: Aptera, Theater
vici:vici-18651.description: Theatre of Aptera in Crete, built c. 3rd century BC and rebuilt in Roman style in the 1st century AD; damaged by a lime kiln erected in its cavea, it was excavated 2008-2015 and reopened in 2016 as Crete's only restored ancient theatre.

vici:vici-18701.label: Théâtre de Cenabum
vici:vici-18701.description: Theatre of Cenabum (Roman Orléans), built in the 1st century AD and enlarged in the 2nd, with a diameter exceeding 100 m and an orchestra c. 38 m across; unearthed in 1821 during quay construction, then demolished and its stone reused.

vici:vici-19259.label: Teatro romano (Montegrotto Terme)
vici:vici-19259.description: A small theatre/odeon within the Roman thermal bath complex at Montegrotto (ancient Aquae Patavinae), built from the later 1st century BC and used into the 3rd century AD; first uncovered in excavations of 1781–1788.

vici:vici-19265.label: Teatro romano (Asolo)
vici:vici-19265.description: Roman theatre of Acelum (ancient Asolo), with seating for about 1,000; discovered in the late 19th century by local pharmacist Pacifico Scomazzetto and largely uncovered in excavations led by Guido Rosada, 1988–1993.

vici:vici-19321.label: Ai Khanum, theater
vici:vici-19321.description: Hellenistic theatre at Ai-Khanoum (Alexandria on the Oxus) in Bactria, about 84 m in diameter with three royal loges and seating for 4,000–6,000; built under Seleucid/Greco-Bactrian rule and excavated by a French mission, 1965–1978.

vici:vici-19357.label: Aegae, Theater
vici:vici-19357.description: Theatre of Aigai (Vergina), built alongside the royal palace in the later 4th century BC; here King Philip II of Macedon was assassinated by his bodyguard Pausanias in 336 BC during his daughter's wedding celebrations.

vici:vici-19371.label: Théâtre d'Amel
vici:vici-19371.description: Gallo-Roman theatre at Amel-sur-l'Étang, forming a roughly 20-hectare suburban sanctuary complex with five temples and baths, revealed by aerial and geophysical surveys (2004–2011) near the neighboring Senon settlement.

vici:vici-19373.label: Théâtre de Senon
vici:vici-19373.description: Gallo-Roman theatre identified by aerial and geophysical survey at the Senon vicus (Meuse), part of a paired sanctuary agglomeration with the nearby Amel theatre-and-temples complex, occupied 1st–4th centuries AD.

vici:vici-19498.label: Teatro romano de Córdoba
vici:vici-19498.description: Augustan-era theatre of Roman Corduba (built before c. 5 BC), the largest in Hispania and second only to Rome's Theatre of Marcellus in the empire, seating about 15,000; rediscovered in 1994 beneath the city's Archaeological Museum.
vici:vici-19498.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman theatre in Cordoba, Spain

vici:vici-19606.label: Olba Theatre
vici:vici-19606.description: Roman theatre at Olba in Cilicia, built during the joint reign of emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus (161–169 AD) with seating for about 2,000, standing near the city's nymphaeum and Temple of Zeus.

vici:vici-19889.label: Stadium NICOPOLIS
vici:vici-19889.description: Stadium built at Nicopolis for Augustus's Actian Games, inaugurated in 27 BC to mark his victory at Actium. Its two rounded ends (sphendonai) made it a transitional 'stadium-amphitheater' form, seating roughly 10,000.

vici:vici-19924.label: Diocletian’s palace amphitheatre
vici:vici-19924.description: A c. 50-metre Roman amphitheatre outside Diocletian's palace walls, built alongside the palace in the early 4th century AD; long mistaken for a theatre's seating, confirmed as an amphitheatre by 2013 excavations north of the old town.

vici:vici-19940.label: Cyrene, theater
vici:vici-19940.description: Greek theatre cut into Cyrene's acropolis slope in the late 6th century BC, the oldest and largest of the city's five theatres, seating over 1,000; converted into a Roman amphitheatre in the 2nd century AD.

vici:vici-21686.label: Tiberias
vici:vici-21686.description: Roman theatre at the foot of Mount Berenice near Tiberias, built in the early 1st century AD close to the city's founding by Herod Antipas and enlarged in the 2nd century; seated over 7,000, excavated from 1990.

vici:vici-23250.label: Theatre of Klitoria
vici:vici-23250.description: Theatre of the Arcadian city of Kleitor, in its southwestern quarter; already ruined and stripped of stone in Roman times, with its cavea and part of the seating only brought to light by recent excavation.

vici:vici-23252.label: Kos
vici:vici-23252.description: Roman Imperial-period theatre at Ambavri south of Kos town, about 108 m wide with capacity for up to 13,000, likely tied to festivals of the nearby Asklepieion; Hellenistic 'almond stone' seating hints at a 3rd-century-BC predecessor.

vici:vici-23293.label: Oiniades
vici:vici-23293.description: Theatre of ancient Oiniadai in Acarnania, first excavated in December 1900 by American archaeologist Benjamin Powell, who uncovered the stage, orchestra, and much of the cavea; fully cleared by Greek archaeologists in 1987.

vici:vici-23299.label: Herakleia Salbace
vici:vici-23299.description: Carian city near modern Vakıf in the Tavas district, on the Phrygia-Caria border; Christianised early, its bishop Polychronius attended the Council of Ephesus in 431 AD, and it later became a titular Catholic see.
vici:vici-23299.wikidataDescription: ancient city of Caria, in modern-day Turkey

vici:vici-23313.label: Aigaiai [Aeolis]
vici:vici-23313.description: Theatre of the Aeolian hilltop city of Aigai, excavated since 2004 by Ege University; its vomitorium (entrance passage) was uncovered in 2018 alongside the bouleuterion and odeon.

vici:vici-23561.label: Alexandria Troas
vici:vici-23561.description: Large theatre of Alexandria Troas, built in the Greek tradition and embellished under Hadrian in the 2nd century AD; 2024 excavations estimated its capacity at roughly 12,000 spectators.

vici:vici-23820.label: Theatre Amphiaraion
vici:vici-23820.description: 2nd-century BC theatre at the healing sanctuary of Amphiaraos near Oropos; its Doric stage building survives along with five inscribed marble priests' thrones, seating about 300.

vici:vici-23987.label: Abila of Decapolis
vici:vici-23987.description: Roman theatre built into a hillside at Abila, one of the ten cities of the Decapolis; partially excavated since 1980 by John Brown University alongside a nymphaeum and Byzantine churches.

vici:vici-24006.label: Sebastia
vici:vici-24006.description: Theatre at Samaria-Sebaste with a semicircular, two-tier cavea built against the north slope during the Severan dynasty (early 3rd century AD), after Septimius Severus granted the city colonia status; excavated in the 1930s.

vici:vici-24023.label: Pessinus in Phrygia
vici:vici-24023.description: Monumental theatre-shaped stairway and colonnaded square in the sanctuary quarter of Pessinus, the Phrygian cult center of the mother goddess Cybele; excavated in the 1970s next to a Roman-period temple.

vici:vici-24175.label: Stadium of Miletus
vici:vici-24175.description: Stadium of Miletus, built in the first half of the 2nd century BC under Eumenes II of Pergamon; 191 m long with seating for roughly 15,000 on twelve tiers, and given a monumental colonnaded gate in the early 3rd century AD.

vici:vici-24210.label: Asclepieion of Messene
vici:vici-24210.description: Ekklesiasterion (assembly-hall theatre) within the Asclepieion complex at Messene, first built in the late 3rd century BC for civic assemblies and performances honoring Messene and Asclepius; its proscenium and orchestra were repaired in the 1st and 3rd centuries AD.

vici:vici-24275.label: Smyrna Theatre
vici:vici-24275.description: Built on the north slope of Mount Pagos in the 3rd century BC and enlarged under Hadrian, Smyrna's theatre seated roughly 20,000 and hosted the provincial 'Asian Games'; abandoned in the 4th century AD and buried until excavations resumed in 2012-2016.

vici:vici-24291.label: Philadelphia [Alaşehir]
vici:vici-24291.description: A small Roman-period theatre on the north edge of Toptepe Hill, the only visible survivor of Philadelphia (founded c. 159-138 BC by Attalus II of Pergamon), one of the Seven Churches of Revelation addressed by John.

vici:vici-24336.label: Apollonia in Lycia
vici:vici-24336.description: A small Hellenistic theatre with about ten rows of seats at Apollonia in Lycia, a minor city that by the Roman period belonged to a sympoliteia led by Aperlae within the Lycian League.
vici:vici-24336.wikidataDescription: ancient city of Lycia, in modern-day Turkey

vici:vici-24368.label: Odeon of Selge
vici:vici-24368.description: An odeon on the acropolis of Selge, a rugged Pisidian mountain city on the Eurymedon river that struck its own coinage and, alongside its better-known theatre and stadium, hosted civic assembly and musical performances.

vici:vici-24426.label: Stadium of Sillyon
vici:vici-24426.description: A roughly 10,000-seat stadium at Sillyon, built starting in the 1st century AD and used into the 5th century for athletic contests and festivals; only about a quarter has been excavated as of the 2020s.

vici:vici-24446.label: Kadyanda in Lycia
vici:vici-24446.description: A small south-facing theatre with 18 rows of seats at Kadyanda, dated to the late 2nd or early 1st century BC, part of a hilltop Lycian city discovered by Charles Fellows and identified by its native name Kadawanti.

vici:vici-24450.label: Stadium of Sagalassos
vici:vici-24450.description: A 1st-century AD stadium on the western edge of Sagalassos seating about 9,000 - far more than the city's own population - built to host athletic and gladiatorial events for the wider province of Pisidia.

vici:vici-24463.label: Heloros [Eloros]
vici:vici-24463.description: A theatre, popularly nicknamed 'Colisseo' by locals, is the most conspicuous ruin of Heloros, a coastal Syracusan colony that stayed loyal to Hieron II until Rome retook it from Carthaginian sympathies in 214 BC.

vici:vici-24624.label: Iulia Concordia Sabittaria theatre
vici:vici-24624.description: Theatre of Iulia Concordia (modern Concordia Sagittaria), a Roman colony founded 42 BC where the Via Annia crossed the Via Postumia; its remains survive in Parco Signini alongside the forum and baths.

vici:vici-24654.label: Balsa amphitheatre
vici:vici-24654.description: Amphitheatre of Roman Balsa (Luz de Tavira, Algarve), identified only through non-invasive geophysical survey of the largely unexcavated town; local inscriptions record residents funding naumachiae and boxing bouts.

vici:vici-24662.label: Olisipo
vici:vici-24662.description: Theatre of Felicitas Iulia Olisipo, built under Augustus and enlarged in AD 57 by the benefactor Caius Heius Primus; held roughly 4,000-5,000 spectators. Rediscovered in 1798, excavated from 1964, now the Museu do Teatro Romano.

vici:vici-24663.label: Bracara Augusta
vici:vici-24663.description: Roman theatre of Bracara Augusta (Braga), the only one known in the northwestern Iberian Peninsula; found by chance in 1999 beside the Maximinos baths, with a cavea about 72.6 m across seating roughly 4,000-4,500.

vici:vici-24664.label: Bracara Augusta
vici:vici-24664.description: Roman theatre of Bracara Augusta (Braga), the only one known in the northwestern Iberian Peninsula; found by chance in 1999 beside the Maximinos baths, with a cavea about 72.6 m across seating roughly 4,000-4,500.

vici:vici-24702.label: Theatre of Kremna
vici:vici-24702.description: One of two theatres at Kremna, a Pisidian hill city made the Roman colony Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Cremnena after King Amyntas's death in 25 BC; the site later withstood the rebel Lydius's siege in the 270s AD.

vici:vici-24713.label: Bararus
vici:vici-24713.description: Roman theatre of Bararus (Henchir Rougga) in Byzacena, sited across the wadi from the town's forum; a stage roughly 29x30 m is still traceable, though the structure is heavily ruined after stone-robbing and the earthquake of 365 CE that devastated the city.

vici:vici-24714.label: Thugga
vici:vici-24714.description: Theatre of Thugga, built 168-169 CE under Antoninus Pius and personally funded by local magnate Publius Marcius Quadratus; its 19 tiers seated about 3,500 spectators, making it one of the best-preserved theatres of Roman Africa.

vici:vici-24718.label: Utica
