vici:vici-24718.description: One of two Roman theatres at Utica, the Phoenician-founded city that briefly served as first capital of Africa Proconsularis after Carthage's fall; the site's Roman quarters were only uncovered by excavation starting in 1948-58.

vici:vici-24719.label: Utica
vici:vici-24719.description: One of two Roman theatres at Utica, the Phoenician-founded city that briefly served as first capital of Africa Proconsularis after Carthage's fall; the site's Roman quarters were only uncovered by excavation starting in 1948-58.

vici:vici-24720.label: Utica
vici:vici-24720.description: One of two Roman theatres at Utica, the Phoenician-founded city that briefly served as first capital of Africa Proconsularis after Carthage's fall; the site's Roman quarters were only uncovered by excavation starting in 1948-58.

vici:vici-24722.label: Sicca Veneria
vici:vici-24722.description: Roman theatre at Sicca Veneria (modern El Kef), a hill city on the road linking Carthage to Theveste, sited near the Casbah; the structure remains largely unpublished, with no established construction date or capacity.

vici:vici-24748.label: Kourion, Stadium
vici:vici-24748.description: The only fully excavated stadium on Cyprus, built near Kourion under Antoninus Pius in the 2nd century CE; a U-shaped track about 217 m long with seven rows of seating for c. 6,000 spectators, used for pentathlon events until the 4th century CE.

vici:vici-24756.label: Paphos, Roman theatre
vici:vici-24756.description: Theatre of Nea Paphos, cut into the bedrock of Fabrika hill and first built c. 300 BCE under the Ptolemies; monumentally expanded under the Antonines to seat up to 8,500, it stayed in use for over six centuries until earthquakes ended performances in the late 4th century CE.

vici:vici-24767.label: Kydonia
vici:vici-24767.description: Roman-period theater of Kydonia (ancient predecessor of Chania, Crete); the standing building was demolished in 1583 when Venetian authorities quarried its stone to reinforce the town's fortifications.

vici:vici-25175.label: Mopsouhestia [Mopsuestia]
vici:vici-25175.description: Roman-era theater of Mopsuestia (modern Misis/Yakapınar) on the Pyramus (Ceyhan) River, part of the city's public architecture alongside a stadium, colonnaded street, and the city's well-known Roman bridge; Mopsuestia prospered as a grain-exporting center after Pompey's annexation of Cilicia in 67 BC.

vici:vici-25185.label: Scavi archeologici di Via G. Marconi
vici:vici-25185.description: Site near Pozzuoli's former Marconi school, proposed by archaeologist Davide Peluso (2008) as the location of Puteoli's lost Roman theatre, based on the area's topography and nearby inscriptions of theatre-linked musicians' guilds (tibicines, scabillarii); unconfirmed and never excavated as such.

vici:vici-25212.label: Phlious - Φλειοῦς
vici:vici-25212.description: Theatre of the Peloponnesian city-state of Phlius, noted by Pausanias below the acropolis near temples of Asclepius and Demeter; excavations behind its stage building found twin stone foundations interpreted as supports for a mechane used for 'deus ex machina' stage entrances.

vici:vici-25517.label: Ekklesiasterion of Morgantina
vici:vici-25517.description: Hellenistic assembly hall of Morgantina in Sicily, a fan-shaped flight of monumental steps in the agora built for meetings of the citizen assembly (ekklesia), dated to the mid-3rd century BC and uncovered by the Princeton University expedition (1955-1968).

vici:vici-25533.label: Stadium of Kadyanda
vici:vici-25533.description: Rock-cut stadium of the Lycian hill city of Kadyanda, roughly 100 m long and 9-10 m wide with six surviving rows of seating on its north side, known from numerous inscriptions honoring victors of two local athletic festivals.

vici:vici-25556.label: Bargilia
vici:vici-25556.description: Bargylia, a Carian coastal city with a temple of Artemis Cindyas, sheltered Philip V of Macedon's fleet in 201/200 BC while it was blockaded there by Rhodian and Pergamene warships; its ruins include a theatre, defensive walls, and a palaestra.

vici:vici-25559.label: Iasos (Iasus) - Bouleuterion
vici:vici-25559.description: Council house (bouleuterion) of Iasos in Caria, first built in the 4th century BC near the agora's south stoa; rebuilt in the 1st century AD with a three-quarter-circle cavea, functioning as a small covered theatre embellished under Hadrian.

vici:vici-25618.label: Euromos
vici:vici-25618.description: Hellenistic theatre of Euromos in Caria, carved into a hillside and dating to about the mid-3rd century BC; originally seated roughly 2,000 spectators, though only five rows of seating survive above ground pending further excavation.

vici:vici-25709.label: Corinthos - Korinthos
vici:vici-25709.description: Theatre of ancient Corinth, built c. 400 BC and enlarged to seat up to 18,000; rebuilt under Rome and later used as a beast-fight arena, abandoned after Alaric's 396 AD sack. The nearby 'Erastus pavement' is linked by many scholars to the Erastus of Romans 16:23.

vici:vici-25758.label: Patra, Roman Amphitheatre
vici:vici-25758.description: A Roman amphitheatre (200 x 90 m) raised at Patrae under Domitian in the late 1st century AD, reputedly marking the colony's centenary; it hosted the renowned Caesarea games of racing, pentathlon, boxing and wrestling.

vici:vici-25778.label: Keryneia Achaias
vici:vici-25778.description: Theatre of Ceryneia, an Achaean League city on a height above the Cerynites river; in myth the home of the Ceryneian Hind captured by Heracles, and a member state when the League revived around 280 BC.
vici:vici-25778.wikidataDescription: town and polis (city-state) of ancient Achaea

vici:vici-25784.label: Leontio
vici:vici-25784.description: Small theatre of Leontion excavated in 1958 by N. Gialouris on Kastritsi Hill, its nine surviving rows of seats built into the fortified Achaean city's defences; Leontion was destroyed by Philip V after 217 BC.

vici:vici-25903.label: Şarköy, Tufanbeyli
vici:vici-25903.description: Roman theatre of Comana Cappadociae (Şar), the Cataonian temple-state sacred to the moon goddess Ma, visited by Strabo and Julius Caesar; excavated from 1967 alongside a monumental Roman gate and Byzantine church remains.

vici:vici-25987.label: Balbura, Upper Theatre
vici:vici-25987.description: One of two theatres at Balboura, cut into the steep southern slope of the acropolis about 70 m above the valley; its cavea is unusually interrupted by a block of natural rock, and it remains unexcavated with no inscriptions found.

vici:vici-25989.label: Balbura, Lower Theatre
vici:vici-25989.description: Balbura, in the Cabalian district of northern Lycia, had two theatres: this lower one lies in a natural hollow before the mountain south of the stream, opposite the upper theatre whose cavea is split by a rock outcrop.

vici:vici-25996.label: Bubon, Theatre
vici:vici-25996.description: Bubon's small sandstone theatre, at Dikmen Tepe near Ibecik in the Cabalian hills, preserved an inscribed letter of Commodus praising the city for repelling bandit raids and gaining a third vote in the Lycian League.

vici:vici-26013.label: Olympia, Hippodrome
vici:vici-26013.description: South of the stadium, Olympia's hippodrome staged four- and two-horse chariot and horse races from the 7th century BC; Pausanias described its starting gates and turning posts, but Alpheios river silt has buried all trace of it.
vici:vici-26013.wikidataDescription: ancient track for chariot and horse racing at the Olympic games

vici:vici-26035.label: Rhamnous, Theatre
vici:vici-26035.description: The small theatre of the fortified Attic deme of Rhamnous, near the sanctuary of Nemesis, doubled as public meeting space and lay within the settlement's extended 4th-century BC fortification circuit.

vici:vici-26053.label: Arcadian Orchomenos
vici:vici-26053.description: Cut into the acropolis slope of Arcadian Orchomenos around 300 BC, this 40-plus-row theatre held over 4,000 spectators for games honoring Dionysus; first excavated in 1913 by G. Blum and A. Plassart.

vici:vici-26099.label: Parion, Odeon
vici:vici-26099.description: The odeon of Parion, the Hellespontine city made a Roman colony under Augustus, stands among the site's well-preserved Roman public buildings alongside its theatre and baths.

vici:vici-26152.label: Nysa ad Maeandrum, Bouleuterion
vici:vici-26152.description: Nysa's bouleuterion, or gerontikon, in the northwest corner of the agora seated 600-700 people in a 12-row semicircular auditorium later reused as an odeon; recent scholarship dates the surviving building to the Antonine period, with no earlier phase.

vici:vici-26180.label: Amantia, Stadium
vici:vici-26180.description: Hellenistic stadium of the Illyrian city of Amantia, built on a terraced hillside in the first half of the 3rd century BC; c. 60m by 12.5m with 17 rows of seats on one side, holding about 4,000 spectators for footraces, boxing and discus.

vici:vici-26182.label: Bylis, Theatre
vici:vici-26182.description: Hellenistic theatre of the Illyrian city of Byllis, built in the 3rd century BC; about 78m across and 16m high with roughly 40 rows of seating, holding up to 7,500 spectators.

vici:vici-26261.label: Nicopolis of Epirus, Amphitheatre
vici:vici-26261.description: Roman theatre of Nicopolis, founded by Augustus after his 31 BC victory at Actium; hosted the quadrennial Actian Games and, per orchestra-barrier net-anchor holes and an inscribed invitation, was later adapted for gladiatorial and animal-hunt spectacles.

vici:vici-26289.label: Sparta, Theatre of Artemision
vici:vici-26289.description: Roman-period theatral structure built around 3rd century AD around the altar of the Sanctuary of Artemis Orthia at Sparta, giving spectators seating to watch the ritual flogging (diamastigosis) of Spartan youths; excavated by the British School at Athens, 1906–10.

vici:vici-26364.label: Smyrna, Stadium
vici:vici-26364.description: U-shaped stadium on the slope of Mount Pagos (Kadifekale) in ancient Smyrna, traditionally identified as the site where bishop Polycarp was martyred by Proconsul Statius Quadratus in the mid-2nd century AD.

vici:vici-26435.label: Sidyma, Theatre
vici:vici-26435.description: Small Roman-period theatre of the Lycian hill town of Sidyma, described by 19th-century explorer Charles Fellows as diminutive but finely built; the site has never been officially excavated.

vici:vici-26610.label: Thassos - Odeon
vici:vici-26610.description: Roman-period odeon (small roofed hall for music and oratory) in the agora of ancient Thasos, uncovered during French School at Athens excavations of the agora that began in 1911.

vici:vici-26778.label: Notion, Theatre
vici:vici-26778.description: Theatre in the eastern quarter of Notion (New Colophon), near the North Gate; first noted in the early 20th century, investigated by Erol Atalay in the 1980s and surveyed by a University of Michigan–Brown University team in 2014–2018.

vici:vici-26782.label: Panionion, Theatre
vici:vici-26782.description: Small rock-cut theatre or odeon (about 32 m across, 11 seat rows) at the foot of the Panionion hill on Mt Mycale, presumed to be the bouleuterion where the twelve-city Ionian League met for the Panionia festival of Poseidon Helikonios.

vici:vici-26837.label: Metropolis, Reception Hall
vici:vici-26837.description: Frescoed reception hall of the Roman theatre at Metropolis in Ionia, paved with a mosaic (its figures debated as either a Four Seasons allegory or Dionysiac scene), uncovered during excavations running since 1989.

vici:vici-27446.label: Amphitheatre of Tusculum
vici:vici-27446.description: 2nd-century AD amphitheatre outside the walls of Tusculum, roughly 80 x 53 m with a capacity of about 3,000; its entrances were excavated in 1820 and the rest in 1867.

vici:vici-27607.label: Durovernum Theater
vici:vici-27607.description: Roman theatre at Durovernum Cantiacorum (Canterbury): an earthen-banked timber theatre built under the Flavians (AD 69-96) was replaced around AD 220 by a stone theatre seating roughly 3,000, one of the largest in Britain.

vici:vici-27806.label: Camulodunum Circus
vici:vici-27806.description: The only confirmed Roman circus (chariot-racing track) in Britain, built in the early 2nd century AD, possibly under Hadrian, south of the Colchester colonia; about 450 m long with eight starting gates and seating for 8,000+, discovered in 2004-05 at the former Colchester Garrison.

vici:vici-27807.label: Camulodunum Theater
vici:vici-27807.description: Roman theatre at the Gosbecks religious complex near Colchester (Camulodunum), Britain's largest at about 82 m diameter and c.5,000 seats; a timber theatre was replaced by one of turf, clay and stone revetment, demolished by the mid-3rd century.

vici:vici-27961.label: Bouleuterion  of Cnidus [Knidos]
vici:vici-27961.description: A Roman-period council house on a terrace east of Knidos's Harbor Street; a raised central podium and traces of a colonnaded, timber-roofed hall identify it as the city's bouleuterion.

vici:vici-27979.label: Theatre of Cnidus [Knidos]
vici:vici-27979.description: One of two theatres at Knidos, cut into the hillside above the harbor; the excavated, harbor-side theatre held roughly 5,000 spectators, with a temple of Dionysos standing nearby.

vici:vici-28127.label: Theodosiopolis [Perperene]
vici:vici-28127.description: Site of ancient Perperene, an Aeolian colony in Mysia on the Kozak plateau near Pergamon, noted for copper mines and vineyards; later renamed Theodosiopolis and became a Christian bishopric.

vici:vici-28392.label: Nemea, Hippodrome
vici:vici-28392.description: No hippodrome has actually been located at Nemea; its existence and the lengths of its horse and four-horse chariot races are known only from ancient literary sources, not excavation.

vici:vici-28395.label: Stadium of Isthmia
vici:vici-28395.description: Early stadium of the Panhellenic sanctuary of Poseidon at Isthmia, built around 550 BC with a stone-and-rope starting mechanism (hysplex); excavated by Oscar Broneer from 1952, it hosted the biennial Isthmian Games.

vici:vici-28465.label: Iato, Bouleuterion II
vici:vici-28465.description: One of the civic assembly buildings on Monte Iato, the Hellenistic-Roman hill city of ancient Ietas in western Sicily, excavated by the University of Zurich since 1971.

vici:vici-28578.label: Theatre, Mylasa [Milas]
vici:vici-28578.description: Theatre of ancient Mylasa, Caria's largest city; built on the east slope of Topbaşı Hill, it survives only as an eroded hollow in the bedrock, with no seating visibly preserved today.

vici:vici-28630.label: Bargilia [Bargylia], Odeum
vici:vici-28630.description: A small, hillside-cut odeum among the acropolis ruins of Bargylia, a Carian coastal city near modern Boğaziçi; the site is privately owned and unexcavated, so the structure survives only as surface remains.

vici:vici-28677.label: Theangela
vici:vici-28677.description: Carian city founded (or renamed) by the Hecatomnid dynast Mausolus in the mid-4th century BC via synoecism of the Lelegian town of Syangela; subjected to Halicarnassus after Alexander's conquest, and birthplace of the historian Philippus of Theangela.

vici:vici-28743.label: Kastabos, Theatre
vici:vici-28743.description: Theatre built into the hillside within the sanctuary of the healing demigoddess Hemithea (Molpadia) at Kastabos, used for her festival, the Kastabeia; the sanctuary's main buildings date to c.300 BC and were excavated by J.M. Cook and W.H. Plommer from 1960.

vici:vici-28777.label: Amyzon, Theatre
vici:vici-28777.description: Carian sanctuary city of Zeus, enclosed by massive isodomic fortification walls; excavated and published by Louis and Jeanne Robert, who recorded inscriptions including a 351/341 BC dedication by the Hecatomnid Idrieus and a 203/190 BC letter from the Seleucid official Zeuxis.

vici:vici-28822.label: Colossae, Theatre
vici:vici-28822.description: Roman-period theatre on Colossae's eastern slope, estimated to have seated around 5,000; the Phrygian city is best known as recipient of the Apostle Paul's Epistle to the Colossians. Systematic excavation began only in 2021, led by Pamukkale University.

vici:vici-28847.label: Myrina, Theatre
vici:vici-28847.description: Aeolian coastal city whose theatre has been located northwest of Beriki Tepe hill, though little survives visibly; excavations in 1880-82 uncovered roughly 4,000 Hellenistic-period tombs with terracotta figurines, most now in the Louvre.

vici:vici-28850.label: Chrysavgi
vici:vici-28850.description: Well-preserved Hellenistic theatre at the fortified hilltop settlement known as the "Castle of Veliani" (identified as ancient Elaea) near Chrysavgi in Thesprotia, above the Acheron-Kokytos valley, alongside an adjacent Hellenistic arcade and semi-underground storage rooms.

vici:vici-28854.label: Pitane
vici:vici-28854.description: Aeolian city founded by colonists from Lesbos, notable for its two harbours and as birthplace of the philosopher Arcesilaus, founder of the Middle Academy; theatre and stadium remains survive, and the town suffered a severe earthquake under Titus.

vici:vici-28864.label: Klazomenai - Clazomenae
vici:vici-28864.description: Ionian city and birthplace of the philosopher Anaxagoras; after relocating from the mainland to an offshore island during the Ionian Revolt, it built a north-facing theatre there alongside a paved street and a temple.

vici:vici-28891.label: Theatre Florentia
vici:vici-28891.description: Roman theatre of Florentia, built beneath what is now Palazzo Vecchio in the 1st century AD; excavated 1876–2010, its cavea held an estimated 10,000–15,000 spectators, comparable to Rome's Theatre of Marcellus.
vici:vici-28891.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman theatre in Florence, Italy

vici:vici-28915.label: Notion [Notium], Bouleuterion
vici:vici-28915.description: Bouleuterion of the Ionian city of Notion, one of the largest known Hellenistic council houses (c. 30.5 x 24.3 m, seating ~500); excavated by the University of Michigan from 2023 after prior illicit digging.

vici:vici-28981.label: Marcellum (Sebatum)
vici:vici-28981.description: Marketplace (macellum) at Sebatum, a Roman road station on the Via Julia Augusta near modern St. Lorenzen in South Tyrol, where the settlement's weekly nundinae (markets) were held; now the Mansio Sebatum museum site.

vici:vici-29006.label: Samaria - Sebastia
vici:vici-29006.description: Roman theatre at Sebaste (Samaria), built by Herod the Great after Augustus granted him the city in 27 BC; part of Herod's Augustan forum complex, it could seat up to about 6,000 spectators.
vici:vici-29006.wikidataDescription: municipality in Nablus, West Bank, Palestine

vici:vici-29249.label: Aquinum, Amphitheatre
vici:vici-29249.description: Amphitheatre of Aquinum, a Roman colony traditionally considered the birthplace of the poet Juvenal; only scant remains survive within the walled site alongside temples, a basilica and the Porta Capuana gate.

vici:vici-29257.label: Bouleuterion of Pamphylian Seleucia - Lybre
vici:vici-29257.description: Bouleuterion (also used as an odeon) in the agora of Seleucia/Lyrbe in Pamphylia, a six-row council chamber that hosted both civic assembly meetings and musical performances.

vici:vici-29316.label: Terracina Amphitheater
vici:vici-29316.description: Amphitheatre in the harbour district of Roman Terracina, an imperial-period building of which little survives; a marble bust of Sophocles found nearby in 1838 is now in the Vatican Museums.

vici:vici-29358.label: Stadium of Selge
vici:vici-29358.description: Selge's Roman-era stadium, cut into the hillside with a U-shaped track and a single sphendone; only a few tiers of seating survive from a renovation programme that also rebuilt the city's agora and theatre.

vici:vici-29362.label: Mailand - Turm der Carceres (Circus von Mediolanum)
vici:vici-29362.description: The starting-gate tower of Mediolanum's circus, built for Maximian around 293–305 AD as part of Milan's imperial building programme; later converted into the bell tower of the church of San Maurizio, now within the Archaeological Museum.

vici:vici-29423.label: Theater of Issos
vici:vici-29423.description: A small Hellenistic theatre at Issus, identified with Kinet Höyük near İskenderun, site of Alexander the Great's decisive 333 BC victory over Darius III; excavated during the Bilkent University campaigns of 1992–2012.

vici:vici-29764.label: Ascalon Theater
vici:vici-29764.description: A Roman-era odeon at Ascalon (Tel Ashkelon) built mainly for musical performances, excavated alongside Herod's basilica and restored during the Israel Nature and Parks Authority's park renovation begun in 2008.

vici:vici-29785.label: Stadium of Amrit
vici:vici-29785.description: A Phoenician stadium at Amrit carved from bedrock, about 230 m long with seven rows of seats partly preserved; dated to the 4th–3rd century BC, it is among the oldest stadiums known, likely used for sacred and funerary games.

vici:vici-29799.label: Pinara, Odeoum
vici:vici-29799.description: The ruined odeon of Pinara, one of the six chief cities of the Lycian League (three votes), stands near the site entrance; the city's better-preserved theatre lies nearby.

vici:vici-29803.label: Sphendone
vici:vici-29803.description: The Sphendone, curved southern end of the Hippodrome of Constantinople, rests on 25 vaulted arches that leveled the track toward the sea slope; its remains, excavated by Stanley Casson's British team in 1927, are the hippodrome's most substantial survival.

vici:vici-29810.label: Vise Odeon
vici:vici-29810.description: A 2nd-century AD Roman theatre at Bizye (modern Vize), the only theatre known in ancient Thrace, with marble seating for about 4,000; excavated in 1998 and further studied in 2003, its finds are held in Kırklareli Museum.

vici:vici-29835.label: Apollonia Theater
vici:vici-29835.description: A Hellenistic Greek theatre cut into Apollonia's hillside north of the Agora, buttressed by an artificial bank; now under excavation by a joint German-Albanian team, it fell from use in late antiquity when a church was built over its reused seating blocks.

vici:vici-29836.label: Apollonia Odeon
vici:vici-29836.description: Small odeon on the north side of Apollonia's Agora, built around the mid-2nd century AD with sixteen rows of seats for roughly 300 spectators and a shrine faced by two Ionic columns; excavated 1978, restored 1984-87.

vici:vici-29842.label: Oricum Theater
vici:vici-29842.description: Theatre built at Oricum by the 2nd-century AD senator and benefactor Herodes Atticus, later destroyed by an earthquake; a nearby monumental fountain (nymphaeum) used as a rainwater cistern was long mistaken for a second theatre.

vici:vici-29881.label: Idebessiois, Theatre
vici:vici-29881.description: Small Hellenistic-style theatre with only seven or eight rows of seating, built into the northwest slope of Idebessos's acropolis hill; the city has never been excavated, known only from Akdeniz University surveys in 2000 and 2008.

vici:vici-29912.label: Villa Potenza, Macerata
vici:vici-29912.description: Roman theatre of Helvia Recina, the largest in the Picenum region, which flourished under Augustus and Tiberius; its 71.8m cavea is the only above-ground remnant of the city and today hosts open-air opera performances.

vici:vici-29913.label: Urbisaglia Theatre
vici:vici-29913.description: Roman theatre of Urbs Salvia, built in 23 AD in the Hellenistic tradition on a hillside terrace above the forum; one of the largest theatres in ancient Italy, with a three-tier cavea and colonnaded stage backdrop.

vici:vici-30009.label: Apollonia Ad Rhyndacu Theater
vici:vici-30009.description: Theatre on Zambaktepe's slopes above Lake Uluabat at Apollonia ad Rhyndacum, founded in the late 4th century BC with Hellenistic and Roman building phases; seated about 6,000 in an 80m cavea; excavation since 2021 uncovered an inscribed reserved seat naming a priestess.

vici:vici-30088.label: Tiermes Theatre
vici:vici-30088.description: One of the largest Roman theatres in Spain, partly carved into the sandstone hillside of Tiermes (Termantia), a Celtiberian hillfort allied with Numantia that became a Roman municipium in 98 BCE.

vici:vici-30154.label: Karatas Stadium - Magarsus
vici:vici-30154.description: Theatre of Magarsus, the port-sanctuary of Mallos where Alexander the Great sacrificed to Athena Magarsis before Issus; excavations uncovered a c. 30m-wide, 150m-long theatre seating roughly 3,000, with a rare sea view.
vici:vici-30154.wikidataDescription: ancient city of Cilicia in modern-day Turkey

vici:vici-30167.label: Sulun Theatre - Prymnessos
vici:vici-30167.description: Small, still-unexcavated theatre (estimated capacity c. 2,000) on a hillside at Prymnessos, a Phrygian town near Sülün that later served as a Christian bishopric attested at councils from 381 to 787 CE.

vici:vici-30170.label: Astra Theatre
vici:vici-30170.description: Theatre of Astra, a walled Roman-Byzantine town in Isauria near Tamaşalık whose identity was confirmed by inscriptions first recorded by Sterrett in 1885; rescue excavations there also uncovered a necropolis and church.
vici:vici-30170.wikidataDescription: town of ancient Isauria, inhabited in Roman times

vici:vici-30173.label: Kolybrassos Odeon
vici:vici-30173.description: Small theatre/odeion at Colybrassus, a Cilician hill settlement 1,000m up on Susuz Dağ that also held a Temple of Hercules; the city became a Byzantine bishopric before vanishing from record after 1199 CE.

vici:vici-30176.label: Perpene Theatre
vici:vici-30176.description: Perperene was an Aeolian colony of ancient Mysia on the Kozak plateau near Bergama, known in antiquity for its copper mines and vineyards; specific details of its theatre are not attested.

vici:vici-30195.label: Gigti Theatre
vici:vici-30195.description: Gigthis (Bou Ghrara), a Phoenician trading post absorbed by Rome after Thapsus in 46 BCE and later a municipium under Antoninus Pius; its forum, arch, and temples were cleared by French excavators from 1901.

vici:vici-30379.label: Esenkoy Theatre - Harpasa
vici:vici-30379.description: Carian city founded in the 6th century BCE on the Harpasus river, mentioned by Ptolemy, Stephanus of Byzantium, and Pliny; its late Hellenistic-to-early-Imperial theatre and city walls survive near Esenköy in the Nazilli district.

vici:vici-31066.label: Birketein Theatre - Gerasa
vici:vici-31066.description: Small theatre (capacity roughly 1,000) built into a hillside at the Birketein sanctuary north of Gerasa, part of a 2nd–3rd century AD complex with twin pools and baths; the site hosted the nocturnal Maiuma festival of Dionysus in late antiquity.

vici:vici-31073.label: Assos, Bouleuterion
vici:vici-31073.description: The council house (bouleuterion) of Assos, a square building roughly 21x21m with columns in antis, built in the late 4th century BC by the local benefactor Ladomos and his wife — one of the oldest bouleuteria known in Asia Minor.

vici:vici-31101.label: Thelepte Theatre
vici:vici-31101.description: Theatre of Thelepte, a Roman colonia in Byzacena near modern Fériana; the city became seat of the province's military governor in the 6th century and was refortified under Justinian, per Procopius.

vici:vici-31121.label: Henchir Khima Theatre - Aggar
vici:vici-31121.description: Ruined theatre of Aggar (Henchir Sidi Amara) in the Siliana plain, identified with the ancient town by L. Ladjimi-Sebaï; some cavea seating steps survive. The site also preserves a triumphal arch, forum/capitol, and a Byzantine fort built atop a temple of Juno.

vici:vici-31123.label: Small theatre
vici:vici-31123.description: Small theatre of Seressi, a Roman town near modern El Fahs, standing alongside the settlement's triumphal arch.

vici:vici-31202.label: Theater
vici:vici-31202.description: Theatre associated with Thunigaba, a Roman-Berber town near modern Aïn Laabed in the Nefza region that later became a bishopric; no remains are currently visible above ground.

vici:vici-31205.label: Tebourba Amphitheatre - Thuburbo Minus
vici:vici-31205.description: Amphitheatre of the Roman colonia Thuburbo Minus (Tebourba), partly cut into a hillside and measuring roughly 36x48m, built in the 2nd century AD; one of only three Tunisian amphitheatres, with Uthina and El Jem, known to have underground service galleries. Still standing in the 17th century, it was later demolished for bridge material.

vici:vici-31274.label: Fossa Theatre - Aveia
vici:vici-31274.description: The only surviving public monument of the Vestinian town of Aveia, an early imperial theater built on the middle terrace of the settlement, unusually located outside the city walls.

vici:vici-31276.label: Fermo Theatre - Firmum
vici:vici-31276.description: Built in the 1st century BC on the Colle del Girfalco acropolis, this theater held roughly 2,000 spectators; its buried remains, studied in 1786, 1853, and 1934, lie beneath the church of Madonna del Carmine.
vici:vici-31276.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman theatre in Fermo city centre, Italy

vici:vici-31279.label: Urbino Theatre - Urvinum Mataurense
vici:vici-31279.description: Rediscovered in 1943 and excavated from 2015, the theater of Urvinum Mataurense (1st c. BC-1st c. AD) stood out for its lavish marble revetment sourced from quarries across the Mediterranean, from Carrara to Egypt.

vici:vici-31280.label: Rimini Theatre - Ariminium
vici:vici-31280.description: Probably built under Augustus as part of his urban development of Ariminum, the theater had an external diameter of about 80 meters and a 23-meter-wide stage; its remains are now embedded in later buildings.

vici:vici-31281.label: Galeata Theatre - Mevaniola
vici:vici-31281.description: Theater of the Roman town of Mevaniola, dated to the early 1st century BC; its perfectly circular orchestra follows Greek-Hellenistic rather than standard Roman design. Excavated in the 1950s-60s after the site's 1934 discovery.

vici:vici-31282.label: Bologna Theatre - Bononia
vici:vici-31282.description: Begun around 88 BC as part of Bononia's transition to a Roman municipium, this was the first stone theater in Roman architecture, predating Pompey's theater in Rome by decades. Discovered in 1977 during restoration on via Carbonesi.

vici:vici-31283.label: Lucca Theatre - Luca
vici:vici-31283.description: Built in the northwestern part of ancient Luca near the city walls, probably in the early Augustan period; the semicircular cavea had a diameter of about 78 meters, with traces surviving at the Church of Sant'Agostino.

vici:vici-31287.label: Pianosa Theatre - Planasia
vici:vici-31287.description: Part of the villa where Augustus exiled his grandson Agrippa Postumus in 6 AD; the small theatre, alongside a thermal bath and mosaic-floored villa, was uncovered by abbot Gaetano Chierici in the 19th century.

vici:vici-31288.label: Cosa Bouleuterion - Cosa
vici:vici-31288.description: The council house of the Roman colony of Cosa (founded 273 BC), excavated by the American Academy in Rome under Frank E. Brown; the original timber-and-stone curia was rebuilt as a three-part hall around 173 BC.

vici:vici-31290.label: Assisi Theatre - Asisium
vici:vici-31290.description: Asisium's theatre is known only from two inscriptions found near Santa Maria Maggiore naming the gens Propertia as builders, possibly linking it to the poet Sextus Propertius; its physical remains have never been located.

vici:vici-31291.label: Spello Theatre - Hispellum
vici:vici-31291.description: Part of a public sacred precinct with an amphitheatre and temple below the later Villa Fidelia, on the road from Porta Venere toward Assisi; demolished by the early 20th century, leaving only a buried pillar core visible today.

vici:vici-31292.label: Bevagnia Theatre - Mevania
vici:vici-31292.description: Built in the 1st century AD against the hillside above the Via Flaminia; its curved cavea foundations and two supporting ambulatories survive embedded in later houses, one now the Redibis restaurant.

vici:vici-31293.label: Todi Theatre - Tuder
vici:vici-31293.description: Ancient Tuder's Roman theatre was partly overbuilt by the early medieval circuit walls; a 2012 archaeological reassessment (Chiaraluce) reinterpreted the structural relationship between the theatre remains and the later fortifications.

vici:vici-31294.label: Terni Theatre - Interamna Nahars
vici:vici-31294.description: Distinct from the city's amphitheatre, this 1st-century-BC theatre stood near the forum on the Via Flaminia crossing; only fragmentary opus reticulatum walls and one vaulted lateral entrance survive beneath later buildings.

vici:vici-31295.label: Falerii Novi Theatre - Falerii Novi
vici:vici-31295.description: Excavated in 1829, when Augustan-era statues of Livia and her grandsons Gaius and Lucius Caesar were recovered from it; recent ground-penetrating radar survey has since mapped its full structural plan beneath the abandoned city.

vici:vici-31300.label: Casoli Theatre - Cluviae
vici:vici-31300.description: The Samnite-Roman town of Cluviae's theatre, built in opus reticulatum at Piano Laroma and dated to the 1st century BC-1st century AD, had a cavea front over 36m long and a rectangular scaenae building of 24x12m.

vici:vici-31303.label: Corfino Theatre - Corfinium
vici:vici-31303.description: Built in the first half of the 1st century AD with a diameter of about 75m, Corfinium's theatre survives mainly through inscriptions recording its construction and a guild of 23 scabillarii dancers; little remains beneath Piazza del Teatro.

vici:vici-31304.label: Alba Fucens Theatre - Alba Fucens
vici:vici-31304.description: Carved into the slope of Colle Pettorino in two building phases from the late 2nd to mid-1st century BC, the theatre was later restored, reportedly under the usurper Magnentius, and abandoned after Alba Fucens declined post a 6th-century earthquake.

vici:vici-31305.label: Tivoli Theatre of Herucles - Tibur
vici:vici-31305.description: Part of the Republican-era Sanctuary of Hercules Victor (c.120-82 BC), the theatre had three vomitoria, a scaenae frons and an orchestra pit, and abutted the sanctuary's underground Via Tecta road; restored in 2008-09.

vici:vici-31307.label: Tivoli Villa Adriana Greek Theatre
vici:vici-31307.description: A small court theatre with an oval cavea near Villa Adriana's entrance, long quarried for building stone; 18th-century digs by Count Fede found paired herms of Tragedy and Comedy, later restored by Cavaceppi and now in the Vatican Museums.

vici:vici-31310.label: Gabii Sanctuary Theatre - Gabii
vici:vici-31310.description: Part of the sanctuary of Juno Gabina at ancient Gabii: a sacred precinct cut partly into rock, with porticoes, shops, and a theater on its south side facing the late 2nd-century BC temple of Juno.

vici:vici-31311.label: Odeon of Domitian
vici:vici-31311.description: A concert/oratory hall built by Domitian on the Campus Martius, seating up to c.11,000, restored by Apollodorus of Damascus around AD 106; its cavea outline survives in the curved facade of Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne.
vici:vici-31311.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman building on the Campus Martius in Rome

vici:vici-31313.label: Amphitheatre of Commodus - Villa Commodiana
vici:vici-31313.description: A small amphitheater within the Villa of the Quintilii on the Via Appia, seized by Commodus in AD 182 after he had the villa's owners executed; tradition holds he trained and hunted beasts here as a gladiator.

vici:vici-31314.label: Rome Villa of the Quintili Stadium
vici:vici-31314.description: The c.500m hippodrome-shaped garden of the Villa of the Quintilii, expanded under Commodus after his AD 182 seizure of the estate; a porticoed racetrack-garden used for chariot exercise and imperial promenades, lined with statuary and fountains.

vici:vici-31315.label: Castel Gandolfo Theatre - Albano
vici:vici-31315.description: The private theater of Domitian's Alban Villa, built c. AD 81-96 on the middle terrace above Lake Albano; excavated fragments are held in the Antiquarium of Castel Gandolfo, with ruins still visible in the Villa Barberini grounds.

vici:vici-31316.label: Lanuvio Amphitheatre - Lanuvium
vici:vici-31316.description: An elliptical amphitheater (c.56m long) confirmed by 2012-13 excavations as part of the imperial 'Villa degli Antonini' estate at ancient Lanuvium; ancient sources say Commodus earned his nickname 'Roman Hercules' here by killing wild beasts.

vici:vici-31317.label: Lanuvio Theatre - Lanuvium
vici:vici-31317.description: Remains of Lanuvium's Roman theater and its city walls survive in the modern town, near a porticoed precinct in opus reticulatum associated with the city's famed temple of Juno Sospita.

vici:vici-31319.label: Palestrina Theatre - Praeneste
vici:vici-31319.description: The topmost terrace of the late 2nd-century BC Sanctuary of Fortuna Primigenia formed a theater-like cavea crowned by a small circular tholos, reached via the 'Hemicycles' terrace with its oracular sortes well.

vici:vici-31322.label: Venafro Theatre - Venafrum
vici:vici-31322.description: Built in the early Augustan period on the slopes of Monte Santa Croce, the theatre had a roughly 60m stage front and seated about 3,500; an inscription credits a member of the gens Vibia with funding it. Abandoned after the destructive 346 CE earthquake.

vici:vici-31324.label: Roccavecchia di Pratella Theatre - Callifae
vici:vici-31324.description: Theatre of the Samnite hilltop town identified as Callifae, with a masonry stage and a cavea cut directly into the rock following the terrain — only the second rock-cut Samnite theatre found after Pietrabbondante. The settlement was destroyed after the Social War (88 BC).

vici:vici-31329.label: Alife Theatre - Allifae
vici:vici-31329.description: Theatre of Allifae, built inside the walls near today's Piazza del Vescovato; recorded still standing with two arcades in the 18th century before being demolished in 1836 for cathedral stone. Fragments including marble portrait heads re-emerged in 1965 and 1989.

vici:vici-31330.label: Tregli Theatre - Trebula Balliensis
vici:vici-31330.description: Theatre of the Samnite-Roman town of Trebula Balliensis, excavated in its southwestern quarter, where statues and public inscriptions (now largely in the Museo Campano, Capua) suggest the town's forum also stood. The Roman-era settlement developed here from the 2nd century BC.

vici:vici-31332.label: Trebula Balliensis
vici:vici-31332.description: A theatre known only from inscriptions at ancient Telesia (Telese Vetere/San Salvatore Telesino), recorded as roughly 48.7m in diameter with a 37.7m orchestra; despite this epigraphic evidence, excavation has never located its physical remains.

vici:vici-31333.label: Formia Theatre - Formiae
vici:vici-31333.description: Augustan-era theatre in Formia's Castellone district, locally called 'Gliu Canciegl'; its cavea faced south toward the sea and its stage was about 24m long. Tradition places the martyrdom of St Erasmus here in 303 CE; the ruins are now built over by a residential quarter.

vici:vici-31336.label: Santa Maria Capua Vetere Early Amphitheatre - Capua
vici:vici-31336.description: Capua's Republican-era amphitheatre (130-90 BC), sited about 20m from its later Flavian successor and holding an estimated 20,000 spectators; likely the site of the gladiatorial school from which Spartacus's revolt broke out in 73 BC. Demolished to build the standing amphitheatre.

vici:vici-31338.label: Cassino Spinelli Theatre - Suessula
vici:vici-31338.description: Scholars believe the 18th-century Casina Spinelli hunting lodge was built directly over the remains of Suessula's Roman theatre; excavations beneath and around it exposed part of the ancient city's forum.

vici:vici-31339.label: Acerra Theatre - Acerrae
vici:vici-31339.description: Elliptical opus reticulatum/opus mixtum walls of a 1st-century AD theatre were found in 1982 under the stables of Acerra's Castello dei Conti; inscriptions record Gnaeus Stennius Egnatius, priest of Isis and Serapis, funding a day of games.

vici:vici-31341.label: Miseno Theatre - Misenum
vici:vici-31341.description: A 2nd-century AD theatre built against the hillside at Punta Sarparella served the sailors of the Classis Misenensis, Rome's principal imperial fleet based at Misenum; bradyseism has submerged part of it below sea level.

vici:vici-31344.label: Sorrento Theatre - Surrentum
vici:vici-31344.description: A small Roman theatre was uncovered in 1855 beneath the terrace of Sorrento's Hotel Victoria, alongside a long wall thought to belong to an imperial-era residence, with a rock-cut tunnel descending toward the sea.

vici:vici-31351.label: Castiglione di Paludi Theatre - Cossa
vici:vici-31351.description: A rock-cut and sandstone-block semicircular theatre seating roughly 200 was built into the hillside of this Brettian hilltop settlement (4th century BC), tentatively identified with Cossa, and served as a communal meeting place.

vici:vici-31355.label: Vicenza Theatre - Vicetia
vici:vici-31355.description: The Teatro Berga, Vicetia's Roman theatre, was built in the 1st century BC with a cavea about 82 m across seating over 5,000; adorned with marble statues of the Julio-Claudian family, it was surveyed by Andrea Palladio before being built over in the 17th century.
vici:vici-31355.wikidataDescription: ancient Roman theatre in Vicenza, Italy

vici:vici-31356.label: Altino Odeon - Altinum
vici:vici-31356.description: The smaller of Altinum's two Roman theatres, identified as an odeon through geophysical resistivity survey within the city's monumental centre; unlike its larger neighbour it had not been excavated as of 2026.

vici:vici-31357.label: Altino Theatre - Altinum
vici:vici-31357.description: The larger of Altinum's two Roman theatres, first mapped by geophysical prospection; a 2025-26 excavation campaign uncovered sections of its cavea walls near the city's forum and the Via Annia.

vici:vici-31358.label: Ivrea Theatre - Eporedia
vici:vici-31358.description: Remains of a Roman theatre at Eporedia, distinct from the town's better-known amphitheatre, first catalogued by Carlo Promis in his 1883 study of its surviving traces; little is visible above ground today.

vici:vici-31361.label: Palma de Majorca Theatre
vici:vici-31361.description: A theatre proposed for Roman Palma (Palmaria) in a 1997 architectural hypothesis applying Vitruvian design criteria to the city's ancient street grid; unlike the excavated theatre at Pollentia in northern Mallorca, no dig has confirmed the structure.
vici:vici-31361.wikidataDescription: hypothetical Roman theatre in Palma de Mallorca, Spain

vici:vici-31362.label: Akmonia - Traianopolis Theater
vici:vici-31362.description: An unexcavated theatre cavity at Akmonia (Ahat Köyü, Uşak province), a Phrygian city mentioned by Cicero; visible remains include two temple podiums and gymnasium foundations alongside the theatre pit, with no standing structure surviving.

vici:vici-31364.label: Bolu Stadium - Claudiopolis
vici:vici-31364.description: U-shaped stadium of Claudiopolis (Bithynium), built in the 2nd century AD, probably under Hadrian; inscriptions naming priests Secundus and Anatole record gladiatorial games held there. Originally ~190m long; excavated since 2008, now the best-preserved Roman structure in Bolu.

vici:vici-31365.label: Izmit Theatre - Nicomedia
vici:vici-31365.description: Roman theater of Nicomedia, capital of the Roman Empire under Diocletian from 284 AD; reportedly among antiquity's largest theaters, it lies mostly unexcavated beneath İzmit's Orhan neighborhood, exposed by rubble-clearance after the 1999 earthquake.

vici:vici-31371.label: Ephesus, Theatre Gymnasium
vici:vici-31371.description: Bath-gymnasium complex built in the 2nd century AD by Publius Vedius Antoninus and his wife Flavia Pappiana, dedicated to Artemis and Antoninus Pius; its 70x30m palaestra beside the Great Theatre is thought to have trained actors.
vici:vici-31371.wikidataDescription: bath-gymnasium located across the street from the theater in Ephesus

vici:vici-31392.label: Ciavieja Amphitheatre
vici:vici-31392.description: At the Roman civitas of Murgi (Ciavieja, El Ejido), georadar survey detected a curved wall interpreted as a possible amphitheatre, supported by a 2nd-century inscription honoring Porcia Maura referencing circus games; identification remains provisional.

vici:vici-31393.label: Castulo Theatre - Castulo
vici:vici-31393.description: Remains of the Roman theatre of Castulo survive near the acropolis of this Iberian-Roman city by Linares (Jaén), part of a public complex with baths, forum and an amphitheatre built as Castulo adopted the Roman urban model.

vici:vici-31394.label: Alhambra Circus - Laminium
vici:vici-31394.description: Roman circus of Laminium (Alhambra, Ciudad Real), identified in the late 1990s during roadworks on the N-340; a rectangular structure with a central longitudinal wall interpreted as the spina, now buried beneath the road.

vici:vici-31396.label: Arcobriga Theatre - Arcobriga
vici:vici-31396.description: Theatre of the Celtiberian-Roman hilltop city Arcóbriga (Cerro Villar, Monreal de Ariza), built on the slope between the acropolis and the public-buildings plateau; the site was excavated by the Marquis of Cerralbo in the early 20th century.

vici:vici-31397.label: Bilbilis Theatre - Bilbilis
vici:vici-31397.description: Theatre of Bílbilis, birthplace of the poet Martial, linked to the forum by porticoes and stairs faced with marble from Carrara and Chemtou; a two-story scaenae frons with Corinthian capitals gave the venue a capacity near 4,500.

vici:vici-31398.label: Coruna del Conde Amphitheatre - Clunia
vici:vici-31398.description: Rock-cut theatre of Colonia Clunia Sulpicia, built under Emperor Tiberius with capacity for c. 10,000 spectators — one of the largest in Hispania — remodeled in the 2nd century for amphitheatre-style spectacles.

vici:vici-31399.label: Lugo Amphitheatre - Lucus Augusti
vici:vici-31399.description: Amphitheatre of Lucus Augusti (Lugo), built outside the city walls near a gladiatorial palaestra and the temples of Isis and Venus; its modest size (c. 2,800 capacity) matched the town's population.

vici:vici-31400.label: Leon Amphitheatre - Legio
vici:vici-31400.description: Legionary amphitheatre of Legio (León), one of only five known legionary amphitheatres in the Roman Empire; begun by Legio VI Victrix in the 1st century and enlarged by Legio VII Gemina to seat up to 8,000.

vici:vici-31401.label: Arzila Theatre - Augusta Zilil
vici:vici-31401.description: Roman theatre of the colonia Iulia Constantia Zilil (Dchar Jdid, near Asilah), sited just outside the west gate of the 3rd-century town wall; today only the cavea depression and stage-wall foundations survive.

vici:vici-31402.label: Setif Circus - Sitifis
vici:vici-31402.description: Roman circus of Sitifis (Sétif), a chariot-racing track roughly 450m long and 70m wide, likely built or restored in late antiquity; largely built over today, with only its curved southern end still visible.

vici:vici-31404.label: Lissos Theatre - Lissos
vici:vici-31404.description: Small 1st-century AD theatre or odeion (23m diameter) beside the Asclepieion of ancient Lissos, likely used for performances tied to the sanctuary's healing cult.

vici:vici-31405.label: Lyttos Theatre - Littos
vici:vici-31405.description: Roman theatre of Lyttos (Lyktos), described by 16th-century drawings and recent excavation as the largest theatre on Crete; nearby a civic hall dedicated to Hadrian was completed in 118 AD.

vici:vici-31406.label: Lato Theatre - Lato
vici:vici-31406.description: Rock-cut theatral area of the Doric city of Lato, with stone benches for about 350 spectators beside the agora, used for civic assembly as much as performance.

vici:vici-31410.label: Lykossoura Theatre - Lycosura
vici:vici-31410.description: A stepped, uncurved stone seating area of about ten rows (21-29 m long) set into the hillside beside the 4th-century BC temple of Despoina at Lycosura, likely for spectators of the goddess's mystery rites; the sanctuary held Damophon's colossal cult statue group, found in 1889.

vici:vici-31414.label: Lykaion Hippodrome - Lykaion
vici:vici-31414.description: The only substantially preserved hippodrome from Greek antiquity (roughly 250 x 50 m), built after the 7th century BC in the Lower Sanctuary of Zeus on Mount Lykaion, where the quadrennial Lykaia games staged chariot and horse races into the 3rd century BC.

vici:vici-31416.label: Platana Theatre - Typaneae
vici:vici-31416.description: A 4th-century BC theatre (its stage rebuilt around 245 BC) attached to the fortified hill-city of Typaneae in Triphylia, one of only two known ancient theatres in Elis Prefecture; part of its cavea, retaining wall, and a proedria throne survive in place.

vici:vici-31417.label: Elis Theatre - Elis
vici:vici-31417.description: Theatre of Elis, built mainly in Hellenistic times on the acropolis slope near a temple of Dionysus that housed a statue by Praxiteles (Pausanias); excavated by the Austrian Archaeological Institute in 1910-1914 and again from 1960, with an estimated capacity of 5,000-8,000.

vici:vici-31418.label: Tripotama Theatre - Psophis
vici:vici-31418.description: A theatre at Psophis in northwestern Arcadia, near the confluence of the Erymanthos and Aroanios rivers; noted by 19th-century traveller William Martin Leake on a hillside but, despite being a modest settlement described by Pausanias, it has not been securely relocated by later excavation.

vici:vici-31425.label: Makyneia Theatre - Makyneia
vici:vici-31425.description: A small 4th-3rd century BC theatre at the foot of the fortified hill of ancient Macynia in Aetolia, with an unusual layout combining a 14-row curved cavea and an adjoining 3-row straight wing forming a single-row proedria, built using the Doric-foot module.

vici:vici-31426.label: Pleuron Theatre
vici:vici-31426.description: Theatre of New Pleuron in Aetolia, built around 230 BC contemporary with the city walls after Demetrios II of Macedon destroyed old Pleuron in 234 BC; a well-preserved five-section cavea with six staircases and a six-columned proscenium abut the city wall.

vici:vici-31429.label: Lefkada Theatre - Leucas
vici:vici-31429.description: Theatre of ancient Leucas, built c. 4th century BC on Koulmos Hill; rediscovered in 1997 and systematically excavated from 2015, with 21 seat rows for c. 3,500 spectators and carved marble thrones.

vici:vici-31430.label: Kassiopi Theatre - Nikopolis
vici:vici-31430.description: Roman theatre of Nikopolis, built in the early 1st century AD as part of Augustus's building program for the city founded after Actium; capacity c. 5,000, renovated under Hadrian in the 2nd century AD.

vici:vici-31431.label: Kassiopi Odeon - Nikopolis
vici:vici-31431.description: Roman odeon at Nikopolis, built in the 1st century AD with its cavea carried on three semicircular stoas since the ground lacked a natural slope; remained in use until the later 3rd century AD.

vici:vici-31432.label: Arta Theatre - Ambracia
vici:vici-31432.description: Small theatre-odeon-bouleuterion of Ambracia, capital of Pyrrhus of Epirus, built late 4th-early 3rd century BC over an earlier bathhouse; the smallest known Greek theatre, seating only about 500.

vici:vici-31438.label: Igoumenitsa Theatre - Gitana
vici:vici-31438.description: Theatre of Gitana, capital of the Thesprotian League, built mid-3rd century BC and destroyed by Rome in 167 BC; 65m diameter with 28 seat rows, many inscribed with acts of manumission.

vici:vici-31439.label: Tanagra Theatre - Tanagra
vici:vici-31439.description: Ancient theatre of Tanagra, a Boeotian city famed for its Geometric-to-Hellenistic cemetery and Tanagra terracotta figurines; the theatre remains only partly uncovered, cut through by a later water-supply channel.

vici:vici-31443.label: Volos Theatre - Demetrias
vici:vici-31443.description: Theatre of Demetrias, built with the city's founding by Demetrios Poliorketes in 294-292 BC; a Hellenistic cavea and stage over 24m across, seating upward of 2,500, excavated from 1907 onward.

vici:vici-31445.label: Skotoussa Theatre - Scotoussa
vici:vici-31445.description: Theatre of Thessalian Scotussa, built into a natural hollow inside the city's southwest wall; the polis, home of Olympic pankratiast Polydamas, lay near the 197 BC Battle of Cynoscephalae and is under excavation by a Greek-Italian team since 2014.

vici:vici-31448.label: Dion Bouleterion - Dium
vici:vici-31448.description: A council hall built within Dion's Great Thermae bath complex in the later 2nd century AD; the roughly 400-seat odeon-style room hosted musical and poetic performances and likely doubled as the city's bouleuterion (assembly hall).

vici:vici-31453.label: Andros Theatre - Andrus
vici:vici-31453.description: Theatre of Palaiopoli, the fortified Classical-Hellenistic capital of ancient Andros founded in the 7th-6th century BC on the island's west coast; only fragmentary remains survive, and the site today hosts summer performances of ancient Greek drama.

vici:vici-31456.label: Delos Stadium - Delos
vici:vici-31456.description: Track and seating built in Delos's sanctuary of Apollo in the early 3rd century BC for the athletic contests of the Delia festival; at roughly 270 m it is among the smallest stadia known from ancient Greece.

vici:vici-31457.label: Santorini Theatre - Thera
vici:vici-31457.description: Theatre of Ancient Thera, the Dorian city on Mesa Vouno founded by Theras of Sparta in the 9th century BC; excavated by Friedrich Hiller von Gaertringen (1895-1904), it seated up to about 1,500 spectators near the agora.

vici:vici-31461.label: Kefalos Theatre - Kephalos
vici:vici-31461.description: Hellenistic theatre of Astypalaia (Isthmos), Kos's capital until 366 BC, near the acropolis and a temple of Asklepios and Hygieia; the orchestra retains its Dionysus altar (thymele), and the stage building's Doric foundations survive.

vici:vici-31464.label: Kardamena Theatre - Alasarnas
vici:vici-31464.description: Hellenistic theatre of Halasarna near Kardamaina, part of the Sanctuary of Apollo complex; excavated by the Italian Archaeological Mission in 1928, it preserves three cunei of turf-cut seating and a Roman-period stage platform, though nothing is visible today.

vici:vici-31465.label: Kos Roman Theatre - Kos
vici:vici-31465.description: Large Roman theatre at Ambavri south of Kos town, about 108 m wide and seating up to 13,000 for events linked to the Temple of Asklepios; built in the 1st century AD and partly excavated by the Italian Mission in 1922 and 1930.

vici:vici-31466.label: Kos South Stadium - Kos
vici:vici-31466.description: Findspot of Kos's Hellenistic athletics stadium, built in the first half of the 2nd century BC (roughly 180 x 30m, without a curved sphendone); German archaeologist R. Herzog excavated the site in 1899–1900, locating its aphesis (starting line).

vici:vici-31467.label: Kos Northern Stadium - Kos
vici:vici-31467.description: Findspot of Kos's Hellenistic athletics stadium (built first half of the 2nd century BC, track roughly 180 x 30m); Italian archaeologist Luciano Laurenzi excavated here in 1928, uncovering rows of travertine seating that confirmed the stadium's identification.

vici:vici-31468.label: Samothraki Theatre - Paleapolis
vici:vici-31468.description: Theatre of the Sanctuary of the Great Gods at Samothrace, built around 200 BC on the Western Hill; it staged mythological performances during the Mysteries, with an orchestra roughly 12.5m across and polychrome seating of red rhyolite and white limestone.

vici:vici-31469.label: Avdera Theatre - Abdera
vici:vici-31469.description: Badly damaged theatre on the north side of Abdera, the Thracian colony founded by settlers from Teos; topographic and geophysical survey (University of Thessaloniki) plus trial trenching have begun defining its plan, though excavation remains at an early stage.

vici:vici-31472.label: Ariassos Bouleuterion - Ariassos
vici:vici-31472.description: Council house (bouleuterion) of Ariassos, a Pisidian hill city occupied from the 3rd century BC to the 7th century AD; survey by Stephen Mitchell's team identified a squarish hall with a semicircular tiered bench, possibly an odeion, fronted by a hexagonal-facade atrium.

vici:vici-31473.label: Ariassos Theatre - Ariassos
vici:vici-31473.description: Theatre of Ariassos, a Pisidian city on the Antalya–Burdur road that minted coins in the late Hellenistic period; only partial foundations of the cavea survive, recorded during Stephen Mitchell's Pisidia Survey Project alongside the city's bouleuterion, nymphaeum and baths.

vici:vici-31475.label: Karaot Theatre - Osia
vici:vici-31475.description: At Sia (also read Osia), a minor Pisidian town near Karaot attested only by a boundary inscription, one surviving structure preserves eight or nine straight rows of stone seating above a paved area, probably a small theatre or council hall.

vici:vici-31476.label: Cremna Eastern Theatre - Cremna
vici:vici-31476.description: One of two theatres at Cremna, a Pisidian hilltop city on the Cestrus gorge that Augustus refounded as the Roman colony Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Cremnena; the city's public buildings flourished from Hadrian's reign into the Severan period.

vici:vici-31477.label: Bayat Theatre - Claudioseleucia
vici:vici-31477.description: Theatre of Seleucia Sidera (Claudioseleucia) on Hisar Tepe, built to the Greek plan with a largely destroyed cavea; its stage building dates to the Roman Imperial period, 2nd–3rd century CE.

vici:vici-31478.label: Dinar Theatre - Apamea
vici:vici-31478.description: Theatre of Apamea Kibotos (Cibotus), the Seleucid city Antiochus I founded on the site of Phrygian Celaenae; its remains lie beneath modern Dinar and have seen little systematic excavation.

vici:vici-31479.label: Ballihisar Theatre - Pessinus
vici:vici-31479.description: Theatre-stairway of Pessinus, built beside the sanctuary of Cybele as monumental steps to the Tiberian-era temple, with an orchestra used for religious rites and gladiatorial shows; last major restoration under Hadrian.

vici:vici-31480.label: Soli Theatre - Pompeiopolis
vici:vici-31480.description: Theatre of Soli-Pompeiopolis, the Rhodian colony Pompey refounded in 64 BC to resettle surrendered Cilician pirates; recorded by early 19th-century travelers, it is no longer visible above ground and remains under excavation.

vici:vici-31481.label: Mut Theatre - Claudiopolis
vici:vici-31481.description: Theatre of Claudiopolis (Colonia Ninica Claudiopolis), a Claudian colony in the Calycadnus valley; seating fragments and scaenae column drums survive west of modern Mut amid an otherwise built-over ancient site.

vici:vici-31482.label: Syedra Theatre - Syedra
vici:vici-31482.description: Theatre of Syedra, a Greek foundation traced to the 7th century BC that flourished under Rome; the roughly 3,000-year-old structure is under active excavation via a Turkish-French research project (TUBITAK-backed).

vici:vici-31484.label: Yenicikent Hippodrome - Tripolis
vici:vici-31484.description: Stadium of Tripolis on the Meander (Apollonia/Antoniopolis), a city on the Caria-Lydia-Phrygia border; its 2nd-century-CE public buildings, including this stadium, are under ongoing excavation by Pamukkale University.
vici:vici-31484.wikidataDescription: ancient city at the crossroads of Caria, Lydia, and Phrygia in modern-day Turkey

vici:vici-31487.label: Haydere Theatre - Bargasa
vici:vici-31487.description: Theatre of Bargasa, a minor inland Carian town of Hellenistic and Roman date near Haydere/Kavaklı in the Harpasos valley; its ruins are poorly preserved and hidden in woodland.

vici:vici-31491.label: Bozyurt Theatre - Mastaura
vici:vici-31491.description: Theatre of Mastaura, a small Roman-era theatre near Nazilli seating an estimated 1,600, with a partially preserved two-tiered arched stage building; the city also has a recently unearthed Severan-era amphitheater.

vici:vici-31493.label: Çamyayla Theatre - Kyon
vici:vici-31493.description: Roman-period theatre of Kyon, built against a hillside near Çamyayla village (ancient Paliapolis in Byzantine times); only 13 rows of seating survive and the city, known for its coinage, has never been formally excavated.

vici:vici-31494.label: Alasehir Stadium - Philadelphia
vici:vici-31494.description: Stadium of Philadelphia in Lydia, founded 189 BC by Eumenes II of Pergamon and later one of the Seven Churches of Revelation; the U-shaped cavea survives cut into a hillside, but the structure remains unexcavated and its stone seating stripped.

vici:vici-31495.label: Blaundos Theatre - Blaundus
vici:vici-31495.description: Theatre of Blaundus, a hilltop city founded by Macedonian settlers under Alexander's successors and rebuilt as a Roman center after earthquakes; the theatre sits on the southern slope outside the walls with its stage destroyed but seating rows partly preserved.

vici:vici-31496.label: Blaundos Stadium - Blaundus
vici:vici-31496.description: Stadium of Blaundus, a 1st-century AD structure roughly 140 by 37 meters excavated in recent seasons, notable for a stepped entrance and a male statue found reused as filler stone in its wall.

vici:vici-31497.label: Menemen Theatre - Temnos
vici:vici-31497.description: Theatre of Temnos, an Aeolian city mentioned by Herodotus near modern Görece; built on the acropolis' north slope with an estimated capacity of about 2,800, its cavea partly visible but never scientifically excavated.

vici:vici-31498.label: Nemrud Kalesi Theatre - Aigai
vici:vici-31498.description: Theatre of Aigai in Aeolis, a member of the Aeolian dodecapolis and seat of a noted Apollo sanctuary that flourished under the Attalids of Pergamon; the theatre has been under excavation since the site's 2004 research program began.

vici:vici-31499.label: Nemrud Kalesi Stadium - Aigai
vici:vici-31499.description: One long wall survives from the stadium of Aigai (Aeolis), a Greek city atop Gün Dağı in Manisa province; excavated since 2004 by Ege University under Ersin Doğer alongside the city's agora, theater, and Temple of Demeter.

vici:vici-31506.label: Tell Abil Theatre - Abila
vici:vici-31506.description: The Roman-Byzantine theater of Abila of the Decapolis (Tell Abil/Quwaylibah) in northern Jordan, part of the ten-city Decapolis league; the site's structures were largely leveled by the earthquake of 747 CE.

vici:vici-31508.label: Jericho Theatre - Jericho
vici:vici-31508.description: Herod the Great built a small theater, seating about 3,000, at Tell es-Samrat north of his winter palace at Jericho; Josephus records the dying Herod ordering Judean notables assembled there executed at his death.

vici:vici-31509.label: Jericho Circus - Jericho
vici:vici-31509.description: The hippodrome (racecourse) at Tell es-Samrat formed part of Herod the Great's theater-stadium complex north of his winter palace at Jericho, excavated by Ehud Netzer; Josephus sets here Herod's deathbed order to execute assembled notables.

vici:vici-31510.label: Tel Dor Theatre - Dor
vici:vici-31510.description: Dor's Roman theater, built in the late 1st or early 2nd century CE north of the tell, was about 72 m in diameter and seated roughly 4,000; partly excavated in the 1950s by Ja'acov Leibowitz.

vici:vici-31515.label: Sebastopol Theatre - Chersonisus Taurica
vici:vici-31515.description: The only excavated ancient Greek theater in the northern Black Sea region, built in the Hellenistic period within Chersonesus Taurica near Sevastopol; it was later remodeled into an arena for gladiatorial combat under Roman rule.
vici:vici-31515.wikidataDescription: ancient Greek theatre in Chersonesus in today's Sevastopol, Crimea

vici:vici-31516.label: Olbia Theatre - Olbia
vici:vici-31516.description: Ancient sources place a theatre, hippodrome, and gymnasium around Olbia Pontica's agora, but despite more than a century of excavation at this Greek colony on the Southern Bug estuary, the theatre's physical remains have never been located.

vici:vici-31518.label: Kostolac Hippodrome - Ciminacium
vici:vici-31518.description: Geophysical survey has traced a hippodrome for chariot racing among the public buildings of Viminacium, capital of Roman Moesia Superior near modern Kostolac, though like most of the 450-hectare site it remains unexcavated.

vici:vici-31521.label: Klos Theatre - Nikaea
vici:vici-31521.description: Built into a hillside in the 3rd century BC, this theatre at Nikaia had a 53m cavea seating about 800 in 17 rows; its parodos wall preserves 14 inscriptions recording grants of citizenship to the city.

vici:vici-31522.label: Bylis Stadium - Bylis
vici:vici-31522.description: Built around the mid-3rd century BC, Byllis's roughly 190m stadium ran beside the theatre for standing spectators; a 51m rainwater cistern fed by its steps and the Great Stoa's roof survives alongside one bank of seating.

vici:vici-31523.label: Messina Theatre - Messana
vici:vici-31523.description: Plutarch's Life of Timoleon implies a theatre or arena at Messana, where the deposed tyrant Hippon was lynched before the crowd, but no excavation has ever confirmed or located a Hellenistic theatre in the city.

vici:vici-31525.label: Prizzi Theatre - Hippana
vici:vici-31525.description: Excavated in 2007 at Montagna dei Cavalli, this Greek theatre — among the earliest known in Sicily — was built in the later 4th century BC and destroyed in 258 BC when Rome sacked Hippana during the First Punic War.

vici:vici-31526.label: Agrigento Bouleuterion - Agrigento
vici:vici-31526.description: Uncovered in the 1960s on the San Nicola hillock, this 4th–3rd century BC semicircular assembly hall — cut into tufa, seating roughly 3,000 — served Akragas's popular assembly and was later refashioned as a Roman-era odeon called the comitium.

vici:vici-31535.label: Ampfitheater
vici:vici-31535.description: Antioch's amphitheater, built around the mid-1st century BC — one of the earliest in the Roman world — but its exact location was never securely fixed and may be confused in the ancient sources with a nearby reservoir.

vici:vici-31536.label: Hipodrom
vici:vici-31536.description: Built around 50 BCE on an island in the Orontes, the Circus of Antioch stretched over 490 m and could seat up to 80,000 spectators for chariot racing, among the largest hippodromes in the Roman world.
vici:vici-31536.wikidataDescription: Roman hippodrome in Antakya, Hatay, Turkey

vici:vici-31606.label: Neandreia Theater
vici:vici-31606.description: Archaeological survey has identified traces of a theater among the remains of Neandreia, an Aeolian Greek city on Çığrı Dağ in the Troad founded around 700 BC and largely depopulated after Alexandria Troas absorbed it c. 310 BC.

vici:vici-31610.label: Yenicikent Theatre - Tripolis
vici:vici-31610.description: The Hellenistic-Roman theater of Tripolis ad Maeandrum, near modern Yenicekent, is built into a hillside at a steep 50-degree incline, dates to around the 2nd century AD, and remains largely unexcavated.

vici:vici-31611.label: Bergama Odeon - Pergamum
vici:vici-31611.description: The odeon of Pergamon's Upper Gymnasium was a roofed recital hall about 36 m across with 14 rows of seating in five wedges, seating roughly 1,000; built in the 2nd century CE, it may also have served as a bouleuterion.

vici:vici-31612.label: Bergama Stadium - Pergamon
vici:vici-31612.description: Pergamon's roofed 'Basement Stadium', about 212 m long, lay between the middle and upper terraces of the 2nd-century-BC gymnasium complex on the acropolis, used for athletic training and competitions.

vici:vici-31632.label: Tlos Stadium
vici:vici-31632.description: Tlos's Roman-era stadium, about 148 m long with shops opening onto it, hugs the acropolis slope; excavations since 2005 under Akdeniz University have exposed nine of its original seating rows and an adjoining paved street.

vici:vici-31633.label: Sutlegen Theatre - Nisa
vici:vici-31633.description: The small Roman-period theater of Nisa, a minor Lycian League city near modern Sütleğen that minted its own coins in the 2nd century BC, has 22 surviving rows of seating and is the best-preserved structure at the unexcavated site.

vici:vici-31846.label: Heraclea ad Latmum, Bouleuterion
vici:vici-31846.description: Hellenistic bouleuterion of Heraclea ad Latmum in Caria, sited at the northeast corner of the agora with U-shaped stone council seating comparable to the bouleuteria at Priene and Miletus; probably 2nd century BC.

vici:vici-32383.label: Helicon Theatre
vici:vici-32383.description: Theatre in the Valley of the Muses on Mt Helicon, built for the musical and dramatic contests of the Mouseia festival hosted by Thespiae; dated to the late 3rd–early 2nd century BC, excavated by the French School at Athens in 1888–1890.

vici:vici-32560.label: Paramythia Theatre - Elea
vici:vici-32560.description: Theatre of ancient Elea (Elaea), capital of the Thesprotian koinon from its mid-4th-century BC foundation; the cavea spanned 45–50 m and stood 8–9 m high, seating an estimated 3,000–4,000. Excavation of the site began in 1985.

vici:vici-32922.label: Archanes Theatre
vici:vici-32922.description: Minoan 'theatral area' within the Tourkogeitonia palace complex at Epano Archanes: a paved court crossed by raised walkways, with a stepped altar and sacred horns; excavated from 1964 by Yannis Sakellarakis alongside the Bronze Age palace.

vici:vici-33216.label: Kalydon, theatre
vici:vici-33216.description: The Pi-shaped theatre of Calydon, unusual among Greek theatres for its square orchestra and rectilinear stone benches; found in 1967 during roadworks and fully excavated by a Danish-Greek team 2001-2014, with the stage building dated to the mid-3rd century BC.

vici:vici-34119.label: Theater of Halaesa
vici:vici-34119.description: Hellenistic-Roman theater of the Sicilian polis Halaesa Archonidea near Tusa; rediscovered in the 2010s and under active excavation since the 2020s by archaeologists from Amiens University with Palermo and Messina, noted for its scale and preservation.

vici:vici-34988.label: Odeon
vici:vici-34988.description: The Odeon of Hippos (Sussita), a Decapolis city above the Sea of Galilee, was a small roofed venue (c. 27 x 21 m, semicircular) for poetry readings and recitals before a privileged audience, uncovered in excavations announced in 2009.

vici:vici-35024.label: Ulpia Augusta Traiana Theater
vici:vici-35024.description: The theatron of Augusta Traiana (Roman Beroe, renamed for Trajan after 106 CE) was built with marble seats under Marcus Aurelius (161-180 CE) for gladiatorial contests, processions, and civic assemblies.

vici:vici-37325.label: Ampfitheater of Issos
vici:vici-37325.description: A small Hellenistic theatre survives at Issus (Kinet Höyük, near Yeşilköy, Hatay Province), site of Alexander's decisive 333 BC battle against Darius III; the mound was excavated by Bilkent University between 1992 and 2012.

vici:vici-40183.label: Krommyon theater
vici:vici-40183.description: At Krommyon (modern Agioi Theodoroi) on the Corinthian coast, 1961 excavations uncovered a small circular structure of the late Archaic period (late 6th c. BC); whether it served as a tiny theatral area or a place of worship remains undetermined.

vici:vici-40184.label: Argos. the Roman odeon.
vici:vici-40184.description: Around 120 CE, under Hadrian's building program, the smaller of Argos's two ancient theatres — a 5th/4th-century BC archaic theatre seating roughly 2,500 — was roofed over and converted into a Roman odeum with brick seating faced in mosaic.

vici:vici-40185.label: Argos.the small theater in agora
vici:vici-40185.description: Argos's second, smaller theater, cut into the lower slope near the agora in the 5th century BC and seating around 2,500; under Hadrian the Romans roofed and remodeled it into an odeon for musical and rhetorical performances.
vici:vici-40185.wikidataDescription: ancient odeion and theater of Argos, Greece

vici:vici-4140.label: Amphitheatre Diocletianopolis
vici:vici-4140.description: Built at the end of the 3rd century AD within the walls of Diocletianopolis (modern Hisarya, Bulgaria), this irregular pear-shaped amphitheatre seated roughly 3,000 and is among the best-preserved in Bulgaria; its unusually central, intramural location and late Christian-era operation suggest bloodless spectacles.

vici:vici-4147.label: Amphitheatre Calleva Atrebatum
vici:vici-4147.description: Built around AD 55-75 outside the walls of Calleva Atrebatum (Silchester), this earthwork amphitheatre held roughly 3,500-7,000 spectators; rebuilt in stone in the 3rd century, it later saw post-Roman British and Anglo-Saxon reuse before an 1147 medieval fortification atop it.

vici:vici-4149.label: Amphitheatre Deva Victrix
vici:vici-4149.description: The largest Roman amphitheatre known in Britain, built outside the legionary fortress of Deva Victrix (Chester) by Legio II Adiutrix in the late AD 70s and rebuilt in stone by Legio XX Valeria Victrix around AD 100, seating an estimated 7,000-12,000 for entertainment and military training.

vici:vici-4150.label: Amphitheatre Durnovaria
vici:vici-4150.description: A Neolithic henge at Dorchester (Durnovaria) remodeled by the Romans around AD 60-70 into an amphitheatre, likely by Legio II Augusta, with its banks lowered and an oval arena cut for military displays and public spectacle; later reused as a Civil War fort and 17th-18th century execution site.

vici:vici-4152.label: Amphitheatre Isurium Brigantum
vici:vici-4152.description: An amphitheatre serving Isurium Brigantum (Aldborough), one of Roman Britain's civitas capitals, confirmed only by geomagnetic scanning in 2011; its earthworks were later reused as the motte of a Norman castle on Studforth Hill.

vici:vici-4154.label: Amphitheatre Noviomagus Reginorum
vici:vici-4154.description: Built c. AD 70-90 outside the walls of Noviomagus Reginorum (Chichester) near Stane Street, this timber-lined amphitheatre measured about 70 by 60 metres; discovered in 1935 by Raymond Carlyon-Britton and excavated by G. M. White, it was then backfilled and is now a shallow depression in a public park.
vici:vici-4154.wikidataDescription: Roman amphitheatre in Chichester, Chichester, England, UK

vici:vici-4158.label: Amphithéâtre Agedincum
vici:vici-4158.description: The amphitheatre of Agedincum (Sens), capital of the Senones in Gallia Lugdunensis; only its foundations survive, buried beneath the modern Rue des Arènes, whose curving course still traces the arena's outline.

vici:vici-4159.label: Amphithéâtre Aginnum
vici:vici-4159.description: The amphitheatre of Aginnum (Agen), built between the Augustan period and the later 1st century AD, measured about 115 x 100 m and held an estimated 12,000-15,000 spectators; its remains were only confirmed by rescue excavations in 1988-1989.

vici:vici-4161.label: Amphithéâtre Argentomagus
vici:vici-4161.description: Part of the secondary Gallo-Roman town of Argentomagus (Saint-Marcel, Indre), the amphitheatre stood alongside two successive theatre buildings and was used for hunts, animal displays, and gladiatorial combat.

vici:vici-4166.label: Amphithéâtre Burdigala
vici:vici-4166.description: Known since the Middle Ages as the Palais Gallien, this amphitheatre of Roman Burdigala (Bordeaux) was built in the late 1st or early 2nd century AD, measured 132 x 111 m, and held roughly 22,000 spectators; it is Bordeaux's only visible ancient monument today.

vici:vici-4171.label: Amphithéâtre Divodurum
vici:vici-4171.description: The amphitheatre of Divodurum (Metz), built between the late 1st and mid-2nd century AD, measured about 148 x 124 m with capacity near 25,000 and ranked among the largest in the Roman world; its plan was recovered from remains found in 1902 during railway station construction.

vici:vici-4173.label: Amphithéâtre Geinum
vici:vici-4173.description: A semi-amphitheatre built into the Mazerolles hillside at Gennes (ancient Geinum) in the late 1st century AD, with a cavea about 94 m across holding an estimated 5,000 spectators; used into the early 3rd century and first reported by antiquarians in 1837.

vici:vici-4174.label: Amphithéatre Grannus
vici:vici-4174.description: The amphitheatre at Grand (Andesina), built c. 80-140 AD beside the sanctuary of the healing god Apollo Grannus, had a major axis of 148 m and seated roughly 17,000-20,000, making it one of the ten largest amphitheatres of the Roman world; abandoned in the late 4th century.

vici:vici-4177.label: Amphithéâtre Limonum
vici:vici-4177.description: One of the grandest amphitheatres of Roman Gaul, built at Limonum (Poitiers) in the 1st-2nd century AD and measuring roughly 156 x 130 m, it may have held 22,000-30,000 spectators and was reportedly refortified as a citadel by the Visigoths in the 5th century.

vici:vici-4183.label: Amphithéâtre Samarobriva
vici:vici-4183.description: Unusually built at the very heart of Samarobriva (Amiens) beside the forum rather than on the city's edge, this amphitheatre (built late 1st-mid 2nd century AD, c. 113 x 99 m) could hold up to about 15,000 spectators; its remains lie buried beneath the modern city hall.

vici:vici-4184.label: Amphithéâtre Sanxay
vici:vici-4184.description: Semi-circular theatre-amphitheatre hybrid seating up to 6,600, part of the Gallo-Roman sanctuary of Sanxay, a 1st–2nd-century healing-water cult complex centered on an octagonal temple; excavated by Camille de La Croix from 1881.

vici:vici-4187.label: Amphithéâtre Vesontio
vici:vici-4187.description: Amphitheatre of Roman Vesontio, built in the 1st century AD on the Doubs's far bank with capacity of roughly 20,000, among Gaul's largest; abandoned by the 4th century and later quarried for the citadel and churches of Besançon.

vici:vici-4190.label: Amphitheatre Gortyn
vici:vici-4190.description: Elliptical amphitheatre (c.100m long) built in 2nd-century AD Gortyn, Roman capital of Crete and Cyrenaica; ten Christians were reportedly killed there by beasts in 249 AD during the Decian persecution.

vici:vici-4204.label: Amphitheatre Aquileia
vici:vici-4204.description: Amphitheatre of Aquileia, the Roman colony founded 181 BC that grew into a city of some 100,000 with its own circus and port; its remains survive only below ground after the site was sacked by Attila in 452 AD.

vici:vici-4211.label: Amphitheatre Caralis
vici:vici-4211.description: Rock-cut amphitheatre of Roman Caralis (Cagliari), built in the 2nd century AD partly carved from the limestone bedrock, seating around 10,000 for gladiatorial combats, beast hunts, and public executions.

vici:vici-4212.label: Amphitheatre Cales
vici:vici-4212.description: Amphitheatre of the Roman colony of Cales, dug into the tuff bedrock and built around the 1st century BC for gladiator shows, distinct from the city's separate stone theatre nearby.

vici:vici-4213.label: Amphitheatre Canusium
vici:vici-4213.description: Amphitheatre of Roman Canusium (Canosa di Puglia), an Apulian municipium on the Via Traiana near Trajan's arch; ancient descriptions record it as larger than the amphitheatre at Pompeii.

vici:vici-4220.label: Amphitheatre Egnatia
vici:vici-4220.description: So-called amphitheatre of Egnatia (ancient Gnathia); its small size (37 x 25 m) and lack of seating tiers or underground chambers have led some scholars to reinterpret it as a market plaza rather than a spectacle building.
