vici:vici-4221.label: Amphitheatre Eporedia
vici:vici-4221.description: The amphitheatre of Roman Eporedia (Ivrea) was built in the mid-1st century AD along the road to Vercelli, an elliptical arena (65m major axis) holding over 10,000 spectators; excavated 1955-1964.

vici:vici-4233.label: Amphitheatre Interamnia Praetutiana
vici:vici-4233.description: The brick-built amphitheatre of Interamnia Praetuttiorum (Teramo), dated to the late 1st-early 2nd century AD, measured 74 by 56 metres and held roughly 3,500 spectators; its remains were identified in 1937.

vici:vici-4245.label: Amphitheatre Neapolis
vici:vici-4245.description: The Roman theatre of Neapolis (1st century BC, rebuilt after the AD 62 earthquake or AD 79 eruption), held about 5,000 spectators and is where, per Tacitus and Suetonius, Emperor Nero made his public performing debut.

vici:vici-4251.label: Amphitheatre Peltuinum
vici:vici-4251.description: An amphitheatre at Peltuinum, a Vestinian town on the Via Claudia Nova founded mid-1st century BC and prosperous under Augustus from livestock, wine and saffron trade; the site declined after the earthquake of AD 346.
vici:vici-4251.wikidataDescription: Roman amphitheatre in San Pio delle Camere, Italy

vici:vici-4252.label: Amphitheatre Pollentia
vici:vici-4252.description: The amphitheatre of Roman Pollentia (Pollenzo), near the site of the 402 AD Battle of Pollentia where Stilicho defeated Alaric's Visigoths; the structure no longer stands, but the town's circular street plan still traces its outline.

vici:vici-42628.label: Saittai [Sidas]
vici:vici-42628.description: Saittai (Setae), a city of Lydia in the Katakekaumene region visited by Hadrian, is known from four 2nd-3rd century AD gladiator funerary stelae naming fighters Metbysos, Amphiaros, Maternos and Rhodon, alongside a large stadium.

vici:vici-4270.label: Amphitheatre Tutere
vici:vici-4270.description: The amphitheatre of Tuder (Todi), built outside the walls in the Augustan-period urban expansion; its remains are partly incorporated into the church of San Nicolò de Cryptis, built inside the old arena.

vici:vici-4273.label: Amphitheatre Venafrum
vici:vici-4273.description: The Verlasce amphitheatre of Venafrum (Venafro), built in the 1st century AD, measured 110 by 85 metres and is estimated to have held up to 15,000 spectators; an inscription recorded a gens Vibia benefactor's funding of the building.
vici:vici-4273.wikidataDescription: former Roman amphitheatre in Venafro, Italy

vici:vici-4289.label: Amphitheatre Trimontium
vici:vici-4289.description: The most northerly amphitheatre yet found in the Roman Empire, attached to the fort of Trimontium at Newstead; its use was proposed in 1993 and confirmed by a Bradford University excavation in 1996 — an oval arena of 37 by 30m seating about 1,500.
vici:vici-4289.wikidataDescription: Roman amphitheatre in Newstead, United Kingdom

vici:vici-4294.label: Amphitheatre Emerita Augusta
vici:vici-4294.description: Built under Augustus and dedicated in 8 BC beside the adjoining Roman theatre, Mérida's amphitheatre held about 15,000 spectators for gladiatorial combats and beast hunts; it forms part of the UNESCO-listed Archaeological Ensemble of Mérida.

vici:vici-4296.label: Amphitheatre Emporion
vici:vici-4296.description: Oval Roman amphitheatre built for the colonia of veterans Julius Caesar settled behind the older Greek city of Emporion; its 75 by 44m arena held only about 3,300 spectators, a more modest design than originally planned.

vici:vici-4301.label: Amphitheatre Tarraco
vici:vici-4301.description: Built in the 2nd century AD near Tarraco's forum (130 by 102m, c.15,000 seats), this amphitheatre is where bishop Fructuosus and his deacons Augurius and Eulogius were burned alive in AD 259 during Valerian's persecution of Christians.

vici:vici-4303.label: Amphitheatre Aventicum
vici:vici-4303.description: Built c. AD 120 and enlarged about 30 years later, the amphitheatre of Aventicum (capital of Roman Helvetia) seated roughly 9,000 across 24 rows; partly quarried for lime in the 6th century, it is Switzerland's best-preserved amphitheatre.

vici:vici-4305.label: Amphitheatre Julia Equestris
vici:vici-4305.description: Amphitheatre of the Caesarian veterans' colony Colonia Iulia Equestris (Nyon); discovered by chance in 1996, its arena measured about 50 by 36m and dates to the early 2nd century AD, with an inscription linking construction to the reign of Trajan.

vici:vici-4313.label: Amphitheatre Carthago
vici:vici-4313.description: Built in the late 1st or early 2nd century AD with roughly 30,000 seats, one of Roman Africa's largest amphitheatres; traditionally linked to the 203 AD martyrdom of Perpetua and Felicity, commemorated by a 19th-century chapel on the site.

vici:vici-43138.label: Theater
vici:vici-43138.description: Geophysical survey about 300m east of the Palais des Papes revealed a large circular structure at Roman Avenio (Avignon), interpreted as a theatre or amphitheatre; no remains are visible above ground and its precise function is unconfirmed.

vici:vici-4316.label: Amphitheatre at Ksar Lemsa
vici:vici-4316.description: At Roman Limisa (Ksar Lemsa), a small entertainment building — recorded by different sources as an amphitheatre or theatre — stood beside a well-preserved 6th-century Byzantine fortress with intact corner towers; the site was excavated in 1966-69.

vici:vici-4321.label: Amphitheatre Pheradi Maius
vici:vici-4321.description: At Pheradi Maius (Sidi Khalifa, Sousse Governorate), an African town raised to municipium status under Marcus Aurelius, an amphitheatre stood alongside a triumphal arch, Capitol, nymphaeum, and baths within the town's civic complex.

vici:vici-4327.label: Theatre Aquae Segetae
vici:vici-4327.description: The theatre at the Gallo-Roman spa sanctuary of Aquae Segetae (Sceaux-du-Gâtinais), dedicated to the healing goddess Segeta, measured about 104m across and could seat over 10,000 pilgrims visiting its baths and temple, peaking in the 2nd century AD.

vici:vici-4330.label: Amphitheatre Thibaris
vici:vici-4330.description: Thibaris, a town of Africa Proconsularis near ancient galena mines at Djebba, was a Christian bishopric suffragan to Carthage whose bishops attended councils at Carthage in 256 and 411 AD; an amphitheatre also stood among the town's ruins.

vici:vici-4332.label: Amphitheatre Thimisua
vici:vici-4332.description: At Thimisua (Sidi-Bou-Argoub, Siliana Governorate), a civitas of Africa Proconsularis downstream from Thabbora, the amphitheatre is oval with two opposed entrances set along its longitudinal axis; little else about the structure has been published.

vici:vici-4333.label: Amphitheatre Thugga
vici:vici-4333.description: At Thugga (Dougga), Tunisia's best-preserved small Roman town, an amphitheatre stands apart from the site's famous 3,500-seat theatre, built in 168-169 AD by local benefactor P. Marcius Quadratus; the amphitheatre itself is far less studied.

vici:vici-4341.label: Amphitheatre Utica 2
vici:vici-4341.description: One of two Roman amphitheatres identified at Utica, the Phoenician-founded city that became capital of Africa Proconsularis after Carthage's destruction in 146 BC; today largely ruined and unexcavated.

vici:vici-4343.label: Amphitheatre Aizanoi
vici:vici-4343.description: Part of Aizanoi's unique theatre-stadium complex in Phrygia (2nd-3rd c. AD): the theatre and stadium stand directly adjoined, separated only by a colonnaded street, with capacities of roughly 20,000 and 13,500 respectively.

vici:vici-4345.label: Amphitheatre Isca Augusta
vici:vici-4345.description: Built around AD 80 for Legion II Augusta's fortress at Caerleon; timber benches seated up to 6,000 for gladiatorial games. Excavated in 1926-27, it is Britain's most complete Roman amphitheatre, long known locally as 'King Arthur's Round Table'.

vici:vici-43615.label: Obulco Ampfitheatre
vici:vici-43615.description: Amphitheatre of Obulco, rediscovered in 2014 beneath Porcuna's Hoyo Mendo district and excavated from 2022; built c. 1st century BC/AD for a city Caesar used as a base before the Battle of Munda (45 BC), holding over 10,000.

vici:vici-43776.label: Attalea [ Antalya]
vici:vici-43776.description: Attalea (modern Antalya) was founded as a naval base by King Attalus II of Pergamon, probably before 150 BC, and named for him; bequeathed to Rome in 133 BC by Attalus III.

vici:vici-4390.label: Théâtre d'Alésia
vici:vici-4390.description: Gallo-Roman theatre on Mont-Auxois, built in the later 1st century AD within the vicus that grew on the site of Caesar's siege of Alesia (52 BC); semicircular cavea about 81m across, seating an estimated 5,000.

vici:vici-44812.label: Theater Vieux-la-Romaine
vici:vici-44812.description: Theatre of Aregenua, capital of the Viducasses near Caen, built as the town acquired monumental Roman-style buildings in the 1st-3rd centuries AD; its cavea measured about 80 by 67 metres, a mid-sized Gallo-Roman theatre.

vici:vici-44923.label: Megalopolis, Thersilio Vouleftirio
vici:vici-44923.description: The Thersilion, council hall of the Arcadian League built c. 370 BC beside the theatre of Megalopolis and nicknamed the 'Hall of the Ten Thousand'; destroyed by Cleomenes III of Sparta in 222 BC.

vici:vici-45466.label: Castulo Ampfitheater
vici:vici-45466.description: Detected by georadar and LiDAR survey in 2016 within the walled Iberian-Roman city of Castulo (Linares, Jaén), one of several monumental buildings — alongside a theatre, forum and baths — from the city's Roman-era expansion; largely unexcavated.

vici:vici-45510.label: Astigi Amphiteather
vici:vici-45510.description: Its remains lie beneath Écija's 19th-century bullring; at roughly 130 x 107 m with an 80-arch exterior facade modeled on Rome's Flavian Amphitheatre, it likely shared architects with the amphitheatre at nearby Italica.

vici:vici-45568.label: Ampfiteater of Cesaraugusta
vici:vici-45568.description: Unlike the city's well-preserved Roman theatre, the amphitheatre of Caesaraugusta has never been conclusively located; a long-standing theory placing it beneath the Hotel Palafox site has not been confirmed by excavation.

vici:vici-46394.label: Missua Theater
vici:vici-46394.description: Missua (modern Sidi Daoud, Cap Bon) was a Roman port town of Africa Proconsularis with trade ties to Ostia and a Christian bishopric attested from 484 AD; its theatre remains stand near the ancient harbor and breakwater.

vici:vici-48059.label: Circo Romano de Castulo
vici:vici-48059.description: First identified via 2016 LiDAR and georadar survey north of Castulo's walled Iberian-Roman city (Linares, Jaén); its existence had long been suspected but its exact location was only pinpointed through this remote-sensing work.

vici:vici-48683.label: Ampfiteater of Barcino
vici:vici-48683.description: A largely vanished Roman amphitheatre of Barcino; no confirmed remains have been excavated, though archaeologist Jordina Sales hypothesizes a location near Santa Maria del Mar based on the district's oval street pattern.
vici:vici-48683.wikidataDescription: Roman amphitheatre in the Ribera district of Barcelona, Spain

vici:vici-49118.label: Singilia Barba Circus
vici:vici-49118.description: A circus at the Roman municipium of Singilia Barba, identified through epigraphic evidence and geophysical survey near the city's buried theatre (capacity c. 2,200), part of a monumental zone that also included a forum.

vici:vici-49794.label: Théâtre antique de Meaux
vici:vici-49794.description: Gallo-Roman theatre of Iatinum (Meaux), built in the 1st–2nd century AD; a 1993–94 rescue excavation uncovered cavea substructures spanning over 150 m, and an inscription credits its funding to a local notable, Orgetorix.

vici:vici-49922.label: Amphithéâtre Vindunum
vici:vici-49922.description: Gallo-Roman amphitheatre of Vindunum (Le Mans), capital of the Aulerci Cenomani; rediscovered in 1791 by architect Daudin during urban works and destroyed the following year when the Jacobins promenade was laid out.

vici:vici-50043.label: Circus of Contributa Iulia Ugultunia
vici:vici-50043.description: Structure at the Roman town of Contributa Iulia Ugultunia (Medina de las Torres, Badajoz), identified in 2016 via geophysical survey as an amphitheatre, one of the first found this way in Iberia; the site preserves an unusually intact street grid.

vici:vici-50056.label: Astigi Circus
vici:vici-50056.description: Circus of the Roman colony Augusta Firma Astigi (Écija), built outside the walls between the Via Augusta and the road to Augusta Emerita; a semicircular structure near the presumed prima meta was clarified by 2023–2024 excavations.

vici:vici-50062.label: Consuegra Circus
vici:vici-50062.description: Roman circus of ancient Consabura, confirmed by geophysical survey and 2017 excavations; an 18th-century plan recorded it at roughly 370 x 80 m with a capacity near 10,000, one of only about a dozen archaeologically documented circuses in Roman Hispania.

vici:vici-50599.label: Wadi Sabra Theatre
vici:vici-50599.description: Small horseshoe-shaped Nabataean-Roman theater (39 m wide, 11 rows seating 500-800) cut into a gully at Sabra near Petra; built in the 1st century AD with a water-channel system beneath the seating, remaining in use into the late Roman period.

vici:vici-50768.label: Ampfiteater
vici:vici-50768.description: The unfinished Roman theater of Palmyra, built in the Severan 2nd century AD with a cavea of eleven sections/twelve rows never completed; buried in sand for centuries, it was excavated and restored in the 1950s, and its stage facade was destroyed by ISIL in 2017.

vici:vici-52623.label: Thessaloniki, Hippodrome
vici:vici-52623.description: Built in the early 4th century AD under the Tetrarchy, this roughly 450 x 95 m racecourse was the site of the 390 AD massacre in which Theodosius I's Gothic troops killed thousands of citizens after a riot; fragments survive beneath the modern Hippodromiou district.

vici:vici-54949.label: Italica, Circus
vici:vici-54949.description: Geophysical surveys announced in 2023 revealed likely remains of a Roman circus east of Italica's Hadrianic quarter — an exceptionally large structure some 532 m long with capacity for up to 80,000 spectators; a 1799 mosaic of chariot-race scenes and racehorse graffiti in the city's theater had earlier hinted at its existence.

vici:vici-55079.label: Durocortorum, Amphitheater
vici:vici-55079.description: Built around AD 15–45, among the earliest amphitheaters raised in Roman Gaul alongside those of Lyon and Saintes, it stood north of Durocortorum near the road to Boulogne-sur-Mer; its remains had vanished by the mid-19th century and were rediscovered in 2007–08 during tramway construction.

vici:vici-55148.label: Lepcis Magna, Theater Porticus
vici:vici-55148.description: The colonnaded porticus post scaenam behind Leptis Magna's theater enclosed a temple to the Dei Augusti; built by Iddibal of the Tapapius family (who also built the theater itself) and dedicated by the proconsul Quintus Marcius Barea.

vici:vici-55892.label: Bouleuterion, Sia - Taştandam
vici:vici-55892.description: The council house of Hellenistic Sia, a Pisidian city near Bucak founded c. 2nd century BC; it is the only building at the site securely predating Roman rule, when three temples, an agora with Doric stoa, and Byzantine basilicas were added.

vici:vici-55971.label: Remains of Sinuessa amphitheatre
vici:vici-55971.description: Amphitheatre (about 80 by 45 m) of the Roman colony of Sinuessa, founded 296 BC near modern Mondragone; the town was noted for its thermal springs and Falernian wine before coastal erosion later submerged part of the settlement.

vici:vici-57005.label: Sikyon, Stadium
vici:vici-57005.description: Stadium of ancient Sicyon, lying just west of the city's theatre and shaped largely by the hillside; unlike fully excavated Greek stadia, seating did not run the full length of the track, with one end built up on fill.

vici:vici-58188.label: Panathenaic stadium (restored)
vici:vici-58188.description: Athens' Panathenaic Stadium was built c. 330 BC under Lycurgus for the Panathenaic Games, rebuilt entirely in Pentelic marble by Herodes Atticus by 144 AD, and restored again for the first modern Olympics in 1896 as the world's only all-marble stadium.

vici:vici-58426.label: Amfitheater of Treia
vici:vici-58426.description: Amphitheatre of Trea, a Roman municipium on a Picene/Sabine hilltop near modern Treia that flourished from Augustus to Antoninus Pius; its oval outline is still traceable as a crop mark near the Santuario del Santissimo Crocifisso.

vici:vici-58447.label: Theilenhofen Theater
vici:vici-58447.description: Geophysical survey in 2010–11 near the Roman fort Iciniacum (Theilenhofen) on the Raetian Limes revealed a c. 75 m theatre-shaped structure beside a large plaza interpreted as a forum, probably temporary buildings for a single major event.

vici:vici-58541.label: Inveresk Amphitheatre
vici:vici-58541.description: A curving timber structure identified as a possible amphitheatre stood in the civilian settlement outside the east rampart of Inveresk Roman fort near Musselburgh, occupied from Antoninus Pius's AD 139/140 invasion; if confirmed, the empire's northernmost amphitheatre.

vici:vici-58553.label: Forden Gaer Amphitheatre
vici:vici-58553.description: A possible amphitheatre with only scant surface traces, lying east of the mid-1st-century Roman auxiliary fort at Forden Gaer, which guarded a crossing of the River Severn near Montgomery, Wales.

vici:vici-58567.label: Bitburg Theater
vici:vici-58567.description: Known only from inscriptions (CIL XIII 4132, 198 CE, and a text of 253 CE) recording that Lucius Ammatius Gamburio endowed the theatre of Beda (Bitburg) with 50,000 denarii and funded annual games, probably for the Floralia; the building itself has never been located.

vici:vici-58763.label: Ampfitheater of Adria
vici:vici-58763.description: Amphitheatre of Roman Hatria (Adria); its buried foundations near the Canalbianco were found in rescue excavations and later traced by ground-penetrating radar, its superstructure having been stripped away in the Middle Ages.

vici:vici-59657.label: Liffremont
vici:vici-59657.description: Site of a Roman fortified camp at Liffremont; 19th-century finds included gold, silver and bronze imperial coins and the 3rd-century marble 'Venus of Liffremont' (now in Rouen's Museum of Antiquities); the location of a theatre was also identified here, though it remains unexcavated.

vici:vici-60167.label: Tebessa Theatre - Theveste
vici:vici-60167.description: Small theatre in Theveste (Tébessa, Algeria), built after the city was refounded as a base for Legio III Augusta; the colony also has a 3rd-century triumphal arch of Caracalla and a 4th-century amphitheatre.

vici:vici-60175.label: Theatre
vici:vici-60175.description: 1st-century AD theatre of the Roman town of Libarna (Piedmont), with a 22-arch external ambulatory on sandstone-based pillars; the ruins, later damaged by farming and two railway lines, sit beside the town's amphitheatre and baths.

vici:vici-60254.label: Odeon
vici:vici-60254.description: Josephus records that Herod the Great funded a theatre at Damascus, one of several benefactions (gymnasia, temples, colonnades) to Greek cities outside his own kingdom; the structure's physical remains have not been securely located.

vici:vici-60356.label: Amfiteatrul roman de la Casian
vici:vici-60356.description: Not a built amphitheatre but a natural rock formation ('Pietrele Scrise') near Casian in Dobrogea, bearing two Greek boundary inscriptions ('Oroi Kasianon') dated to the 2nd-3rd century AD and first deciphered by Vasile Pârvan in 1912-13.

vici:vici-61475.label: Possible hippodrome
vici:vici-61475.description: Hypothesized Roman circus at Nemausus (Nîmes), proposed by archaeologist Richard Pellé from imported sand deposits found near Rue Cité Foulc matching the arena floor; if real, it would postdate the amphitheatre, built in Beaucaire limestone in the later 2nd century AD.

vici:vici-61640.label: Villa Antonii - Commodus' amphitheater
vici:vici-61640.description: 2nd-century AD amphitheatre at the 'Villa of the Antonines' near Genzano di Roma (ancient Lanuvium), a family estate of the Antonine dynasty; possibly the arena where Commodus killed wild beasts and earned the nickname 'Roman Hercules'.

vici:vici-61935.label: Blicquy
vici:vici-61935.description: A Gallo-Roman theatre discovered in 1993 near the sanctuary of Blicquy, the only known Roman theatre building in Belgium; timber-and-stone construction about 70m across, estimated to have seated 5,000-6,000.

vici:vici-62026.label: Dimal Theatre
vici:vici-62026.description: Theatre of the Illyrian hill city of Dimale (Dimallum), built amid Hellenistic urban expansion in the 3rd-2nd century BC; the fortified city was captured by Rome under L. Aemilius Paullus in 219 BC after a seven-day siege.

vici:vici-62184.label: Pelusium Hipodrom
vici:vici-62184.description: A hippodrome tentatively identified in 1993 from Roman-period brick pillars at Pelusium (Tell el-Farama), one of only two hippodromes known from Roman Egypt, alongside Antinoöpolis.

vici:vici-62185.label: Ampfiteater of Pelusium
vici:vici-62185.description: A large imperial-period amphitheatre at Pelusium (Tell el-Farama), excavated from 1992 and linked to a drainage system serving the surrounding city; identified by archaeologist Ahmed el-Tabai.

vici:vici-62189.label: Holz Amphitheater von Unterkirchberg
vici:vici-62189.description: A modest wooden amphitheatre with a circular palisade ditch built in the southern corner of the timber-and-earth Roman fort at Unterkirchberg (Illerkirchberg) on the Raetian Danube limes, founded under Claudius.

vici:vici-62216.label: Carteia circus
vici:vici-62216.description: The Roman circus of Carteia (San Roque, Cadiz), whose spina and meta secunda were documented in 2017 excavations, confirming a chariot-racing track at this Phoenician-Carthaginian-Roman port city on the Bay of Gibraltar.

vici:vici-62218.label: Valentia circus
vici:vici-62218.description: The Roman circus of Valentia (Valencia), built in the 2nd century AD, measured roughly 350 x 70m and could seat up to 10,000; first identified in 1987, its remains lie beneath several buildings in Ciutat Vella.

vici:vici-62225.label: Consuegra Theater
vici:vici-62225.description: Site of Roman Consabura, predecessor of Consuegra; a rare Roman circus — one of only about a dozen securely attested in Hispania — was excavated here in December 2017 near Viriato Park.

vici:vici-62499.label: Amphitheater
vici:vici-62499.description: Oval Roman amphitheatre of Divona Cadurcorum (Cahors), c. 110 by 90 metres, built in the 1st century AD; its buried remains were found beneath Place Gambetta during car-park construction and opened to visitors in 2009.

vici:vici-62501.label: Theatre
vici:vici-62501.description: The Roman theatre of Augustodunum (Autun), built into a hillside in the later 1st century AD, spanned some 148 metres and held up to c. 14,000 — the second-largest theatre in the Roman world after Pompey's in Rome.

vici:vici-62995.label: Possible stadium
vici:vici-62995.description: Located within the Hellenistic-Roman city of Zeugma on the Euphrates, a Seleucid foundation that became a Roman legionary base and major commercial hub; the stadium is among the site's identified but still largely unexcavated public buildings.

vici:vici-63003.label: Pompeiopolis-Odeon I
vici:vici-63003.description: Small odeon at Pompeiopolis, the Paphlagonian capital founded by Pompey the Great in 64 BCE (modern Taşköprü); German-led excavations resumed here in 2024 and exposed the structure beneath a roughly two-metre-thick ash layer.

vici:vici-63321.label: Amphitheater
vici:vici-63321.description: Roman-era remains found in 1908 on Pisa's Via San Zeno during foundations work for the Institute of Physiology; a contemporary survey (kept at the Museo di San Matteo) never resolved whether the structure was a theatre or an amphitheatre, and it remains unexcavated, buried beneath the modern city.

vici:vici-63461.label: Hamat Gader Theatre - Emmatha
vici:vici-63461.description: Roman theatre at the Emmatha hot springs (Hamat Gader), built in the 3rd century CE with about 2,000 basalt seats arranged in 15 rows around the orchestra, near baths begun by the Legio X Fretensis garrison from Gadara.
vici:vici-63461.wikidataDescription: human settlement in the Golan Heights

vici:vici-63475.label: Caesarea's Eastern Hippodrome
vici:vici-63475.description: The southern end of Herod's hippodrome/stadium at Caesarea (built 10/9 BC, c.457x76m, seating ~38,000) was rebuilt in the 2nd century CE into an oval amphitheater for gladiatorial combat and venationes.

vici:vici-63557.label: Troy Theater
vici:vici-63557.description: The Great Theatre of Roman Ilium (Troy), first built c.306 BC, was rebuilt under Augustus with a three-tiered scaenae frons (completed 12-11 BC); cavea diameter 98.6m, seating roughly 7,700-9,650.

vici:vici-63803.label: Amphitheater
vici:vici-63803.description: A medium-sized (c.70x100m) amphitheater of Forum Sempronii, identified in 2009 aerial photography near modern Fossombrone; its rubble-core walls faced in opus vittatum remain largely buried and unexcavated.

vici:vici-64584.label: Circus
vici:vici-64584.description: Despite the generic vici label "Circus," this point marks the Roman theatre of Alba Fucens, built 2nd-1st century BC on the Pettorino hill slope east of the Hercules sanctuary; no longer visible above ground today.

vici:vici-64631.label: Calatis
vici:vici-64631.description: Greek Calatis (Heraclea Pontica colony, founded 6th c. BC; modern Mangalia, Romania) is attested by inscriptions as having had a theatre, but the building's physical remains have never been located archaeologically.

vici:vici-64633.label: Curubis
vici:vici-64633.description: A late 2nd-century CE inscription honoring citizen Marcus Manlius Modestus Quietianus records his private funding of a theatre at Curubis (modern Korba, Tunisia); the building itself has never been located.

vici:vici-64635.label: FURNOS MINUS
vici:vici-64635.description: Theater of the Romano-Berber town Furnos Minus, identified with Henchir-el-Msaadine near Tebourba; a bishopric of Africa Proconsularis whose Christian cemetery yielded a celebrated 5th–6th-century mosaic of Daniel in the Lions' Den, now in Tunisia's Bardo Museum.

vici:vici-64636.label: Gurza
vici:vici-64636.description: Theater of Gurza, a civitas of Roman Byzacena at modern Kalâa Kebira and later seat of an episcopal see (revived in 1933 as a Catholic titular bishopric); the theater is catalogued in Lachaux's survey of Proconsular African theaters.

vici:vici-64639.label: Valis theater
vici:vici-64639.description: Theater of Vallitanus (Sidi Medien), a Romano-Berber colonia and Africa Proconsularis bishopric under Carthage; the theater ruins there are documented in Frank Sear's architectural survey of Roman theaters, alongside inscriptions naming local officials.

vici:vici-64641.label: Kisamos
vici:vici-64641.description: Roman theater of Kissamos (Kastelli Kissamou), the free Roman city (civitas libera) that succeeded Hellenistic Kisamos as Polyrrhenia's port; first noted by 16th-century observer Onorio Belli, its seating and stage-building stones mapped by Thomas Spratt in the 19th century are now lost.

vici:vici-64642.label: ANTINOOPOLIS
vici:vici-64642.description: Theater of Antinoöpolis, the city Hadrian founded on 30 October AD 130 on the Nile in memory of his drowned companion Antinous; its ruins near the southern gate, still visible to Napoleonic surveyors and recorded in the Description de l'Égypte, were later quarried away for building stone.

vici:vici-64643.label: CROCODILOPOLIS THEATER
vici:vici-64643.description: Theater of Crocodilopolis/Arsinoe (Medinet el-Fayum), the Ptolemaic-Roman capital of the Faiyum and cult center of the crocodile god Sobek, whose sacred pool-kept crocodile Petsuchos, adorned with gold pendants, drew pilgrims and tourists into Roman times.

vici:vici-64645.label: OXYRHYNCHUS THEATER
vici:vici-64645.description: A vast 2nd-century AD Roman theatre excavated by Flinders Petrie, estimated to have seated up to 11,000 spectators — among the largest in Roman Egypt; later stripped as a stone quarry, leaving only fragmentary remains.

vici:vici-64647.label: Daphne theater
vici:vici-64647.description: The chronicler John Malalas records that Vespasian built this theatre on the site of a former synagogue using spoils from the Jewish War; American and French teams excavated it in 1932-1940.

vici:vici-64648.label: Seleucia ad Calycadnum theater
vici:vici-64648.description: Roman-era theatre of Seleucia ad Calycadnum (modern Silifke); largely unexcavated, overgrown and built over, with its orchestra long used as a depot for local buses.

vici:vici-64650.label: CITIUM THEATER
vici:vici-64650.description: A theatre has long been conjectured for Hellenistic-Roman Kition (Larnaca) but has never been definitively located or excavated; most of the ancient city lies buried beneath the modern town.

vici:vici-64653.label: Ampfitheater
vici:vici-64653.description: This 2nd-century Roman amphitheatre of Narbo Martius measured about 122 x 93 m and could hold an estimated 25,000 spectators; its buried remains, located via 1838 surveys, underlie modern Narbonne's street plan.

vici:vici-64666.label: Amphitheater
vici:vici-64666.description: Amphitheater of the Roman spa town Aquae Statiellae (modern Acqui Terme), built on the settlement's outskirts near the Via Aemilia Scauri and identified by excavation in the 1960s alongside the town's thermal baths.

vici:vici-65356.label: Amphitheater
vici:vici-65356.description: Amphitheater of Roman Carpis (colonia Iulia Carpitana), a Cape Bon coastal town possibly founded under Caesar or Augustus; its rubble-masonry remains stand beside a large cistern that received an aqueduct at El Mraissa.

vici:vici-65977.label: Ampfitheater
vici:vici-65977.description: Amphitheater of Roman Parma, known as the 'Arena' in ancient and medieval sources; sections of its perimeter wall found in 1846 and 1933 suggest a capacity near 25,000 seated spectators before its destruction in the 6th century.

vici:vici-66000.label: Circus
vici:vici-66000.description: Ancient Panormus is attested to have had a circus and amphitheater by a 2nd-century AD inscription honoring one Aurelianus for staging games; aerial-photo analysis has proposed a curving structure in the Loggia/Vucciria quarter, though the site remains debated.

vici:vici-66001.label: Ampfitheater
vici:vici-66001.description: Panormus's amphitheater is attested by a 2nd-century AD inscription from San Cataldo recording gladiatorial games and animal hunts sponsored by one Aurelianus; its exact location is debated, with this Loggia/Vucciria-quarter site suggested by aerial-photo curvature analysis.

vici:vici-66293.label: Amphitheater
vici:vici-66293.description: Roman amphitheater of Augustodunum (Autun), built in the second half of the 1st century AD next to the city's famous theater; at roughly 154x130m it ranked among the largest in the Roman Empire, but was fully quarried away by the 18th century and rediscovered only through 1832 and 1844 excavations.

vici:vici-66294.label: Amphitheater
vici:vici-66294.description: The Grohan amphitheater of Juliomagus (Angers), built around AD 115 with capacity for roughly 6,000 spectators; unusually well-documented from a 1637 survey by Claude Ménard, it survived until the 17th century before being destroyed, with the last traces lost to 19th-century street works.

vici:vici-66413.label: Nevers
vici:vici-66413.description: Nevers occupies the site of Noviodunum, an Aeduan oppidum on the Loire where Caesar stockpiled Gallic hostages, grain, army pay and cavalry horses in 52 BC; the Aedui massacred the Roman garrison there and burned the town during the revolt recounted in his Gallic War, book VII. No specific theater structure at the site is confirmed by excavation.

vici:vici-66417.label: Possible amphitheater
vici:vici-66417.description: Remains of a spectacle building at Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence), discovered only in 2004; the curvature of its excavated seating rows has not settled whether it was a semicircular theater or an oval amphitheater.

vici:vici-66446.label: Theater
vici:vici-66446.description: Roman theater of Tolosa (Toulouse), built under Augustus between the Place du Pont-Neuf and La Daurade with seating for about 8,000; its foundations were located in 1869 during construction of rue de Metz, but virtually nothing survives above ground today.

vici:vici-66499.label: Theater
vici:vici-66499.description: Square Castan in Besançon (Roman Vesontio): a semicircular hemicycle roughly 54m across, ringed by eight re-erected Corinthian columns, uncovered by Auguste Castan in 1870. Long identified as a Roman theater, specialists now favor reading it as a colonnaded podium of uncertain function tied to the Arcier aqueduct's water-distribution basin.

vici:vici-66536.label: Ambracia.Great theater .(ruins)
vici:vici-66536.description: The Great Theatre of ancient Ambracia, discovered in 1981 near Arta's Tsakalov Street; the Corinthian colony became King Pyrrhus of Epirus's capital in 295 BC, who adorned it with theatres and palaces.

vici:vici-67575.label: Stadium
vici:vici-67575.description: The stadium of Antioch in Pisidia (near Yalvaç), a Hellenistic-period structure restored in the 2nd century AD and later dismantled by Christians in late antiquity, served the Roman colony founded by Augustus in 25 BC.

vici:vici-67867.label: Odeon
vici:vici-67867.description: The Hellenistic odeon of Selinus in Cilicia, cut into a rectangular cavea seating roughly 1,000, stands near the spot where Emperor Trajan died on 8 August 117 AD, after which the town was briefly renamed Trajanopolis.

vici:vici-67883.label: Lamos-Stadion
vici:vici-67883.description: A stadium associated with the fortified Roman/Byzantine city of Lamos in Rough Cilicia, whose surviving gate bears a dedication to Emperor Gallienus; most standing remains date to the 2nd-3rd centuries AD.

vici:vici-68504.label: Misis Theatre
vici:vici-68504.description: The theatre of Mopsuestia (Misis) on the Pyramus (Ceyhan) river, a Cilician city legendarily founded by the seer Mopsus, whose surviving ruins also include a Roman bridge, stadium and colonnaded street.

vici:vici-68517.label: Circus
vici:vici-68517.description: The stadium of Apamea Kibotos (Celaenae) in Phrygia, founded by Antiochus I Soter and site of the 188 BC Treaty of Apamea between Rome and the Seleucids; partial remains survive near modern Dinar.

vici:vici-69769.label: Théâtre gallo-romain de Saint Paulien
vici:vici-69769.description: Theatre of Ruessium, Gallo-Roman capital of the Vellavi civitas, apparently built around AD 50 under Claudius; its site was recently proposed via archival and cadastral research, comparable in scale to the theatres of Moingt and Javols.

vici:vici-69855.label: HYPAİPA Theater
vici:vici-69855.description: Theatre of Hypaepa, a Lydian city in the Cayster valley regarded as second only to Ephesus in regional importance; the theatre stood on the western slopes of the acropolis within the fortified city.

vici:vici-70239.label: Corinth circus
vici:vici-70239.description: Remains of Corinth's Roman circus, identified as the 'Apsidal Building' uncovered in the 1967-68 Gymnasium-area excavations; planned into the Caesarian city's Augustan design, it hosted equestrian events of the Caesarea and Isthmian games.

vici:vici-70249.label: Circus of Carmona
vici:vici-70249.description: Roman circus of Carmona, an estimated 290 m long and built into the local slope, part of the city's spectacle complex with its amphitheatre and necropolis; poorly documented and its construction date still uncertain.

vici:vici-70582.label: Hipodrome
vici:vici-70582.description: Roman circus of Corduba (Cordoba), capital of Baetica, built between the reigns of Nero and Domitian at roughly 400 x 100 m with an ornamented spina; abandoned after structural failure by the mid-2nd century AD.

vici:vici-70674.label: Trigarium
vici:vici-70674.description: Open equestrian training ground in the Campus Martius, named for the triga (three-horse chariot); first attested under Claudius and used into the 4th century, kept free of permanent structures near the Tiber bend.

vici:vici-70699.label: Artaxata theatre
vici:vici-70699.description: Theatre of Artaxata, the Hellenistic Artaxiad capital founded c. 176 BC on the Araxes; excavations have identified it as Armenia's earliest known theatre, evidence of the city's Greek-influenced civic and cultural life.

vici:vici-71499.label: Sitzstufe des Theaters
vici:vici-71499.description: Inscribed stone seating steps from the Roman theatre of Lopodunum (Ladenburg), found in the Burgacker district and identified in the 1960s by archaeologist Berndmark Heukemes; donor inscriptions name citizens such as Optatius Tetricius.

vici:vici-71652.label: Ostra Theater
vici:vici-71652.description: The Roman theatre of Ostra, excavated in 1903–04 and restored in 2020, measured only 44.6 m across with three tiers of seating — the smallest Roman theatre known in the Marche region.

vici:vici-71807.label: Potentia Theater
vici:vici-71807.description: Theatre remains within Potentia, a Roman colony founded 184 BC on the Adriatic coast to settle Punic War veterans; the town prospered on the terracotta trade before a 56 BC earthquake devastated it.

vici:vici-73115.label: Neung- sur- Beuvron
vici:vici-73115.description: The Gallo-Roman theatre of Neung-sur-Beuvron, dated late 1st–early 2nd century AD, formed part of a rural sanctuary with a temple and spring; c. 100 m across, it held perhaps 7,000 spectators and was used until the 3rd century.

vici:vici-73117.label: Neuvy-sur-Barangeon
vici:vici-73117.description: A Gallo-Roman theatre discovered in 1834 near the probable site of Noviodunum of the Bituriges, but never excavated or documented since.

vici:vici-73275.label: Antibes Theater
vici:vici-73275.description: The Roman theatre of Antipolis is attested chiefly by the funerary stele of the child performer Septentrion, who ‘danced and was applauded’ on its stage; sited near the Porte Royale, it was demolished in 1691.

vici:vici-73276.label: Antipolis Ampfitheater
vici:vici-73276.description: A Roman amphitheatre at Antipolis is known only from its oval outline on 17th–18th-century fortification plans of Antibes; its physical remains vanished during the town's refortification, and scholars still debate whether it truly existed.

vici:vici-73280.label: Theatre of Thouria
vici:vici-73280.description: An early Hellenistic theatre unearthed in 2016 by archaeologist Xeni Arapogianni on the Ellinika ridge at Thouria, near Kalamata; its 16.3 m limestone orchestra and first row of seats survive from when Thouria was the leading city of western Messenia.

vici:vici-73281.label: Theatre of Panormos Fiskardo
vici:vici-73281.description: A Roman-era theatre with orchestra, stone-backed seating and a niche was found in 2006 beside a Roman mausoleum and cemetery at Fiskardo (ancient Panormos), Kefalonia, during hotel construction.

vici:vici-73330.label: Savatra
vici:vici-73330.description: Roman-period theatre at Savatra (Soatra), an autonomous Lycaonian city near modern Yağlıbayat, Turkey; excavations from 2021 exposed its stage, orchestra and cavea steps — a rare central-Anatolian example, said to have doubled as the city's council hall.
vici:vici-73330.wikidataDescription: titular see of Galatia, in modern-day Turkey

vici:vici-73352.label: Stadium of Dion
vici:vici-73352.description: Earthen stadium in the sanctuary quarter of Dion, Macedonia, tied to the "Olympia" games traditionally founded under Archelaus I (late 5th c. BC); excavated in 1995, with coin finds spanning Alexander I to Philip V.

vici:vici-73353.label: Stadion Molykreion
vici:vici-73353.description: A ~32m stadium with three rows of stone seating, the only one known in western mainland Greece besides Olympia's, found in 2014 in the sanctuary of Athena and Poseidon on the acropolis of ancient Molykreion, Aetolia.

vici:vici-73358.label: hippodrome of Delos
vici:vici-73358.description: U-shaped horse- and chariot-racing course on Delos (west side ~300m long), edged by a terrace wall built for Athens' 5th-century BC revival of the games, with a horse-watering well near the presumed starting line.

vici:vici-73370.label: Stadion of Megalopolis
vici:vici-73370.description: Stadium of Megalopolis, capital of the Arcadian League founded 371–368 BC; Pausanias records a temple of Dionysus on its east side and a spring sacred to the god within it, adjoining the city's colossal theatre.

vici:vici-73795.label: Newton Kyme
vici:vici-73795.description: Multi-period site on the River Wharfe with two successive Roman forts, temporary camps and a vicus guarding the Lincoln–Aldborough road crossing; no securely attested Roman theatre survives, though the adjacent Neolithic henge has been speculated to have been reused as an amphitheatre.

vici:vici-74491.label: Antioch on the Maeander
vici:vici-74491.description: Seleucid city (earlier Pythopolis), founded/enlarged by Antiochus I at the Maeander–Orsinus confluence in Caria; ancient sources attest both a theatre and a stadium, of which a stone Roman-period stadium ~200m long survives near modern Kuyucak.

vici:vici-78057.label: ANCIENT THEATRE SYROS
vici:vici-78057.description: Hellenistic-era theatre of ancient Syros; its ashlar seating blocks survive incorporated into later buildings near Ano Syra, one of the few traces of the island's ancient public architecture.

vici:vici-78059.label: Ancient Theatre of Pagai
vici:vici-78059.description: Theatre of Pagai (Pagae), a fortified Megarian harbour city on the Corinthian Gulf near modern Kato Alepochori, strategically important from the Persian Wars through the Peloponnesian War as recorded by Thucydides.

vici:vici-7892.label: Odeum of Amman
vici:vici-7892.description: Small Roman odeon seating about 500, built in the 2nd century CE (likely under Antoninus Pius or Marcus Aurelius) beside the larger Roman Theatre of Philadelphia; used for music, poetry, and lectures.
vici:vici-7892.wikidataDescription: Ancient Roman odeon in Amman, Jordan

vici:vici-78993.label: théâtre gallo-romain de Sainte-Ruffine
vici:vici-78993.description: Gallo-Roman theatre uncovered in a 2022 rescue excavation near Metz, on the Roman road to Reims via Verdun; estimated to have held up to 6,000 spectators, possibly at the site of ancient Ibliodurum.

vici:vici-7905.label: Theatre of Glanum
vici:vici-7905.description: Roman theatre built under Augustus as part of Glanum's monumental rebuilding alongside temples, a basilica, baths, and a triumphal arch, on a Hellenistic town site centered on a sacred healing spring.

vici:vici-80853.label: Circus of Hadremetum
vici:vici-80853.description: Chariot-racing circus at Hadrumetum (Sousse); its existence is attested chiefly by 3rd-century AD mosaics, including one from the House of Sorothus naming winning circus horses such as Adorandus and Crinitus.

vici:vici-80875.label: Hippodrome of Caesarea-Mazaca)
vici:vici-80875.description: Roman hippodrome of Caesarea Mazaca (Kayseri), capital of Roman Cappadocia from Tiberius's reign; buried beneath the modern city, its roughly 450 m track was located in 2024 via old maps and geophysical survey.

vici:vici-81143.label: Sirmium Hipodrome
vici:vici-81143.description: The imperial hippodrome of Sirmium, built c. 312–324 under Licinius or Constantine beside the tetrarchic imperial palace; roughly 450 x 150 m and seating up to 10,000, it is the only known unexcavated Roman hippodrome, lying buried beneath modern Sremska Mitrovica.

vici:vici-8145.label: Kastell Zugmantel - nördliches Amphitheater
vici:vici-8145.description: One of a rare pair of earthen amphitheatres in the vicus of the Flavian-era auxiliary fort Zugmantel on the Upper Germanic Limes; an oval roughly 50 m across ringed by a 13 m-wide, 1.5 m-high earth bank, likely combining spectacle with troop training ground.

vici:vici-8146.label: Kastell Zugmantel - östliches Amphitheater
vici:vici-8146.description: The second of two earthen amphitheatres flanking the civilian settlement of the Roman fort Zugmantel on the Upper Germanic Limes — amphitheatres are very rare on the frontier, and this pair likely served both as performance venues and as training grounds for the garrison.

vici:vici-81558.label: Augusta theater ?
vici:vici-81558.description: Theatre of Roman Augusta in Cilicia, a colony founded in 20 AD and named for Livia; a 1955 rescue survey recorded its open-air auditorium (c. 62 m across) along with a triumphal arch, colonnaded streets, and baths just before the site was submerged by the new Seyhan Dam reservoir.

vici:vici-82733.label: Ampfitheater ?
vici:vici-82733.description: Site of Troesmis, a Roman legionary fortress on the Lower Danube limes, home of Legio V Macedonica (107–163) and later a municipium under Marcus Aurelius (c. 177); no amphitheatre here is independently confirmed in the literature.

vici:vici-82904.label: Theater of Aqua Flaviae
vici:vici-82904.description: Aquae Flaviae, a thermal spa town in Roman Gallaecia named for the Flavian dynasty, raised to municipium status in 79 CE under Vespasian; famed for its hot springs and later spanned by Trajan's bridge over the Tâmega.

vici:vici-83086.label: Theater of Lutetia.
vici:vici-83086.description: Gallo-Roman theatre-amphitheatre hybrid in Lutetia (Paris), built in the 1st century CE and seating up to 15,000; sacked in the 275 raids, later filled in, then rediscovered by Théodore Vacquer in the 1860s and saved after Victor Hugo's campaign.

vici:vici-83134.label: Mušov
vici:vici-83134.description: Hradisko hilltop fortress near Mušov, the principal Roman military base of the Marcomannic Wars (172–180), built deep in Germanic territory under Marcus Aurelius; excavations found a bath complex, but no theatre or amphitheatre is attested at the site.

vici:vici-84196.label: CADYANDA (Üzümlü)
vici:vici-84196.description: Cadyanda's Hellenistic theatre, built late 2nd–early 1st century BCE, was repaired and reused under Roman rule; about 20 rows of seating survive on the hillside above Üzümlü, though the stage building has been destroyed.

vici:vici-84198.label: Hipponion theater
vici:vici-84198.description: Theater identified in 1971 in Vibo Valentia's Terravecchia quarter (ancient Hipponion, a Greek colony of Locri Epizefiri, refounded as the Latin colony Valentia in 192 BC); only retaining walls and part of the lower cavea's steps survive.

vici:vici-84203.label: NEMUS ARICINUM THEATER
vici:vici-84203.description: Part of the Sanctuary of Diana Nemorensis at Lake Nemi (nemus Aricinum), founded c. 300 BC around the cult of Diana of the Wood; the complex also had baths, a nymphaeum and pilgrim lodgings for the annual August Nemoralia festival.

vici:vici-84206.label: SCOLACIUM THEATER
vici:vici-84206.description: Theater of the Roman colony Minervia Scolacium, founded 123-122 BC by Gaius Gracchus on the Greek site of Skylletion; built into the hillside with room for c. 3,500 spectators, it flourished under Nerva's refoundation around AD 96.

vici:vici-84213.label: MONS FERETER  THEATER
vici:vici-84213.description: An AD 148 inscription from the hilltop town of Mons Feretrius (modern San Leo) records a marble-adorned theatre — "theatrum marmoribus ornatum" — the principal evidence for the building, whose remains are not extensively excavated.

vici:vici-84214.label: Pisaurum theater
vici:vici-84214.description: The Roman theatre of Pisaurum (Pesaro) lies beneath the former Filanda silk-mill on Via De Amicis; excavations resumed there in 2021 under the Marche Superintendency as part of plans for a future museum of Roman Pesaro.

vici:vici-84215.label: PITINUM MERGENS THEATER
vici:vici-84215.description: The theatre of Pitinum Mergens, identified near Catirano along the Via Flaminia by University of Urbino excavations, had a stage set parallel to the road and two concentric corridors supporting a cavea about 70 m in diameter.

vici:vici-84216.label: GENUA THEATER
vici:vici-84216.description: Built in the Augustan era on the slope of Genoa's San Giusto hill overlooking the harbor and restored under Trajan by Q. Petronius Modestus, the theatre stayed in use into late antiquity (even hosting gladiatorial shows); identified in 1814, excavated in 1938.

vici:vici-84217.label: Polentia theater
vici:vici-84217.description: Theatre of Roman Pollentia (Pollenzo), built in the earlier 1st century AD with a two-tier cavea about 74 m across and a 34 m orchestra, seating roughly 6,000 — the largest Roman theatre known in Piedmont.

vici:vici-84220.label: LAUS POMPEII THEATER
vici:vici-84220.description: Roman theatre of Laus Pompeia (Lodi Vecchio): so little structural fabric survives along the presumed main street that scholars could attempt only a virtual reconstruction of its stage building.

vici:vici-84222.label: Agyrium theater
vici:vici-84222.description: Per Diodorus Siculus, a native of Agyrium, its theatre — part of Timoleon's building program after 339 BC, when he settled 10,000 Greek colonists there — ranked as the finest in Sicily after Syracuse's; little survives beneath modern Agira.

building:118575.label: Arnsburg
building:118575.description: A circular amphitheater in the vicus of Kastell Arnsburg, a Wetterau Limes cohort fort built around AD 90 under Domitian and garrisoned into the 3rd century; the amphitheater was identified by geophysical survey rather than excavation.

building:236512.label: Legio VII Gemina
building:236512.description: The legionary amphitheater of Legio VII Gemina's fortress at Leon, one of only about five known legionary amphitheaters in the Roman Empire; built in phases from the 1st century AD, it held roughly 5,000 spectators across fifteen tiers.

pl-109016.label: Grannum?
pl-109016.description: Ancient Grand grew around a sanctuary of the Gallo-Roman healing god Apollo-Grannus and built the eighth-largest amphitheater in the Roman world (capacity 16,000–20,000); Emperor Caracalla reportedly visited its shrine in 213 AD.

pleiades:802040030.label: Rotes Haus (Tell Schech Hamad)
pleiades:802040030.description: Elite residence of about 90 rooms at Dūr-Katlimmu (Tell Sheikh Hamad), built by Šulmu-šarri, a senior official of Ashurbanipal (r. 668–631 BC), in the late 7th century BC; it outlasted Assyria's fall before burning down in the 6th century BC.

vici:vici-10793.label: Palast der Cercadilla
vici:vici-10793.description: Palatial complex built at Corduba (Córdoba) around 296–297 AD, attributed to the tetrarch Maximian, centered on a 109-m cryptoporticus and audience hall; rediscovered in 1991 during construction of the AVE railway station and later reused as a Christian cult site.

vici:vici-10881.label: ARDAŠIR KHUREH Palace
vici:vici-10881.description: Palace built in AD 224 by Ardashir I, founder of the Sasanian Empire, near his new capital Ardashir-Khwarrah (Gor, modern Firuzabad); its brick domes on squinches over square chambers are among the earliest known examples of this technique.

vici:vici-11534.label: Praetorium CCAA
vici:vici-11534.description: Seat and residence of the Roman governor of Germania Inferior, uncovered by chance beneath Cologne's town hall in 1953; grew to roughly 40,000 m² over four building phases and is the only known praetorium whose name survives in an inscription.

vici:vici-11535.label: Palace of Antiochus
vici:vici-11535.description: Built 416-418 for the powerful chamberlain Antiochus near the Hippodrome of Constantinople; became imperial property after his fall in 421, and part of it was later converted into the Church of St Euphemia.

vici:vici-11739.label: Römischer kaiserlichen Palast in Milano
vici:vici-11739.description: Imperial residence built by co-emperor Maximian after Diocletian made Mediolanum capital of the Western Roman Empire in 286 AD; excavations near Via Brisa since 1951 have uncovered walls, mosaic floors and baths of the vast complex.

vici:vici-17720.label: Praetorium di Muru de Bagiu
vici:vici-17720.description: Secondary residence of the Roman governor of Sardinia at Muru de is Bangius (Marrubiu), built 2nd-3rd century AD with a porticoed courtyard, 16 rooms and private baths with polychrome mosaics; its function was confirmed in 1990 by an inscribed marble plaque.

vici:vici-17806.label: Palace of Galerius
vici:vici-17806.description: Imperial residence begun 298-299 AD for Caesar Galerius, linked by a colonnaded road to the Rotunda and his triumphal arch; its best-preserved hall, the domed Octagon (875 m²), likely served as the throne room.

vici:vici-17843.label: Palace of Nestor
vici:vici-17843.description: Mycenaean palace excavated by Carl Blegen from 1939; a fire around 1180 BC that destroyed the building also baked and preserved its archive of over 1,000 Linear B tablets, the largest such find on the Greek mainland.
vici:vici-17843.wikidataDescription: archaeological site, part of ancient Pylos

vici:vici-17850.label: Palace, Gorsium
vici:vici-17850.description: Governor's residence built in the 4th century on the main street of Gorsium-Herculia, a Roman town in Pannonia that served as the province's religious center and assembly site; excavated from 1958 under archaeologist Jenő Fitz.

vici:vici-17862.label: Northern Palace, Masada
vici:vici-17862.description: Herod the Great's private pleasure palace, added around 25 BC, cascading down three rock-cut terraces on Masada's northern cliff face with a semicircular portico, a Roman bathhouse and mosaic floors, in a style echoing Augustan Rome.

vici:vici-17863.label: Western Palace, Masada
vici:vici-17863.description: Herod's largest structure at Masada (c. 4,000 m², built from 35 BCE), a Middle Eastern/Greek-style administrative and ceremonial palace with a throne room and fine mosaic floors, distinct from the more Roman-styled Northern Palace.

vici:vici-17869.label: Palace of Agrippa II, Caesarea Philippi
vici:vici-17869.description: Built by Herod Agrippa II at Caesarea Philippi (Banias), a roughly 10,000 m² complex with a basilica, mosaic-paved courtyards and opus reticulatum walls, later converted into a bathhouse used through the 2nd–5th centuries CE.

vici:vici-17890.label: Palace, Bustan al-Khan
vici:vici-17890.description: A 2nd-century CE Roman portico of twelve columns south of Baalbek's Temple of Jupiter, likely the sanctuary's southern gate, near a bathhouse modeled on Trajan's Baths in Rome — not a residential palace despite the label.

vici:vici-18005.label: Palace, Apollonia
vici:vici-18005.description: The Palace of the Dux at Apollonia, seat of the Byzantine military governor (dux) of Libya Superior, built late 5th–early 6th century CE; per Procopius, governor Hecebolus's mistress Theodora — later Justinian's empress — lived here.

vici:vici-18045.label: Palace, Ptolemais
vici:vici-18045.description: The Palazzo delle Colonne, a peristyle mansion of some 600 m² near the agora, probably the governor's residence from the late Hellenistic through Byzantine periods; excavated 1936–42, it was destroyed in the catastrophic 365 CE earthquake, which crushed people fleeing through its courtyard.
vici:vici-18045.wikidataDescription: Government building/palace/basilica; Domestic building/villa/house in Libya

vici:vici-18077.label: Palace, Bosra
vici:vici-18077.description: Known as the "Palace of Trajan" from an old (now revised) belief it was built by Trajan on the site of the Nabataean royal palace; archaeology dates it instead to the late 5th century CE, among the largest houses in southern Syria, likely home to Bosra's governor or archbishop.

vici:vici-18102.label: Palace of the Dux Ripae
vici:vici-18102.description: A monumental (87.5 x 62.5 m) Roman military palace built at Dura-Europos under Elagabalus (218–222 CE) as residence of the dux ripae overseeing the Euphrates frontier — inscriptions name officer Domitius Pompeianus — abandoned after the Sasanian capture of the city in 256 CE.
vici:vici-18102.wikidataDescription: former Ancient Roman palace in Dura-Europos

vici:vici-19322.label: Ai Khanum, palace
vici:vici-19322.description: Palace complex of the Hellenistic city Ai-Khanoum (Alexandria on the Oxus), with a 27,000 m² courtyard ringed by 118 Corinthian columns; held administrative offices and a treasury where Hellenistic coin hoards were found. Excavated by a French team under Paul Bernard, 1965-1978.

vici:vici-19355.label: Sessorium
vici:vici-19355.description: Imperial residence in south-east Rome, begun under Septimius Severus and completed by Elagabalus; from the early 4th century it housed Helena, mother of Constantine, and part of its great hall became the basilica of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.

vici:vici-19356.label: Aegae, Royal Palace
vici:vici-19356.description: Palace of Philip II at Aegae (Vergina), ancient capital of Macedon -- the largest building of Classical Greece, probably designed by the architect Pytheos. Alexander the Great was proclaimed king here in 336 BC. Excavated by Manolis Andronikos through 1970; reopened after restoration in 2024.

vici:vici-19486.label: Praetorium Londinium
vici:vici-19486.description: A lavish late-1st-century AD building complex (c.130 x 100 m) beneath Cannon Street Station, with reception halls, mosaic floors and an ornamental pool. Excavator Peter Marsden read it as the governor's palace, though scholars now favor an administrative function.

vici:vici-20282.label: Constantinople, Bucoleon Palace
vici:vici-20282.description: Byzantine palace on the Sea of Marmara shore south of the Hippodrome, probably built under Theodosius II in the 5th century, enlarged by Theophilos and walled by Nikephoros II in 969; the emperors' favored seaside residence until eclipsed by Blachernae.

vici:vici-20319.label: Constantinople, Blachernae Palace
vici:vici-20319.description: Byzantine imperial residence on Constantinople's northwestern hill, developed from Late Antiquity and vastly expanded by the Komnenoi from the 11th century, becoming the main imperial seat after the Great Palace's decline; restored by the Palaiologoi after 1261, destroyed in 1453.

vici:vici-20325.label: Constantinople, Triklinos of the Candidati
vici:vici-20325.description: A reception hall in Justinian's Great Palace of Constantinople housing the Candidati imperial guard, likely built during the rebuilding after the Nika riots of 532; known mainly from the 10th-century ceremonial protocols of the De Ceremoniis.

vici:vici-20445.label: Persepolis, Apadana
vici:vici-20445.description: Monumental audience hall of Persepolis, begun by Darius I and finished by Xerxes I in the early 5th century BC; 72 columns 24 m tall roofed its 1,000 m², with reliefs of 23 subject nations bearing tribute. Burned in 331 BC.
vici:vici-20445.wikidataDescription: large hypostyle hall, the best known examples being the great audience hall and portico at Persepolis and the palace of Susa

vici:vici-20447.label: Persepolis, Palace of Darius
vici:vici-20447.description: Darius I's private residence, called Tachara ('winter palace'), finished after his death by Xerxes I. Built in the finest gray stone, it was one of the few structures to survive Alexander's fire of Persepolis in 330 BC largely intact.

vici:vici-20449.label: Persepolis, Palace of Xerxes
vici:vici-20449.description: Xerxes I's private residence, called Hadish ('dwelling place'), twice the size of Darius's Tachara and built on Persepolis's highest terrace; tradition holds the fire that destroyed the city in 330 BC began here.

vici:vici-20450.label: Palace, Treasury
vici:vici-20450.description: Persepolis's fortress-like treasury and armory, begun by Darius I and enlarged by Xerxes; excavations by Ernst Herzfeld and Erich Schmidt (1933-1938) recovered the Persepolis Treasury Archive, roughly 750 tablets recording silver payments to workers.

vici:vici-20454.label: Persepolis, Hall of a Hundred Columns
vici:vici-20454.description: Persepolis's second-largest building, the Throne Hall, begun by Xerxes I and finished by Artaxerxes I; a 68.5m-square hall of 100 columns later used as a storeroom for the overflowing Treasury.

vici:vici-20459.label: Pasargadae, Residential Palace
vici:vici-20459.description: Cyrus the Great's private residence at Pasargadae, built of pale stone kept naturally cold; an Old Persian inscription naming Cyrus was later added under Darius I, whose reliefs also depict a king leaving the hall with an attendant.

vici:vici-20460.label: Pasargadae, Audience Palace
vici:vici-20460.description: Cyrus the Great's audience hall at Pasargadae, centered on the oldest known free-standing stone column in Iran (over 13m); its doorway reliefs of a fish-man and bull-man are among the earliest Achaemenid sculptures.

vici:vici-20461.label: Pasargadae, Gate Palace
vici:vici-20461.description: Monumental free-standing gatehouse of Cyrus the Great's palace at Pasargadae; one door jamb preserves the famous four-winged 'genius' relief, once mistakenly thought to be a portrait of Cyrus himself.

vici:vici-20464.label: Susa, Achaemenid Audience Palace
vici:vici-20464.description: Apadana (audience hall) of Darius I's palace at Susa, built after 515 BC; excavated by Marcel and Jane Dieulafoy (1884-1886), whose glazed-brick friezes of archers and lions are now in the Louvre.

vici:vici-20467.label: Susa, Apadana
vici:vici-20467.description: Achaemenid audience hall built by Darius I at Susa from 518 BC as part of his palace complex; a 36-column hypostyle hall nearly 109 m square, its walls faced with glazed-brick friezes of archers and lions, damaged by fire under Artaxerxes I.

vici:vici-21310.label: Ebla Royal Palace G
vici:vici-21310.description: Early Bronze Age royal palace at Ebla, built c. 2400 BC and destroyed c. 2300 BC; excavated from 1964 by Paolo Matthiae, its archive rooms yielded over 1,000 cuneiform tablets, among the oldest state archives known.

vici:vici-21491.label: Palace of Amenhotep III - Malkata [Malqata]
vici:vici-21491.description: Vast mud-brick palace city built by Amenhotep III on Thebes' west bank from his 11th regnal year (c. 1370s BC), the largest royal residence of its time, with residential palaces, a temple to Amun, and an artificial lake; abandoned after Akhenaten moved the capital to Amarna.

vici:vici-21577.label: Caesarea Maritima, palace
vici:vici-21577.description: Herod the Great's Promontory Palace projected on an artificial platform into the sea, its lower terrace centred on a rock-cut swimming pool ringed by porticoes; later served as the praetorium of Roman governors, including Pontius Pilate.

vici:vici-21736.label: Mamshit, Palace
vici:vici-21736.description: Known as Beit HaAmidim ("House of the Pillars"), a three-storey mansion built around a central courtyard in the Nabataean-turned-Roman town of Mamshit (Mampsis), likely the residence of a local governor, 2nd century AD.

vici:vici-21769.label: Nimrud, Palace of Assurnasirpal II
vici:vici-21769.description: The Northwest Palace at Nimrud (ancient Kalhu), built by Ashurnasirpal II from c. 878 BC as his royal residence, roughly 200 by 130 m and lined with alabaster reliefs; inaugurated with a ten-day feast for over 69,000 guests per his own inscription, excavated by Layard from 1845.

vici:vici-22779.label: Afrosiab, Sogdian palace
vici:vici-22779.description: Palace of the Sogdian ruler Varkhuman at Afrasiyab (old Samarkand); its Hall of Ambassadors was decorated c. 648-651 AD with murals of foreign envoys from China, Korea, and Iranian lands, discovered in 1965 and destroyed by Arab forces c. 675-677 AD.

vici:vici-23038.label: Pula Arena
vici:vici-23038.description: Built c. 27 BC–68 AD under Augustus through Vespasian, Pula Arena is the sixth-largest surviving Roman amphitheatre, holding roughly 20,000 spectators for gladiatorial games; its full elliptical outer wall survives intact.

vici:vici-24796.label: Gortyn, Praetorium
vici:vici-24796.description: Seat of the Roman governor of Crete and Cyrenaica at Gortyn, built in the 1st century AD with a second building phase in the 2nd century; part of the civic center alongside the Nymphaeum, Roman baths, and temple of Apollo Pythios.

vici:vici-24844.label: Knossos Little Palace
vici:vici-24844.description: Multi-story Minoan elite residence northwest of the main palace at Knossos, first excavated by Arthur Evans from 1905; destroyed by fire in Late Minoan IIIA2, which baked and preserved Linear B tablets and clay sealings on site.

vici:vici-24880.label: Palace of Archelaos in Pella
vici:vici-24880.description: Royal residence built for Archelaus I of Macedon at Pella around 400 BC, replacing Aigai as the main royal seat; Archelaus had it decorated by the painter Zeuxis and hosted the playwright Euripides there. Later enlarged into a c. 75,000 sq m complex under Philip II; birthplace of Alexander the Great.

vici:vici-25107.label: Palace at Megiddo
vici:vici-25107.description: Tel Megiddo's Iron Age stratum (VA-IVB) contained two monumental ashlar-built palaces, Palace 6000 and Building 1723, excavated by Yigael Yadin in the 1960s; once attributed to Solomon's 10th-century BC building program, they are now generally redated to the 9th-century BC Omride dynasty.

vici:vici-25109.label: Megiddo, Solomon`s Palace
vici:vici-25109.description: Palace 6000 at Megiddo, an ashlar-built structure traditionally attributed to King Solomon's 10th-century BC building program and excavated by Yigael Yadin in the 1960s; radiocarbon dating and stratigraphy now place it in the 9th century BC, the Omride era.

vici:vici-25143.label: Carchemish – Kargamiš -  Karkemish
vici:vici-25143.description: Hittite provincial capital and later a major Neo-Hittite/Luwian city on the Euphrates; excavated 1911-1914 and 1920 by the British Museum under D. G. Hogarth and Leonard Woolley, with T. E. Lawrence as assistant, uncovering relief-carved Iron Age processional ways and palace remains.

vici:vici-25297.label: Palace of Gordian, Volubilis
vici:vici-25297.description: Largest building at Volubilis (74 rooms), formed by joining two earlier houses and rebuilt by Marcus Ulpius Victor under Emperor Gordian III (238-244 AD); likely served as the imperial procurator's residence, named for an inscription found there.

vici:vici-25415.label: Mari, Palace of Zimrilim
vici:vici-25415.description: Royal Palace of Mari (Tell Hariri), Syria: a c. 2.5-hectare complex reaching its final form under King Zimri-Lim in the 18th century BC; discovered in 1935 and excavated by André Parrot, its burnt archive yielded more than 20,000 cuneiform tablets.
vici:vici-25415.wikidataDescription: royal palace of the kingdom of Mari in eastern Syria

vici:vici-84223.label: Gela theater
vici:vici-84223.description: No physical remains of a theatre have ever been found at Gela; its existence is known only from literary tradition. The tragedian Aeschylus, active across Sicily, died in Gela in 456 BC.

vici:vici-84224.label: Henna theater
vici:vici-84224.description: In 214 BC, during the Second Punic War, the Roman garrison under Lucius Pinarius massacred Henna's citizens after gathering them in the town's theatre on suspicion of planning to defect to Carthage (Livy 24.37–39).

vici:vici-84225.label: Cassinomagus theater
vici:vici-84225.description: Part of Cassinomagus's monumental Gallo-Roman sanctuary at Chassenon, this horseshoe-shaped spectacle building ("la Léna"), roughly 70–80m across, stood alongside the site's famed 2nd-century thermal baths and temple complex.

vici:vici-84227.label: DERVENTUM THEATER
vici:vici-84227.description: Built in successive phases from the 1st to 3rd century AD, the Gallo-Roman theatre of Derventum (Drevant) measured 85m in diameter and held an estimated 5,300 spectators, remaining in use into the 4th century.

vici:vici-84233.label: BELGINUM THEATER
vici:vici-84233.description: Excavations in 1969–73 at the Treveran vicus Belginum (Wederath) uncovered a small Gallo-Roman cult theatre within its temple precinct, part of a settlement occupied continuously from about 600 BC to 400 AD.

vici:vici-84234.label: CONTIOMAGUS THEATER
vici:vici-84234.description: At the vicus Contiomagus (Pachten, Dillingen/Saar), inscribed sandstone seating blocks excavated in 1961–63 are interpreted as remains of a small 2nd-century cult theatre tied to a temple complex — the only confirmed theatre site in the Saarland.

vici:vici-84236.label: VERBINUM THEATER
vici:vici-84236.description: Built in the later 1st century AD at Verbinum, a Gallo-Roman vicus at the crossroads of roads linking Bavay–Reims and Saint-Quentin–Macquenoise, this theatre held several thousand spectators; excavated since 1870, its stage wall bears traces of destruction by fire.

vici:vici-84239.label: FORUM SEGUSIAVORUM THEATER
vici:vici-84239.description: The theater of Forum Segusiavorum (Feurs), chief town of the Segusiavi, is known only from an inscription; as in other small Gallic towns it likely had wooden rather than stone tiered seating.

vici:vici-84253.label: JULIOBONA THEATER
vici:vici-84253.description: Built in the 1st century AD on the hillside above Lillebonne and enlarged in the 2nd-3rd centuries, this hybrid theater-amphitheater measured about 106 x 94 m and seated over 5,000; identified in 1764 by the Comte de Caylus.

vici:vici-84254.label: JULIOMAGUS THEATER
vici:vici-84254.description: Likely the hybrid theater-amphitheater known as 'de Grohan,' built around 115 CE with seating for roughly 6,000; unusually for a Gallo-Roman arena it is documented in records as early as 1529, before its 17th-century destruction.

vici:vici-84255.label: MEDIOLANUM AULERCORUM THEATER
vici:vici-84255.description: Built into a hillside during the reign of Claudius (41-54 CE), with a 75 m facade and a 24 m cavea radius, this theater at Evreux was excavated in 1843 then razed by the property owner.

vici:vici-84268.label: IADER THEATER
vici:vici-84268.description: A Roman theater stood at Iader (Zadar) into the early modern era before being demolished in 1657 to make way for a Venetian fortress built on the site.

vici:vici-84271.label: LUCURGENTUM HISPALENSE THEATER
vici:vici-84271.description: A theatre is attested for Lucurgentum (Roman-era Morón de la Frontera, near Hispalis in Baetica), inferred from ancient literary/epigraphic testimony catalogued in Sear's 'Roman Theatres'; no physical remains have ever been identified or excavated.

vici:vici-84272.label: TUCCI THEATER
vici:vici-84272.description: A theatre is recorded for Tucci (Colonia Augusta Gemella Tuccitana, modern Martos, Jaén) purely from literary and epigraphic references to spectacles; no physical remains have been found, and Sear's catalogue lists it among Hispania's inferred, unexcavated theatres.

vici:vici-84273.label: MAGO THEATER
vici:vici-84273.description: A theatre is listed for Roman Mago (modern Mahón, Menorca) in Sear's catalogue of Roman theatres, broadly dated to the 1st century; no remains have been located, and its existence rests on inference rather than excavation.

vici:vici-84274.label: PANOPOLIS THEATER
vici:vici-84274.description: The theatre of Panopolis (Akhmim), a city associated with the cult of Pan, is attested in Roman-period papyri as a venue for festivals and athletic games, but its physical remains have never been substantially excavated or located.

vici:vici-84275.label: ANTIPATRIS THEATER
vici:vici-84275.description: A small semicircular Roman odeon-theatre was excavated at Antipatris (Tel Afek), a city founded by Herod the Great and named for his father Antipater; it stood at the end of the site's colonnaded cardo and hosted musical performances.

vici:vici-84276.label: Elusa theater
vici:vici-84276.description: The only known theatre of the central Negev, excavated in part by Avraham Negev at the Nabataean-Roman-Byzantine city of Elusa (Haluza); built on a roughly 27 m axis with a maximum diameter of about 34.5 m, oriented southeast-northwest.

vici:vici-84277.label: ARETHUSA THEATER
vici:vici-84277.description: At Arethusa (modern Al-Rastan on the Orontes), a Seleucid foundation traditionally credited to Seleucus I Nicator, the French archaeologist Edmond Frézouls recorded surviving cavea seating rows of a Roman theatre in his 1952 survey of Syria's theatres.

vici:vici-84278.label: Maximianopolis in Arabia Theater
vici:vici-84278.description: At Shaqqa, renamed Maximianopolis in AD 287 for co-emperor Maximian and raised to colonia and probable garrison-town status, a Roman theatre built of local black basalt survives among the town's well-preserved kalybe, 'Kaisariye', and temple of Zeus Megistos.

vici:vici-84294.label: CERAMUS THEATRE
vici:vici-84294.description: Theatre of Ceramus (Keramos), a Carian city on the Ceramic Gulf near modern Ören; Hellenized by the 6th century BC, it joined the Athenian League and later the Chrysaoric League, minting its own coinage in Roman times.

vici:vici-84300.label: Aegina theater
vici:vici-84300.description: Ancient theatre on the acropolis hill of Kolonna, Aegina, described by Pausanias (2nd century AD) as comparable in size and workmanship to the theatre of Epidaurus; the hill has been excavated since Charles Robert Cockerell's 1811 dig.

vici:vici-84301.label: Aegina stadium
vici:vici-84301.description: Ancient stadium adjoining the theatre on the Kolonna acropolis at Aegina, part of the sanctuary complex first explored in Cockerell's 1811 excavation and further investigated in 1903, 1924 and 1966.

vici:vici-8508.label: Theatre Scolacium
vici:vici-8508.description: Roman theatre at Scolacium (Colonia Minervia Scolacium, built over the Greek city of Skylletion), raised on a hillside in the 1st century AD with seating for roughly 5,000; it stands within the archaeological park near Roccelletta di Borgia, Calabria.

vici:vici-8516.label: Theatre Odeon
vici:vici-8516.description: Odeon of Roman Catania, probably built in the 2nd century AD beside the main theatre on ground once linked to a sanctuary of Demeter and Kore; it seated about 1,500 for musical and poetic contests and rehearsals, and was fully excavated in the 19th century.

vici:vici-87102.label: Kitanaura Antik Tiyatrosu
vici:vici-87102.description: Theatre of Kitanaura, a Lycian hill city near Saraycık in Antalya's Kumluca district, unmentioned by any ancient author; its identity was fixed only through a 1998 coin study and a Roman milestone found at Patara in 1993, with fortifications spanning Hellenistic to Byzantine phases.

vici:vici-87375.label: Kıran Gölü Antik Tiyatrosu
vici:vici-87375.description: A theatre within a sanctuary north of ancient Loryma on the Bozburun Peninsula, likely predating the Hellenistic period. Its wall construction matches 4th-century-BCE work at nearby Amos, and its plan exceeds a semicircle; no stage building has been found.

vici:vici-9852.label: Roman theatre Capitolias
vici:vici-9852.description: Roman theatre of Capitolias (Beit Ras), a Decapolis city founded c. 97-98 CE under Nerva or Trajan and named for Jupiter Capitolinus. Archaeoseismic study identified at least two ancient earthquake phases that damaged and helped end its use.

building:118337620.label: Commercial Stoa of Mytilene
building:118337620.description: A c. 150 m long Hellenistic commercial stoa excavated at Epano Skala in Mytilene, next to the moles of the city's ancient North Harbour, its principal commercial port.

dare-42919.label: Basílica de Son Peretó
dare-42919.description: Paleochristian basilica (5th-7th century) near Manacor, Mallorca, showing Syrian-Palestinian architectural influence, with a baptistery holding two fonts and an associated necropolis; excavated from 1912 under the initiative of Monsignor Aguiló.

dare-17481.label: Pompeiacum/Vernemetis
dare-17481.description: A sanctuary named Pompeiacum or Vernemetis in antiquity (Antonine Itinerary, Venantius Fortunatus); a basilica was raised in the early 5th century over the newly discovered tomb of St Vincent, whose relics were later moved to escape Viking raids. Its precise modern location (Caumont-sur-Garonne vs Le Mas-d'Agenais) is debated by scholars.

dare-17717.label: S. Quiricus, Mon.
dare-17717.description: A monastery dedicated to St Quiricus, mentioned by Gregory of Tours, localized near modern St-Cirgues-sur-Couze in the Puy-de-Dôme (Barrington Atlas / Pleiades gazetteer).

dare-21296.label: Baldersdorf
dare-21296.description: An 11th-century circular church, excavated in 1995–97, that held the stone tomb of Benno of Molzbichl (ministerial of the Bishop of Brixen); rebuilt in late-Gothic style in the 15th century, with 1739 Baroque frescoes by Balthasar Klenkh.

building:188321148.label: Forum of Pompeii
building:188321148.description: Pompeii's civic forum, laid out as a pedestrian-only piazza in the 2nd century BC and flanked by the Capitolium (Temple of Jupiter), basilica, comitium, macellum, and Eumachia building; sealed and preserved by the AD 79 eruption.

dare-42918.label: Son Bou Basilica
dare-42918.description: A three-aisled 5th-century paleochristian basilica rediscovered in 1951-52 near Son Bou beach, Menorca, with an adjoining rock-cut necropolis; recent Sanisera Institute excavations suggest a later, 7th-8th century construction date.

dare-18657.label: Villa gallo-romaine de Barat de Vin
dare-18657.description: Gallo-Roman villa or roadside inn on the Bordeaux–Astorga road near Sorde-l'Abbaye; its baths were built in the 3rd century and remodeled in the 4th, with mosaic pavements from the later 4th century; listed a monument historique in 1997.

dare-22923.label: S. Passera
dare-22923.description: A church on the Tiber opposite the Basilica of St Paul Outside the Walls, traditionally marking where relics of the Alexandrian saints Cyrus and John landed c. AD 400; the present building (9th century) incorporates an earlier Roman tomb, and its name is a corruption of "Abbas Cyrus."

dare-37324.label: S. Cornelia, Mon.
dare-37324.description: A rural monastic estate (the domusculta of Capracorum) 15km north of Rome between Veii and Formello, founded c.780 by Pope Hadrian I; rediscovered in the 1958 South Etruria Survey and excavated by Charles Daniels in 1962-64.

building:437043462.label: Chiesa di San Paolo di Peltuinum
building:437043462.description: A church built perhaps in the 7th-8th century on the ruins of the Roman town of Peltuinum on the Via Claudia Nova, reusing two Roman columns with capitals and limestone blocks from the site; badly damaged in the 2009 L'Aquila earthquake.

building:66838501.label: Forum of Col. Augusta Raurica
building:66838501.description: Main forum of the Roman colony Augusta Raurica near Basel, founded c. 44 BC by Lucius Munatius Plancus; housed the temple of Jupiter, a basilica, and the town council's assembly chamber.

building:688857980.label: Roman forum at Thessalonica
building:688857980.description: Two-terraced Roman forum of Thessalonica with two-storey stoas and baths; its well-preserved Odeon hosted both musical performances and gladiatorial/beast fights, and the complex was uncovered accidentally in the 1960s during construction work.

vici:vici-10280.label: Lutetia, Forum Romanum
vici:vici-10280.description: Lutetia's forum, roughly 178 x 89 m and combining a basilica and temple linked by porticoed galleries, was uncovered in 1867–68 during the cutting of Rue Monge; a Vespasianic coin dates construction to c. AD 69–79.

vici:vici-10380.label: Nida Forum
